26 Fed might be saying goodbye to another agent.

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

Warning! Spoilers ahead for Season 9, Episode 5 of FBI, “Atonement,” streaming now with a Paramount+ subscription.

FBI may be in its ninth season on the 2026 TV schedule, but the series continues to keep fans on the edge of their seats. Following OA’s undercover storyline, one would think that things are back to normal at 26 Fed. Unfortunately, there may be another shakeup coming. After the end of this week’s episode, I’m worried that another major exit is near.

Throughout the Dick Wolf CBS procedural’s run, there have been a handful of exits. In the last couple of years, FBI has seen three big departures. It seemed like the curse could be done after Juliana Aidén Martinez’s addition at the beginning of Season 8, but alas, another could be coming.

In this week’s episode, “Atonement,” Scola (John Boyd) told the team that Nina (Shantel VanSanten) was offered to run her own task force. It was great news, but Scola didn’t seem too sure about it. He later tells Eva (Aidén Martinez) that the job is in San Diego. While at first he told Nina not to take it, he eventually calls her to say that she should after his conversation with Eva.

Scola was scared about uprooting their life and moving across the country, which is why he told Nina not to take it in the first place. His hesitation is understandable. He’s lived in New York his entire life, their son, Dougie, is getting older, and he has his job. That being said, Nina’s worked hard to get to where she is, and it’s a great promotion for her, which is why Scola came to his senses and told her she should take it. They’ll figure it out.

Whether Boyd is actually leaving FBI remains unknown. VanSanten is set to return to the series on Monday, November 16, but little has been shared about the episode beyond the fact that the team will work alongside Nina to intercept a criminal on the Most Wanted list. Scola and Nina have gone through a lot over the last several seasons, between breakups, makeups, near-deaths, and welcoming their son. While I would absolutely hate to say goodbye to Scola, it would only make sense for him to follow Nina to San Diego so they can stay together and raise their son in the same proximity and not 2,800 miles apart.

Nothing is confirmed, and it’s not even clear if Nina will end up taking the job. It’s likely we’ll get more information during VanSanten’s return on November 16, but fans may have to brace themselves. Boyd has been on FBI since Season 2. It’s hard to imagine the show without him, but at this point, unfortunately, anything is possible. For now, we’ll just have to wait and see. New episodes of FBI air on Mondays at 8 p.m. ET on CBS, streaming the next day on Paramount+.

#3638. The Ocarina Of Time Remake Has Claimed 2026’s Review Crown, But GTA 6 Could Have Something To Say About It

Reviews are in for The Legend of Zelda: Ocarina of Time remake, and they're pretty good so far. On GameSpot's sister site Metacritic, Ocarina of Time has a review aggregate score of 96 from 81 reviews, making it the highest-reviewed game of the year so far--and with only a few months to go, it might stay in the top spot.

A few more reviews will likely filter in over the next few days from other sites Metacritic tracks, but don't expect the needle to shift much in either direction, or at all. According to Metacritic, twin-stick shooter Sektori is second for best-reviewed game of the year (93 based on 10 reviews), followed by the Switch 2 Deluxe Edition of the Resident Evil 2 remake (also 93, based on 16 reviews).

But could Grand Theft Auto 6 dethrone Link from the number one spot? Historically, mainline entries of GTA games have reviewed very well, and looking back at previous entries, they've all earned review aggregate scores that are often on par or even higher than Legend of Zelda games. Here's a quick breakdown of how GTA has done over the years:

  • Grand Theft Auto -- No metascore
  • Grand Theft Auto 2 -- 70
  • Grand Theft Auto 3 -- 97
  • Grand Theft Auto: San Andreas -- 95
  • Grand Theft Auto 4 -- 98
  • Grand Theft Auto 5 -- 97

The pattern here is that the games developed from GTA 3 onwards earned the highest metascores, and if the tradition holds, then GTA 6 should also be in the 90s when reviews land and the scores are tallied up. That's depending on if the game is actually good, but considering Rockstar's track record, GTA 6 should be a polished experience, even if the new immersive gameplay mechanics create some sense of friction for players who are used to going on crime sprees in GTA games while not worrying too much about the consequences of their in-game actions.

For now, the Ocarina of Time remake will likely remain the best-reviewed game of 2026, a feat that Nintendo and Rockstar have achieved multiple times. The Switch 2 edition of The Legend of Zelda: Tears of the Kingdom was the best-reviewed game of 2025, and 2017's Breath of the Wild also took the top spot. Rockstar's Red Dead Redemption 2 was 2018's best-reviewed game, as was GTA 4 in 2008 and GTA 5 in 2013. Who will emerge victorious this year? You'll have to wait until November 19 to find out when GTA 6 launches.

#3637. Marshals Season 2 Teases Yellowstone Fans With A Major Character Name-Drop

"Marshals" continues to tease a crossover with "Dutton Ranch," with Luke Grimes' Kayce Dutton name-dropping his sister in the latest episode. By this point, however, fans are surely tired of the references and eager to see the "Yellowstone" cast reunited.

With its Season 1 finale, "Dutton Ranch" gave itself the perfect excuse for a "Marshals" crossover. Meanwhile, "Marshals" did the same, ending its debut season by having Brecken Merrill's Tate Dutton kidnapped and taken to Texas, where, it just so happens, Kelly Reilly's Beth Dutton and Cole Hauser's Rip Wheeler now live. Meanwhile, Hauser and Reilly spoke positively about a "Dutton Ranch"/"Marshals" crossover, suggesting that's exactly what fans would soon be getting — especially considering Reilly referred to the lack of such a thing as a missed opportunity.

Alas, when "Marshals" Season 2 arrived, not only was there no crossover, but Kayce didn't even have to go to Texas, as it turns out Tate was taken to a Wyoming ranch instead. Now, we have the latest example of "Marshals" referencing Beth, which more than anything else serves only to remind us that we're yet to receive the crossover we've been waiting for.

"Marshals" Season 2, Episode 5, "Secret Weapon" picks up in the aftermath of Rudy Carpenter (Braxton Hale) exploding a bomb and taking himself out in the process. After the Marshals track down his accomplice, Derek McCoy, Kayce chases Derek's brother, Will McCoy (Keean Johnson), into a barn that collapses, trapping the pair below ground. It's here that Kayce decides to bring up his family and once again tease audiences with a crossover that is yet to materialize.

In "Secret Weapon," after the barn floor collapses, Will McCoy's leg is badly injured. While trying to find a way out of their predicament, Kayce tries to convince Will to give up details about his brother, who evidently treats Will like a "punching bag." Kayce takes the opportunity to talk about his own brother, Jamie Dutton (played by Wes Bentley on "Yellowstone), and his sister, Beth Dutton, who also treated Jamie like a punching bag. Of course, Beth ultimately kills Jamie Dutton in the final season of "Yellowstone," but Kayce stops short of mentioning that still buried crime.

"You remind me of my middle brother," he tells Will. "Never quite fit in, always on the bad end of a beatdown. My sister made his life hell." Will replies with antagonism. "Picked on by his sister? I'm not that pathetic." But as Kayce quite rightfully points out, "She'd eat you for lunch," adding, "Meaner than any of your brothers, guaranteed."

It's true that Beth Dutton is a force of nature, and that only makes it even more frustrating that she hasn't shown up in "Marshals," which could do with a jolt of energy at this point. Beth and Rip are too busy setting up shop in Rio Paloma, Texas, in the far superior "Dutton Ranch." But this brief mention of Kayce's sister and how she'd eat Will for lunch is a reminder of just how good we once had it with "Yellowstone," and how much "Marshals" is struggling to match the excitement of its predecessor. Of course, "Yellowstone" lost its way at one point, but Beth was never anything less than electrifying, and "Marshals" would benefit from having anyone in its cast with half as much charisma.

For now, these brief references in "Marshals" to beloved "Yellowstone" characters aren't doing the CBS procedural any favors. In "Secret Weapon," Kayce Dutton recalls how fighting wasn't in Jamie Dutton's nature. "He had to be smarter, more cunning," he says, "And eventually he broke from the family, forged his own path." Of course, that path ultimately ended in his death, with Beth taking a knife to the middle Dutton brother's stomach and exacting revenge for the controversial death of Kevin Costner's John Dutton earlier in "Yellowstone" Season 5.

The thing is, being reminded of the "Yellowstone" years is bad enough on a show that clearly struggles to match the quality of Taylor Sheridan's original neo-Western. But when you take into account the anticipation for a "Dutton Ranch"/"Marshals" crossover, it's just downright frustrating.

The "Marshals" Season 1 finale seemed to set up a perfect crossover with "Dutton Ranch," but in the end we got nothing of the sort. We could still see Beth show up later in the season, but for now all we know is that another "Yellowstone" fan-favorite character will be appearing in "Marshals" when Jefferson White's Jimmy Hurdstrom makes his return to the Montana plains. In the meantime, let's hope the show finds a way to keep the "Yellowstone" connection alive without reminding us of what we're missing out on.

#3636. Hasan Piker’s Lawyer Says Suing Scott Jennings is Just the Beginning

The clash between left-wing political commentator Hasan Piker and his media detractors is moving from the chatroom to the courtroom. One week after Piker filed a $72.5 million defamation suit against conservative commentator and CNN personality Scott Jennings, his attorney, defamation lawyer Daniel Watkins, tells Vanity Fair Piker is “just getting started.”

“There are other people and other entities that will likely receive outreach from my law firm in the coming days,” says Watkins. “They know they have a reckoning coming.”

The Jennings lawsuit, which accuses the former Republican strategist of falsely telling listeners of his Salem Media podcast that Piker advocated for lynchings, comes at the end of a busy, and tumultuous election cycle for Piker, who—after years of online politicking—became a popular surrogate for far-left insurgents, and a popular boogeyman for virtually everyone else. It’s an apparent payback for the mainstream media, whose obsession with villainizing Piker has meant guilt-by-association for everyone Piker champions (and has far outpaced Piker’s actual name-recognition and influence).

On the podcast, which aired on August 11, Jennings shared a spliced montage of the Twitch streamer appearing to make racist and incendiary remarks, some of them about lynching. It’s packaged as an attempt to dissuade Michigan voters from voting for Senatorial candidate Abdul El-Sayed, Piker’s “best pal and campaign partner,” Jennings said.

I watched the October 2024 stream from which the most inflammatory snippets in Jennings’s sizzle reel were spliced together. On the stream, Piker is live-reacting to a YouTube video from the popular channel Jubilee, in which a Black conservative debates a Black liberal.

At one point, an incredulous Piker pauses the video and very clearly mocks the Black conservative by saying, “Can we go back to a better time when lynchings were happening?” At another point, after a commenter asks why he’s “always doing too much with black people” Piker responds sarcastically, “Yes dude, it’s because I’m racist, that’s why. It’s because I’m fucking racist dude.” Both of these clips are included in the Jennings segment without context.

At the end of August Watkins sent a retraction demand and spoke to Christopher Henderson, Salem Media’s chief legal officer. Absent a reply, they proceeded with a lawsuit. (At the time of publication Henderson and Jennings have not responded to a request for comment.)

Piker’s suit against Jennings is seeking $27.5 million in compensatory damages, and $45 million in punitive damages. Piker says he left it to the lawyers to crunch the numbers. “I don't know what I'm worth, if we're being real,” Piker told Vanity Fair in an interview this week.

“I have been very deliberately anti-litigation for a very long time,” Piker said, “but something shifted that’s been bubbling up where…people like Scott Jennings, and there are others as well,” he claims, “started trafficking in outright lies, defamation, and slander.”

“It is particularly pernicious to misattribute a quote to someone,” Watkins said. He explained that for Piker, “who has built a career at a platform based on advocating for marginalized people and taking stances that are not necessarily popular,” such misattributions are “disgusting and vile and dangerous.”

For Piker, the turn to legal action is partly a pro-truth crusade against “pundits who’ve gotten far too comfortable thinking that they can just get away with making ridiculous claims about people.” He pointed out what he claims is a pattern where outlets circulate clips that omit key words, fundamentally transforming the sentiments of their subjects. “I’ve observed this with the likes of James Talarico, for example. He’ll say something and then they’ll cut it right before you can associate with the full context of the statement,” Piker said.

He also admitted that it’s personal. “First and foremost, [the lawsuit is] for me.” He cited what he alleges is “reputational harm,” “emotional harm,” and “financial damages,” sharing that the lynching comment had spurred someone to “stalk a public event [he] was at.”

“When is the last time you experienced eight consistent months of [mainstream media] having one primary villain?” Piker asked. “It’s not fun at all. It sucks.”

Discussing the Michigan race where the controversy with Jennings began, Piker noted El-Sayed’s primary opponent Haley Stevens’s surprising Sunday endorsement of Republican nominee Mike Rogers. Explaining her party defection, Stevens made specific reference to Piker, criticizing El-Sayed for associating with him.

Piker believes Stevens’s statements will backfire in El-Sayed’s favor as the votes are tallied in Michigan.

“Okay, a Twitch streamer is the reason why you’re endorsing ICE raids in every city?” Piker said, referencing Rogers’s platform. “That’s ridiculous.”

Piker maintains, as he has since July, that his political interventions do more good than harm—for everyone except him. In the case of his surrogacy for El-Sayed, he said, “The only person who got attacked in the process was me. I was the one who had his reputation destroyed in the process.”

As for Piker’s own relationship with El-Sayed, he admits it’s not quite as buddy-buddy as Jennings suggested. Piker stumped for the Michigander in the primaries before receding somewhat. “My relationship with him has always been one of…a transactional nature,” he said.

Piker will spend election night streaming live from his home in LA and checking in periodically with candidates. When the midterms are over, he seems prepared to continue delivering comeuppance to those he feels have unfairly represented him during this election cycle.

So who else can expect to get hit with a lawsuit?

Piker didn’t say, exactly, but he did note that Ronna McDaniel, the former chair of the RNC, who, on C-Span last week, repeated the claim that Piker supports reinstating lynchings. He also pointed to Sen. Ted Cruz, who re-shared the clip from Jennings on X. Last week, Piker responded to the X post with a link to the news of his lawsuit against Jennings and wrote, “hey ted you seen this ?” (Cruz and McDaniel did not respond to a request for comment.)

When asked if Piker’s post on X was a clue as to a future lawsuit against Cruz, Watkins answered: “Buckle up.”

Piker did not disclose other specifics regarding future litigation, saying only this: “if you felt as though you could outright fabricate quotes and make up totally ridiculous claims about me, you should probably work on your retractions immediately.”

Mckenna Grace has been working since she was a little kid, and at 20 years old, it feels like she’s done a bit of everything. She’s done drama, action, horror, romance and more, and in her next project, the book-to-screen adaptation of Sunrise on the Reaping, she’ll play out a deeply intense tragedy that also features massive action. However, while it’s clear she’s open to many kinds of projects and work, there is one thing she says no to: nudity. Surprisingly, her reasoning has to do with Disney.

As I said, when it comes to Grace's career, she's explored lots of different genres, which have put her in many different situations. I mean, in the last year alone, she’s worked on Regretting You, Five Nights at Freddy’s 2, Scream 7, PAW Patrol: The Dino Movie, The Last Kiss, Nimrods and Sunrise on the Reaping. Those are all very different movies, and during an interview with Cosmopolitan, she was asked if there are any kinds of roles she’d say no to. Here’s how she responded, and how nudity and Disney came into the conversation:

At this point, I definitely don’t do nudity or very hypersexual things. I respect anybody who can, but it’s terrifying to me. I don’t know if that’ll ever change. It’s not like I only do wholesome things—my character literally gets gutted by Ghostface in Scream—but my dream is to try and be a Disney princess someday.

See, it’s obvious from her explanation that she has nothing against intimacy or nudity. And it seems like she has a lot of respect for actors who do work on projects that require it or very sexual sequences, like Off Campus, for example. However, it’s not her cup of tea, and I do see why.

As she said, she wants to be a Disney princess someday. If you’ve seen the best Disney movies, you know there’s a certain level of wholesomeness involved. That’s not to say an actor who participates in a project that involves sex scenes or nudity wouldn’t get a role as a Disney princess or prince. However, it’s clear Grace is trying to create an image for herself that makes her an unquestionable fit for one of these very wholesome roles.

I think she’s doing a good job at that too. I mean, before Teagan Croft and Milo Manheim were cast as Rapunzel and Flynn Rider for the live-action Tangled, Mckenna Grace and Mason Thames were popular fan casts for the parts. She legitimately looks like a princess, and her bubbly and bright personality fits right in with that kind of character too.

Now, getting back to what she said, she made it clear she’s not only going to do wholesome roles, and her work on the 2026 movie schedule clearly showcases that. I mean, Scream 7 is a horror movie, and as she said, she gets brutally murdered in it. Also, Sunrise on the Reaping is not for the faint of heart. As a fan of the book, I know how brutal the story is, and I know we’ll see Grace acting out some truly violent and intense moments.

However, while she’s willing to do work like that, she does have boundaries she does not want to cross. That means she’ll say no to projects that are hypersexual or involve nudity, which is totally respectable.

With that said, hopefully someday she’ll get her wish of being a Disney princess. While we wait for that to happen (because I do feel like it’s inevitable), you can catch Mckenna Grace in Sunrise on the Reaping on November 20.

#3634. Cillian Murphy's Overlooked 2024 Drama With A 94% Rotten Tomatoes Score Is A Must-Watch

We may receive a commission on purchases made from links.

Many of Cillian Murphy's best characters are either American, like J. Robert Oppenheimer or Jonathan Crane, or British, like Jim from "28 Weeks Later" or the immortal (?) Thomas Shelby from "Peaky Blinders." But as Murphy himself will remind you, he's Irish, and one of his most recent films tackles a dark part of his country's history.

That would be 2024's "Small Things Like These" by "Peaky Blinders" Season 3 director Tim Mielants, adapted from author Claire Keegan's 2021 novella. The movie received strong reviews and more than made its modest $3 million budget back with a $15 million gross in theaters, but it's still under-discussed. Sadly, that makes sense, as it's a quiet character study not really designed for a wide audience.

Murphy (who produced the film) plays Bill Furlong, a coal merchant in the Irish town New Ross during the 1980s. He's a moderately successful man, with his own business plus a wife and five daughters. But he remains troubled by his childhood, having been born out of wedlock and never known his father. If not for the kindness of his mother's employer, the widowed Mrs. Wilson (Michelle Fairley), who sheltered Bill and his mother, Sarah (Agnes O'Casey), like her own family, Bill would've likely been put up for adoption and Sarah sentenced to a Magdalene Laundry. What's that?

Until 1996, the Catholic Church in Ireland operated "Magdalene Asylums" for "fallen women" (unmarried women caught having sex or becoming pregnant, even if through sexual assault). These women were put to work to cleanse their supposed sins and basically enslaved. One of these laundries exists in Bill's own town, where everyone keeps their head down and doesn't peek too closely. But Bill, knowing he only has the life he does because of charity, can't look the other way.

Spoilers for "Small Things Like These" ahead.

In the opening shots of "Small Things Like These," church buildings loom over New Ross as their bells ring out. The Church's power is baked into the town and personified by the convent's Mother Superior (Emily Watson). Watson plays the soft-spoken nun as being so powerful that she doesn't have to be loud. Bill can't even meet her gaze as she makes subtle threats behind her niceties.

Bill's work in coal means that he comes home and cleans his hands every night, i.e. exactly the spiritually symbolic labor that the "fallen women" of the laundries are tasked to do. But a small kindness cleans Bill's hands: He saves an imprisoned girl locked in a shed, wrapping her in a coat and taking her to his home. Bill is particularly suited to break this social norm because of his background. The girl Bill saves, Sarah Redmond (Zara Devlin), literally has the same name as his late mother. As Bill walks with Sarah through New Ross, everyone around them looks on in shock and judgment. Yet, they're all out of focus, as if Bill is finally tuning them out.

"The fact was that he would pay for [taking Sarah], but never once in his whole and unremarkable life had he known happiness akin to this," reads one of the novel's closing lines. Speaking to GQ in 2024, Cillian Murphy even said Bill saving Sarah is "not a classically heroic act."

"Small Things Like These" came about in part due to Murphy's work on "Oppenheimer" and not just via his post-Oscar win clout. During that production, Murphy passed along the script to his co-star Matt Damon, who had recently founded the new studio Artists Equity with Ben Affleck.

"[Artists Equity] really let us make the film we wanted to make, because they're filmmakers themselves and writers, and they really understand it," Cillian Murphy told GQ. Indeed, "Small Things Like These" is extremely faithful to its somber source book and trusts its audience to weather the slow pace with Murphy's quiet but steely performance as an anchor.

Actor Eileen Walsh plays Bill's wife, Eileen Furlong, who advises him: "If you want to get on in this life, there are things you have to ignore." Walsh's casting rings hard because she previously appeared in Peter Mullan's 2002 film "The Magdalene Sisters" as Crispina, a woman imprisoned in one of those laundries. One of the greatest Irish films of the 21st Century, "The Magdalene Sisters" brought new attention to the real-life atrocities of the Magdalene Laundries (and was unsurprisingly condemned by the Catholic Church).

That "national reckoning" continues to this day, Murphy told GQ. "There's government commissions and government reports and academic papers on all of these things that you can get your hands on, but the public doesn't really read them. They will consume books and films, and I think it's a gentler way to confront it," he added. After all, "Small Things Like These" has as realistic a happy ending as one could hope for in this story.

In December 2024, shortly after the movie's theatrical release, the "Small Things Like These" novel was selected by Oprah's Book Club. That publicity is another win for civil education about the real history the novel dramatizes, at least the "gentler way." The book is only about 120 pages, and like the movie, it's easy enough to absorb in a single sitting if you set your stomach right for the cruelty inside.

The long wait for All’s Fair’s second season is finally almost over. The Ryan Murphy legal drama is set to return on Wednesday on the 2026 TV schedule, nearly a year after Season 1 ended. Not surprisingly, the cast is making headlines ahead of the new season, and also not surprisingly, everyone is talking about the corset dress Kim Kardashian wore to the premiere. However, can we please talk about Teyana Taylor’s fit, too?

On Monday, Hulu hosted a premiere for All’s Fair Season 2, and the fashion was absolutely on point. Kardashian, as usual, turned heads as she wore a custom Ashi Studio silver strapless corset dress with a matching silver collar, per Law Roach's Instagram. She posted the look on her Instagram Story, and I am positively obsessed:

That being said, her co-star Teyana Taylor might be giving her a run for her money. The Oscar-nominated actress has also been making waves in the world of celebrity fashion, leaving no crumbs at the BET Awards over the summer by rocking a stunning burgundy Stephanie Rolland gown. Now, once again, she proved that she’s a fashion icon at the All’s Fair premiere with a daring low-rise ensemble:

The look is from Nicholas Oakwell Couture, per Women’s Wear Daily. Between the corset sheer top, the large bow over the black pants, and the bolero jacket, the entire ensemble is incredible. You never know what you’re going to get when it comes to Taylor, and she definitely made that point clear with this look. Of course, Kardashian looked great as well; however, the One Battle After Another actress definitely has my vote for best dressed.

However, I have to say that Kardashian and Taylor’s friendship makes this pair of outfits even better. The Rip actress previously opened up about her friendship with the reality star, pointing out that they were already friends before All's Fair. However, she said that doing this series together “really brought [them] closer.” She continued, “We really went into the show friends and finished out the show as sisters.”

#3632. The Martian Author Andy Weir Explains The One Thing He Would Change About The Story [Exclusive]

Looking back at the success of 2015's "The Martian," it's remarkable to realize just how influential this crowd-pleasing blockbuster really was. It helped launch author Andy Weir to the upper echelon of sci-fi writers, paving the way for even bigger box office hits like 2026's "Project Hail Mary." Alongside Christopher Nolan's "Interstellar" in 2014 and Alfonso Cuarón's "Gravity" the year before, Ridley Scott's adaptation also served as a bellwether for the mid-2010s "space race" in film. And, for those of a certain age, there's something genuinely nostalgic about the tone struck by both the source material and the movie — a last gasp of the sense of optimism and unity that defined the Obama-era U.S.

So, when I had the chance to speak with Weir over a Zoom interview, as he's promoting his newest original project as an executive producer on Audible's "Exoplanet" series (due later this month), I jumped at the chance to revisit the whirlwind experience of "The Martian." Has over a decade of hindsight given Weir a different perspective on his game-changing book, now that he's more established as a novelist? In response, the science-abiding author maintained he wouldn't change anything ... except for the natural disaster that sets the plot in motion in the first place on the surface of Mars:

"If I had it to do over again, there's a few minor changes I'd make. I'd probably make the initial problem not be a windstorm, because that windstorm was not physics-accurate. I'd probably have it be — well, I've since learned that there's lightning strikes on Mars, and that could be something. Lightning strikes something, it causes overload here, that causes an explosion there, and then [the other astronauts have] all got to bail, something like that."

When things just happen to fall into place perfectly, you count your blessings and don't look back. That's more or less the mindset Andy Weir has with "The Martian." Unlike his hands-on role with "Project Hail Mary," Weir notes in our conversation, he was much more of a passenger on this first adaptation of his work. As a result, he simply sat back and let director Ridley Scott and screenwriter Drew Goddard do their thing along with some of the best and most talented actors in the world.

Sure, the part of his brain obsessed with making things as realistic and scientifically-accurate as can be may have some corrections or two. In the book, everything goes haywire when astronaut Mark Watney is separated from his fellow crew during a hellish windstorm and is left behind on the surface of Mars, presumed dead. But while there are dust storms on the surface of Mars, Weir is correct to note that the atmosphere and gravity of the planet couldn't sustain one of this magnitude. "But other than that," he tells me, "I don't think I'd change anything."

He goes on to compare the success of "The Martian" to, well, I'll let Weir's quirky sense of humor speak for itself:

"It's like, have you ever been casually talking to a beautiful woman and then you realize she's interested in you, and you have no idea what you did right, but you don't want to jinx it? That's kind of what happened to me with 'The Martian.' I'm like, 'I don't know what I did right, but I'm sure as hell not going to change anything.' [laughs]"

For those interested in more sci-fi approved by Weir, "Exoplanet" hits Audible on November 5, 2026.

#3631. Annie Andrews Flips South Carolina In Senate Race Against Lindsey Graham's Sister

Few people outside South Carolina knew who Annie Andrews was just six months ago. But in the 2026 midterms, she has made history as the first Democrat to win a statewide Senate election in the deeply red state since 1998, according to CNN.

Andrews was poised to take on longtime senator Lindsey Graham when she won the Democratic primary in June. When Graham died unexpectedly in July, it threw “us for a loop,” Andrews told Vanity Fair's Aidan McLaughlin. Andrews pivoted to campaign against Darline Graham, the late senator's sister, who was appointed by Governor Henry McMaster to fill his seat through January 2027.

With the blessing of President Donald Trump, Darline Graham opted to run for a full term, facing off against Andrews three weeks ago in a tense debate, during which the Democrat physician faced off against the political neophyte. “Why would we hand Darline Graham a full term in the US Senate? She is unserious and unqualified,” Andrews—who previously ran against Republican Nancy Mace in the 2022 race for South Carolina’s First Congressional District—said.

“In order for a Democrat to win in South Carolina, you need three things,” Charleston political operative Tyler Jones told Vanity Fair in July. “You need a popular Democrat, you need an unpopular Republican, and you need a favorable national environment." With Trump's support eroding across the US, Andrews has at least one of those—and if the most recent polling numbers are accurate, Andrews' popularity has just continued to grow.

Now, she must make good on her promise to “go to Washington and solve problems.” If Lindsey Graham had remained “a John McCain–style center-right Republican,” Andrews told McLaughlin, “I probably wouldn’t have gotten in this race.”

Grey's Anatomy is one of the most legendary medical dramas of all time, and we're currently in its whopping 23rd season on ABC (and streaming with a Hulu subscription). The beloved medical drama is till going strong, but many fans like to look back at its glory days. Late actor Eric Dane famously played Mark Sloane/ McSteamy during that time, and excerpts from his posthumous memoir got honest about his struggles during that time.

McSteamy is one of the most beloved Grey's character of all time, in no small part thanks to the charisma and heart that Dane brought to the role. In his recently released memoir My Book of Days (via EW) he wrote about an injury and reliance on painkillers resulted in him deteriorating during his time at Seattle Grace Hospital. He wrote:

My body goes to shit. I drop to 170, my face caves in, my eyes cloud, I look gaunt; shit, I look like a drug addict. You can tell. I can tell. My attitude on set changes. I’m no longer bubbly, the fun guy, a ringleader in laughs. I don’t act out. I don’t throw tantrums or chairs. I go the other way. I bring everything inside. I dissolve.

What a heartbreaking recollection. While Grey's fans were still head over heels in love with Sloan, Dane was having a private struggle with his health and substances that was making his job difficult. Rather than acting out he felt himself "dissolving", and not letting it impact this coworkers. Indeed, Grey's Anatomy stars wrote tributes to the late actor following his tragic death in February.

Later in his memoir, the Euphoria star does mention that his coworkers noticed the change in him. He wrote about the dynamic he felt at the time, in a section which reads:

I can’t help it. I feel other members of the cast looking at me. They’re my friends. My work family. No. My family. They don’t judge me. They don’t look angry. They look concerned. They look sad.

It's tough to hear how Eric Dane was struggling during this time, and how he was being so private about it while bringing McSteamy to life. He didn't want to bother his co-workers and chosen family, but they noticed that something was going on. That includes the one and only Shonda Rhimes, who did offer to help the Last Ship actor. As he wrote:

I tell her I’m dealing with it. I lie to her. I lie to myself. I suck it up. Fight through it. I don’t want to be Shonda’s burden. I don’t want to be a problem. But I am. I am a problem.

Clearly Eric Dane took the time to reflect on his years on Grey's Anatomy, and the struggles he was dealing with at the time. In his book he was able to speak honestly about his issues, and take responsibility for being a "problem." It's a powerful testament, one that might help inspire readers who are dealing with similar issues.

New episodes of Grey's Anatomy air Thursdays on ABC as part of the 2026 TV schedule. Folks who want to re-watch Dane's iconic tenure as McSteamy can do so on both Hulu and Netflix. Although after hearing about his experience, it might hit differently.

#3629. 50 Years Ago Today: John Carpenter Directed A Gritty Action Thriller That Became A Cult Classic

We may receive a commission on purchases made from links.

Retired filmmaker John Carpenter is best known for his horror films. After all, we don't have the modern slasher film without "Halloween." But before Michael Myers returned to Haddonfield on Halloween night 1978, Carpenter tried his hand at an action-exploitation film: 1976's "Assault on Precinct 13," which opened in theaters 50 years ago today.

Carpenter was born in 1948, the perfect age to grow up on cowboy movies. He dreamed of going to Hollywood to make Westerns, not horror films. But, by the time he enrolled in University of South California film school in 1968, Westerns had already faded as Hollywood's biggest genre. Throughout his decades-long filmmaking career, Carpenter never directed a Western — but you can see that longing in "Assault on Precinct 13." The movie has a courageous lawman who has to hold his ground against the black hat gangs. The catch? The movie is set in contemporary Los Angeles, not the Wild West.

Lieutenant Ethan Bishop (Austin Stoker) is overseeing the closure of the LAPD's Precinct 13. A prison bus, carrying convicted murderer Napoleon Wilson (Darwin Joston), also stops at the precinct for a respite. Before long, the building is under siege by bloodthirsty gang members. Bishop, Wilson, and surviving secretary Leigh (Laurie Zimmer) are in a literal fight for their lives as unlikely allies.

Made on a meager budget of $100,000, "Assault on Precinct 13" wasn't an instant mega-hit. Reviews weren't too enthusiastic either. Whitney Williams of Variety was ambivalent, writing backhanded praise like, "some exciting action in second half packs enough interest to keep this entry alive for the violence market." Ellen Edwards of The Miami Herald condemned the film for its "hideous, unmotivated violence." But "Assault on Precinct 13" found its audience. It even got a remake in 2005, starring Laurence Fishburne and Ethan Hawke.

One of John Carpenter's acknowledged influences for "Assault on Precinct 13" is one of the most beloved Westerns ever: Howard Hawks' "Rio Bravo," about a sheriff (John Wayne) and his deputies trying to keep a murderer with a rich brother and many hired guns locked up. But "Rio Bravo" is not a tense thriller; often called a hangout movie, it's leisurely paced with only bursts of gun violence.

In "Assault on Precinct 13," the threat is everywhere. There's not even a reason for the siege beyond violence for its own sake; there's nothing of value inside the precinct besides more lives to end. That leads into one of the other movies that inspired Carpenter: George Romero's 1968 "Night of the Living Dead," the first modern zombie movie. When asked if "Night of the Living Dead" inspired "Assault on Precinct 13," Carpenter said, half-seriously, "Everybody who made a low-budget film was inspired by ['Night of the Living Dead']."

The comparison rings even more true here. Both movies are about people trapped inside a small building, surrounded by a horde outside that wants to break in and kill them. Both films also cast a Black man as their hero: Stoker as Lt. Bishop in "Precinct 13" and Duane Jones as Ben in "Night of the Living Dead." That was a bigger deal in the 1960s and '70s than it is now, and one spot where Carpenter's exploitation movie is rather progressive. "Living Dead" ends on a famously cynical note, with Ben shot by white men who mistook him as a threat. In "Precinct 13," Bishop and Napoleon Wilson achieve mutual respect; at the end of the movie, they walk out of the basement together as equals.

After its U.S. theatrical release in 1976, "Assault on Precinct 13" played along the European festival circuit, including the Cannes Film Festival and the London Film Festival. (At the latter, it received "deafening applause" per a contemporary review by The Guardian's Derek Malcolm.) Seeing the movie at Cannes, George Romero paid forward the compliment of Carpenter modeling his movie after "Night of the Living Dead."

The most shocking scene in "Assault on Precinct 13" is when a little girl, Kathy (future reality TV star Kim Richards), is shot in the chest after buying an ice cream cone. It's a jaw-dropping scene, and the movie is clearly having perverse fun turning such a taboo of violence against children into a spectacle and sick joke.

Quoted in Jason Zinoman's "Shock Value: How a Few Eccentric Outsiders Gave Us Nightmares, Conquered Hollywood, and Invented Modern Horror," Romero testified to this scene's impact: "John Carpenter at Cannes wiped us off the face of the earth with 'Precinct 13.' Right from the scene when the little girl gets blown away, I was blown away." (The same book reports that, to get an R instead of an X rating, Carpenter cut the girl's death from the rating review board then added it back in before the film went to theaters.)

This sort of gang violence is echoed in Carpenter's later "Escape From New York," which is all about a future where the gangs like those in "Precinct 13" have taken over the Big Apple. Like "Escape from New York" and many of his other movies, Carpenter also composed the score for "Precinct 13." The title sequence theme, a synthesized anthem of droning dread, is still the most perfect mood setter for an action thriller even 50 years later.

Since Patrick Stewart's death became public knowledge nearly a week ago, many across social media have been taking the time to honor the late actor. Also, a number celebrities have been honoring Stewart, including more than a few of his Star Trek cohorts. On that note, John de Lancie is now adding his voice to the many who've been sharing their memories of the Jean-Luc Picard portrayer. The beloved Q actor paid a fitting tribute to his former co-star and dropped the perfect reference tied to Picard and Q's past tussles.

While he wasn't a main character, John de Lancie's Q became one of Star Trek: The Next Generation's most memorable foes. After many adventures over the years, including Picard, De Lancie posted the following message about Stewart on Facebook:

For forty years, Q has been a thorn in Jean-Luc Picard’s side. And what a pleasure it has been to be that thorn. Patrick Stewart was a wonderful actor. He brought intelligence and depth to every role he played. It was a privilege to have worked with him. The universe is a little smaller and a little less bright today with his passing. Goodbye, Patrick. You touched so many. See you out there, Mon Capitaine.

That "mon Capitaine" brought a tear to my eye when I read it, and reminded me of some of my favorite TNG episodes. While Q and Picard's relationship ran hot and cold, I could always sense that it was always love coming from the former's end. Of course, he was certainly a jerk, putting Picard through some wtf-worthy scenarios, but I always appreciated that there was some mutual love between them at the end of Picard's second season.

I'm A Star Trek Fan, But I'd Never Heard This Cool Story About Patrick Stewart Showing Up On Jeremy Clarkson's Set

For those who haven't streamed Picard Season 2 with a Paramount+ subscription, the storyline ends with Picard's realization that Q has constructed the entire scenario he's put them through in order to help him overcome past trauma. Q then reveals to Picard that he is dying, and the two share a hug before Q sets the timeline right again.

It was emotional for me, even if it was potentially retconned when Picard Season 3 had Q return in a post-credits scene. Fans have, however, theorized that everything from the Q species exists outside of time. Therefore, his death doesn't have to be linear.

Personally, I think Q is not above faking his own death just for the thrill of pulling one over on Picard. The fact of the matter is, we'll likely never know now that Patrick Stewart is gone, though I'm sure he won't be the last to play Picard. Star Trek hasn't been afraid to recast iconic characters, though I think it'll be a challenge for someone to follow in Stewart's footsteps and play the role.

Patrick Stewart's death comes amid the celebration of Star Trek's 60th anniversary, which has been rife with bad news. As far as the franchise itself goes, there is a movie in development, but no TV shows are actively in the works as far as the general public knows. Stewart's passing certainly feels like a gut punch to the fandom and the former actors, many of whom held out hope for positive news before the year's end.

Tributes continue to pour in for Patrick Stewart, and I'm continuing to love every eulogy and story that is shared. Both Star Trek: The Next Generation and Picard are available to stream on Paramount+, so anyone who is missing the great Captain should head over there and watch some classic episodes.

#3625. Marshals Season 2 Episode 5 Exposes A Major Problem With The Yellowstone Spin-Off

"Marshals" Season 2 Episode 4 ended on a deadly cliffhanger that left the fate of Luke Grimes' Kayce Dutton and Ash Santos' Andrea Cruz unclear. Caught in an explosion, the pair were flung through the air just before the episode cut to black. What would become of Kayce and the character with whom he's clearly developing deep feelings? Well, nothing. The latest "Marshals" installment quickly establishes that they were both fine in what is the latest example of one of the show's most frustrating problems.

It's no secret that Grimes' procedural has struggled to live up to "Yellowstone" and its fellow spin-off "Dutton Ranch." There are many reasons why. For one, "Marshals" Season 1 had no idea what it was about, with the show jumping from premise to premise in an attempt to find its footing and ultimately never succeeding. But there are several other issues with this show, and one of them is its proclivity for building things up only to disappoint viewers in the most unnecessary ways.

Consider the Season 2 premiere. "Marshals" Season 1 ended by having Brecken Merrill's Tate Dutton taken captive by investor turned rancher Tom Weaver (Chris Mulkey). Tate was supposedly being shuttled to Texas, where it seemed we might get the first official crossover between "Dutton Ranch" and "Marshals." But in the Season 2 premiere we learned that Tate was having a grand old time fishing on a Wyoming ranch. By the end of the episode, Tom Weaver had been apprehended and Tate was back to barely featuring in the series. Now, we've had yet another cliffhanger undermined and it's starting to get ridiculous.

"Marshals" Season 1 seemed to introduce a love triangle between Kayce Dutton, Andrea Cruz, and Dolly Weaver (Ellyn Jameson). Now that Dolly's out of the picture, however (she died in that disappointing "Marshals" Season 2 premiere), Andrea and Kayce are free to embrace their attraction.

Season 2, Episode 4, "Blast Radius," saw the pair growing closer than ever. Turns out this duo have been executing warrants as an extra-curricular activity to distract them from their sleepless nights. But it's clear there's also a slow-burn romance developing between the two. As such, when they were seemingly blown sky high in the episode's closing moments it looked as though the writers were about to leverage this burgeoning love affair for some dramatic tension. There was no way Kayce was going to die, but perhaps his new love interest's life would be left hanging in the balance?

Nope, they're both fine. Season 2, Episode 5, "Secret Weapon" opens in the immediate aftermath of Rudy Carpenter (Braxton Hale) exploding his bomb in range of Kayce and Andrea. We see the former lying unconscious on the floor, before he wakes up and crawls over to Andrea, who's also coming to. Meanwhile, their fellow Marshals do a sweep of the barn, determine Rudy's gone for good, and after that everything's back to normal. It's a frustrating opening as it calls to mind all the previous "Marshals" cliffhanger moments that have similarly come to nothing.

"Marshals" is a CBS procedural in the vein of "SEAL Team" — the show from which its showrunner Spencer Hudnut hails. As such, we know there's a case-of-the-week format, and we know that a network show isn't necessarily beholden to the production values of, say, an HBO drama. But is there any rule that states the show has to be made with the dimmest possible audience members in mind?

"Marshals" keeps reiterating the plot of each episode in the simplest terms possible, with the latest example coming in "Secret Weapon." After the team finds tire tracks near the barn where Rudy Carpenter died, it becomes clear that someone other than Carpenter is transporting missing bombs elsewhere. Pete Calvin (Logan Marshall-Green) then announces, "Someone's driving this bomb around right now and we got no idea what the target is." Is this like the Netflix thing where they assume people are on their phones and aren't paying close enough attention?

These frequent consequence-free cliffhangers are another aspect of "Marshals" that gives the sense of a show doing an impression of a better show. It's like the writers know cliffhangers can be compelling, but don't want to cause any actual distress to an audience they evidently assume is made up of phone-addicted simpletons barely following the plot. So, we get these half-baked moments of tension, after which nothing changes. Remember when "Marshals" Season 1 introduced a powerful Dutton family rival who'd apparently been at odds with Kayce's family for generations, only for that same rival to be arrested several episodes later, never to be heard from again? It's the same thing. A threat arises, then it's neutralized. I get that "Marshals" isn't "Yellowstone." But does that mean it has to be bad?

Hallmark has produced a slew of popular TV shows over the years including When Calls The Heart to Chesapeake Shores, The Good Witch and The Way Home. Over the past couple of years, the network added a little more greenery to the Christmas schedule with Mistletoe Murders, a holiday series with a little bit of whodunnit flair.The show is back for another round amidst Hallmark's (extremely) popular holiday programming this year, with more intrigue, murder, fun fashion and guest stars than ever before.

A few months ago, I was able to visit the set of Mistletoe Murders in the hot, hot heat of the Toronto summer –yes, filming holiday content in the summer is not for the faint of heart. Ahead of the Season 3 premiere hitting the Hallmark schedule on Thursday, November 5th, I learned a lot about series leads Sarah Drew and Peter Mooney, as well as the big guest stars heading to our TVs this season. Without further ado, let’s talk about the mystery and mayhem coming down the pipeline.

There are a slew of famous names coming to Mistletoe Murders this season, but chief among them is Hallmark regular Holly Robinson Peete. She joins the series as a psychiatrist named Dr. Russo who is helping out a patient in Fletcher's Grove. Peete told CinemaBlend this is her second time playing a psychiatrist after having done so in a sitcom called For Your Love years ago. She’s also no stranger to a good murder mystery, having starred in the popular Morning Show Mysteries series for Hallmark prior.

Her character this time around will be yet another character making Emily “uncomfortable” after the show picks up 11 months after the drama's explosive Season 2 finale. We know very little about Robinson or her character's motivations so far, but she told CinemaBlend fans should prep for some "good drama."

She’s very smart and extremely inquisitive and intuitive. She has a sense about people where she can find out something about yourself that you don’t even know. So that’s like a superpower for her. She’s warm and friendly, but she’s also very sharp and she can see through lies and manipulation very very quickly. The cool thing about the character is that, even though she’s dealing with some of her patients of whom she’s very protective, with Emily she recognizes things that even Emily doesn’t yet. And I think that makes Emily uncomfortable. Which makes for good drama.

When we pick up in Season 3, time has passed in Fletcher’s Grove and some things have changed, including the addition of Peete’s character. There’s no word on whether or not this series is getting renewed for Season 4 yet, but Ms. Peete told CinemaBlend she was watching the show before getting cast, and she’d be game to do more should it continue.

I was a fan of the show, and so when they came to me and said, ‘Hey we’d like you to come on a couple of episodes.’ And then hopefully if we get a Season 4 I’ll be back. We’ll see.

It’s not just Holly Robinson Peete making a splash this season, either.

Alongside Peete, the show has landed more notable guest stars, some of whom had prior Hallmark connections. Showrunner Ken Cuperus told me they were lucky enough to land an absolute Canadian icon for a murder mystery involving Santa’s workshop. They hit up veteran actor Patrick McKenna to join the Season 3 cast, and series lead Peter Mooney was pretty over the moon about it, telling me about the Santa-adjacent episode the team was filming when I was able to head to the set.

It’s really, really nice. Patrick McKenna’s in this episode, he’s Santa. He really is Santa. It’s alarming to see him. I knew him growing up from the The Red Green Show, which is an iconic piece of Canadian television. I loved him growing up.

I always love it when Hallmark holiday content dives into a good Santa theme, and this should be no exception, but I'm also pumped longtime Hallmark fans will get a reunion. Yes, Good Witch's Catherine Bell will be guest starring opposite Kylee Evans, who is already a regular on the show. That's not the end to the Good Witch connections, either. Mooney is actually married to Sarah Power, who was a mainstay on Good Witch during its run!

These connections across Hallmark run deep, and Mooney told me how cool it's been to be a part of that.

You know, the longer I’m in this Hallmark community, the more I realize it’s actually a pretty right community. You get to like overlap with people. Catherine Bell is amazing. My wife is Sarah Power and she was on a series with Catherine Bell for 7+ years. Our daughter was born during that series, so I’d be on set with a little baby Bjorn trying to get out of the way.

If you've wondered why you see so many familiar faces, Hallmark does employ a lot of Canadian stars, and works with a lot of the same people over and over again. It sounds like it works out great for everyone involved.

I’ve been enamored with Emily’s casual but well-tailored Mistletoe wardrobe since Season 1. I was surprised to find out a lot of her looks are high end but thrifted, and the wardrobe team also has to factor in some wild non-clothing items. Think: Ice packs in coats and more. The team is thrifty and crafty, and if you talk to series lead Sarah Drew, they keep her very happy.

On set, I learned that in Season 3 Emily isn’t going to get a statement dress this year given the context of the mysteries she is solving and the storylines this season (boo), but Sarah Drew did tell me Hallmark has yielded her enough coats to last many lifetimes (yay).

I have so many Christmas coats and jeans. I’m set for life. Too many clothes. Turns out, when I go home, I don’t actually want to dress like Emily. Like she looks really cute because she has [wardrobe] tucking her shirt in before every take. When I’m living my life, it’s like a t-shirt that hits the top of the jeans, so no tucking required.

The best news for the actress? The team is always great about sourcing her favorite brand of jeans (also yay).

I pretty much only wear Mother. I’ve gotten now, so, picky about it. Every time I do a new project they’re like, ‘What kind of jeans?’ I’m like, I only wear Mother. They fit me really well, and often they’ll let me take them home so I have many Mother jeans.

As I mentioned before, the fashion is paramount for keeping things cool, particularly when Mistletoe Murders must film in the summer, as happened this year. They'll be more on that and other stories from the set to come, so stay tuned to CinemaBlend, and be sure to check out Season 3 when it hits the fall 2026 TV schedule on November 5th at 8 p.m. ET, with episodes streaming the next day for those with a Hallmark+ subscription.

She oversees news content, hiring and training for the site, and her areas of expertise include theme parks, rom-coms, Hallmark (particularly Christmas movie season), reality TV, celebrity interviews and primetime. She loves a good animated movie. Jessica has a Masters in Library Science degree from Indiana University, and used to be found behind a reference desk most definitely not shushing people. She now uses those skills in researching and tracking down information in very different ways.

#3623. In Ohio, Amy Acton Defeats Vivek Ramaswamy for Governor

Ohio was home to one of the nation’s most competitive races for governor in the 2026 midterm elections, as entrepreneur and former Republican presidential candidate Vivek Ramaswamy and Democrat physician Amy Acton battled to replace term-limited GOP governor Mike DeWine. But on Tuesday, Acton defeated Ramaswamy, according to the AP.

The Buckeye State, which is also home to Vice President JD Vance, hasn’t elected a Democrat to its highest office since 2006. But rising concerns regarding affordability and data centers boosted the campaign of Acton and running mate David Pepper, the former chair of the Ohio Democratic Party. Ramaswamy’s running mate, Rob McColley, is currently the Ohio Senate president.

A $4 million ad campaign from Ramaswamy had also split Republicans. The commercial featured Acton’s mother, from whom Acton has been estranged since her stepfather was reportedly arrested and charged with raping Acton when she was 12 years old. (According to The New York Times, the stepfather, who died in 2004, pleaded not guilty to the charges and then fled the state before trial.) In the ad, Acton’s 82-year-old mother, Donna Arthur, says, “Don’t let her become your governor,” prompting GOP members, including DeWine, to repudiate the commercial.

Meanwhile, Ohio’s US Senate race also went to the Democrats, further cementing their grip on the House. Over $500 million has been spent in the battle for the seat currently held by Republican senator Jon Husted, who was appointed to the role by DeWine in 2025 to replace JD Vance. Husted has been singled out for praise by President Donald Trump in recent weeks, especially when it comes to his physique, but trailed in the polls behind Democrat Sherrod Brown, who lost his previous seat in the US Senate to Republican Bernie Moreno in 2024. The Associated Press and CNN have projected Brown as the winner, giving his party a major win in one of the country's most closely watched Senate contests.

#3622. 10 Hacks Ever Siri AI User Should Know

Khamosh Pathak is a freelance tech journalist with over 13 years of experience writing online. An accounting graduate, he turned his interest in writing and technology into a career. He holds a specialization in user experience design from ISDI Parsons in Mumbai, where he sought to deepen his understanding of UX, consumer devices, and interplay between software and technology.

Khamosh has written thousands of how-tos and guides on every major platform (iOS, macOS, Android, and Windows). He got started writing how-tos and guides for Guiding Tech, where he also published several e-books. His work has also been seen at MakeUseOf, How-To Geek, and PCMag. He is truly passionate about brewing good coffee.

If you're like me, you've spent years ignoring most of Siri's functionality. Sure, it's great for setting timers, making calls, and sending a text. But that's kind of it—Apple's promise of an "always-on" digital assistant never truly delivered.

But that's finally changed with the recent launch of Siri AI. Fifteen years after debuting the app on the iPhone 4S and four years after the release of ChatGPT, Apple has taken the time to build out its own private Apple Foundation Models (with little help from Google) that work both on-device and on Apple's servers to give quick responses to your queries. Siri AI's answers are short, to the point, and actually useful. However, the conversational side isn't the only new thing about Siri AI. In fact, once you scratch the surface, you'll find Siri AI features embedded across the entire iOS and macOS ecosystem. Here's how to get the most out of Apple's new, enhanced digital assistant.

Siri AI is already tuned for brevity. Compared to Gemini or Claude, its responses are short and to the point. But still, if you ask something with your voice, it responds using voice as well. I personally prefer to quickly read through Siri responses. If you’re like me, you can enable a hidden setting that makes sure that Siri always answers silently, no matter if you’re writing to it or using your voice. Go to Settings > Siri > Responses and switch to the Silent Response option.

On the other hand, if you prefer to listen to Siri's responses, it's worth it to spend some time fine-tuning them. If you have an iPhone that’s under two years old, you have access to a more expressive Siri voice. Siri AI has an Expressive Voice feature that works on iPhone 17 Pro and higher, iPhone Air, and Macs with an M3 processor or higher (at least 12GB RAM).

To find this feature, go to Settings > Siri > Voice. Here, you can change the Pace to make Siri faster or slower. The big feature is the Expressivity slider; you can use it to make Siri sound brighter and more enthusiastic, rather than flat. You also have several voice options at the top (color-coded).

Visual Intelligence is deeply integrated into iOS 27 and macOS 27, and it turns anything on your screen into a source that Siri AI can act upon. It can search anything on your screen, and even take action on things it finds out. You can highlight any text on an iPhone, tap and hold, and choose the Ask Siri option. On the Mac, Ask Siri is the first option in the right-click menu. Choose a file, select text, and get started talking to Siri.

But it goes further. Just pull up Siri AI on your iPhone or Mac and start asking questions about what you’re seeing on screen. If you’re seeing a photo of a cafe on Instagram, ask where it is, or ask Siri to open it in Maps. If you’re watching a scene from a movie or a TV show, ask Siri where it’s from.

Clean Up was part of Apple Intelligence features in iOS 18, but it wasn’t great. It used on-device models to remove objects, and the results were lacking. Now that Apple runs its own Apple Foundation Models in Private Cloud Compute, it can securely process images on its servers, and the Clean Up process is much better. It now removes objects from photos very reliably, and even accounts for shadows. But to use this, you have to make sure to use the High Quality feature (instead of the default Auto mode).

Tap the Edit button in a photo, go to Tools > Clean Up, and from the top, switch to the High Quality option. Now brush over or tap an object you want to remove. Then, tap Clean Up and wait for a while until Apple’s servers complete the process. Tap Done to save the changes.

One of the most tedious parts of using the Calendar app is manually entering multiple events from a complicated schedule—say, for a season's worth of your kid’s soccer practices, or your college course's weekly lecture schedule. With Visual Intelligence in iOS 27, this is now table stakes: You can point your iPhone camera towards a schedule or take a screenshot of one, then tap the Add to Calendar button. Siri will recognize all the events, and you’ll get an option to add them to the calendar individually or all at once.

Siri AI's Mail integration is a hidden gem. Once your iPhone or Mac is done indexing your local data from Mail, you can use Siri AI to triage and manage your Mail without even opening the Mail app. In my testing, it works really well, especially because Siri AI understands the context of an email. This means you don't need to remember the exact details about the sender or the subject. You can just ask something like, "Find all emails about my flights from last week and send them to my accountant." You can also ask it to do things for you. For example, you can say, "Archive all the emails from Walmart from last month," and it will give you a one-button option to do just that.

When you start using the new Siri AI more often, you'll realize that it asks for confirmation way too often. For things like deleting mail, that's useful. But for sending messages, less so. There is a hidden setting that removes the extra step when it comes to sending messages via Siri. Go to Settings > Siri > Responses and enable Automatically Send Messages.

After the Siri AI upgrade in iOS 27, I find myself using the Camera Control often, and you should try it too. Just press and hold the Camera Control button to launch the camera's Siri mode. Point towards anything you want to find out more about and tap the big Siri icon. In a second or two, you will get the Siri response at the top, along with relevant actions based on what you're looking at. This feature is genuinely useful, and if you don't like using the Camera Control (or don't have access to it on your iPhone), you can also add the Siri AI shortcut to the lock screen, Control Center, or the Action button.

While Shortcuts has been one of Apple's most powerful features, it's also one of the hardest to use. Making an automation requires setting up steps, selecting variables, and thinking about chronology, and more. With Siri AI, Apple is trying to reduce that burden. And when it comes to simpler stuff that an everyday iPhone user needs, it works.

For example, you can open Shortcuts, create a new shortcut, and use the Describe a shortcut feature to talk about a Shortcut you want to build in natural language. You can ask Siri to create a daily morning Shortcut that shows you the day's weather, upcoming calendar events, and the to-do list for the day. You can also ask it to create a Shortcut that converts images in batches and creates new notes with a pre-made template.

While Apple is now using its own Apple Foundation Models for the new Siri AI, ChatGPT isn’t technically gone. If you have a complex question, or if Siri AI’s answer isn’t doing the trick, you can still summon ChatGPT from the Siri AI app (no need to go to the ChatGPT app for this). Tap on the text field in the Siri app, choose the Ask option and then switch to the ChatGPT service. Siri AI is quite intelligent at routing, so if ChatGPT can’t answer, it will route you back to Siri AI’s own models.

#3621. 25 Years Later, Aragorn's Best Lord of the Rings Quote Still Defines the Entire Trilogy

No other character is doing it quite like Aragorn

Peter Jackson’s adaptation of J.R.R. Tolkien’s The Lord of the Rings trilogy remains one of cinema’s most poignant and beautiful works. For better or worse, the trilogy also helped shape the visual style we now associate with fantasy. No matter how much time has passed, The Lord of the Rings has left a lasting mark on the genre.

However, The Lord of the Rings also proved extraordinary in other ways. For one thing, every character, major or minor, has at least one fantastic quote that adds tremendous depth. Gandalf might have some of the best lines in the franchise, but Aragorn — the cloaked ranger who stole all our hearts the moment he first appeared — also has plenty of quotable zingers delivered perfectly by Viggo Mortensen.

But what is Aragorn’s best quote? That’s a tough one to pick, especially with amazing lines like “For Frodo” and “I do not fear death.” Still, we think we’ve picked Aragorn’s most memorable line, and it perfectly captures the heart of The Lord of the Rings trilogy.

Aragorn is one of Middle-earth’s most honorable characters. Though he has spent much of his life in the background, hoping for something simpler, he will do whatever it takes to do the right thing when push comes to shove. That doesn’t make him a bastion of goodness — he has selfish moments, too — but overall, Aragorn is defined by his loyalty to those around him.

This loyalty is on full display when Frodo approaches Aragorn at Amon Hen during The Lord of the Rings: The Fellowship of the Ring. After seeing a vision of destruction and war, and only shortly after surviving Boromir's attack to seize the One Ring, Frodo is convinced he must head to the fires of Mordor alone. When Frodo tells Aragorn his plan, Aragorn isn’t pleased, but accepts his decision, knowing the Ring is too tempting and can turn people against one another, as it did with Boromir.

Yet before Frodo leaves, Aragorn displays just how noble and reliable he is with this heartfelt quote:

“I would have gone with you to the end, into the very fires of Mordor.”

After losing so many allies, and with the Fellowship breaking apart so soon, Aragorn’s words show that the ranger deeply believes in Frodo’s mission—even if he won’t be there to see it done.

It’s established early in The Fellowship of the Ring that Frodo’s journey will ask those in the Fellowship to endure innumerable hardships, pain, and sacrifice. Even so, what a person must sacrifice — whether it be their sanity or even their life — only becomes apparent as the group continues its journey.

By the time the movie ends, the Fellowship has split up. It would be all too easy for Aragorn, Legolas, and Gimli to rescue Pippin and Merry, then simply wait to see whether Frodo and Sam can evade Sauron’s forces and cast the Ring into the fires of Mordor.

However, Aragorn and the rest of the Fellowship have faith in Frodo, so they would never abandon their mission. When Frodo offers him the Ring, Aragorn feels its temptation, but realizes he can best serve Frodo by letting him go. He acts not out of fear, but from the inner belief that, though he will part ways with Frodo, the hobbit is strong enough to carry on.

Aragorn’s faith in Frodo sustains the Fellowship through doubt and seemingly hopeless odds. At Helm's Deep, despite Legolas's warning that victory is unlikely, Aragorn remains committed to his allies, as he did at Amon Hen when he risked his life to help Frodo escape. Though loved ones depend on him, he believes the risk is worthwhile if Frodo can defeat Sauron and save Middle-earth.

Though Aragorn’s best quote may not feel as badass as the lines he delivers in the heat of battle, it captures the Fellowship’s steadfast belief in Frodo — and remains one of the most definitive lines in The Lord of the Rings.

#3620. Everything You Should See Along With ‘You Can See Everything’

Jeff Somers is a freelancer who has been writing about writing, books, personal finance, and home maintenance since 2012.

Jeff has published nine novels and more than 70 short stories; his story Ringing the Changes was selected for inclusion in The Best American Mystery Stories 2006. In 2018, Jeff published the book Writing Without Rules: How to Write & Sell a Novel Without Guidelines, Experts, or (Occasionally) Pants. He holds a bachelor’s degree in English and previously worked in medical publishing as a production editor.

When not writing, Jeff spends his free time fixing up his old house. He has tackled a wide range of DIY projects, including remodeling a bathroom entirely on his own in two weeks, and building a roof deck that hasn't fallen down yet. You can find him on Bluesky.

This is Streamalikes, where you can find a curated list of recommendations to stream based on what you already like.

You Can See Everything, the new documentary about Theranos founder (and accomplished con artist) Elizabeth Holmes from filmmakers Nathan Fielder and Lance Oppenheim, is breaking records (and brains). Not only is it raking it in at the box office in a way that few documentaries can manage, it’s also dominating the pop culture chat right now thanks to genre-defying techniques; a huge, rule-breaking twist (that I won't spoil); and its unrepentant and inexplicably mesmerizing subject.

While some might argue that you should head into this incredible film experience fresh, if you’re unfamiliar with any of the three major figures involved, you will benefit from a little prep work before you head in—and if you've already seen it, you're no doubt eager to dive even deeper into this truly remarkable (in every sense of the word) story. Here’s what you should watch, read, and listen to before or after You Can See Everything.

To put it simply: There’s a lot going on here. To ensure you can appreciate the film, you should make sure you know at least the basics about three things: Elizabeth Holmes (and why she’s infamous), and the work of both Nathan Fielder and Lance Oppenheim. Here’s the crash course.

The 2019 podcast The Dropout is one of the most efficient ways to get the background on Holmes and Theranos. In the style of a true crime podcast, this show from ABC and journalist Rebecca Jarvis offers a deep dive into Holmes and her crimes that will give you all the background you’ll need.

John Carreyrou is the journalist who broke the Holmes story wide open, and his award-winning book Bad Blood offers a more journalistic and less sensational investigation than other accounts, providing a close-up look at Holmes in her CEO persona—an alternately terrifying and charismatic person who comes across as a “character” Holmes is playing. The book will inform your viewing of the documentary in important ways.

While Nathan Fielder is getting most of the attention for You Can See Everything, co-director Lance Oppenheim brings his signature technique to the film—it wouldn’t be nearly as interesting without his visual sensibility and framing.

Oppenheim has helmed several notable films, as he’s made a name for himself as a brilliant documentarian over the last few years, but to get ready for You Can See Everything, check out Spermworld, his 2024 exploration of unregulated sperm donations (you read that right). The doc deals with people who are as reality-challenged, manipulative, and possibly delusional as Holmes, and it will prep you for his visual style of extreme close-ups and excessive coverage that seems almost impossible in a normal documentary setting. You can stream Spermworld on Hulu.

If you’re unfamiliar with Nathan Fielder’s work, you need to strap in, because he’s unlike any other comedian or documentarian you’ve ever encountered.

To get a sense of his style, start with Nathan for You, a comedy-documentary-reality TV hybrid in which Fielder—as a version of himself—tries to use his business experience to help struggling people and small businesses. Presented as totally sincere, Fielder’s ideas are nevertheless increasingly elaborate and, in a word, unhinged. This show will familiarize you with Fielder’s persona and approach, but if you only have time to cram one episode, check out the series finale, “Finding Frances.” It follows Fielder’s attempts to reunite one of his earlier clients with his long-lost love, and it is a nearly perfect encapsulation of his style and approach. You can stream Nathan for You on HBO Max, Hoopla or Paramount Plus, or rent it episode-by-episode on Prime Video.

You should also watch at least some of Fielder’s other series, The Rehearsal. Here, Fielder (again, portraying a version of himself) attempts to help people prepare for difficult conversations utilizing increasingly outlandish techniques and scenarios that spiral into comedic insanity, including building sets, hiring actors, and immersing himself and his subjects in an alternate reality of sorts—an approach that will prepare you for some of You Can See Everything’s swerves. If you don’t have time to watch the whole thing, just check out the first episode, “Orange Juice, No Pulp.” It’s a self-contained chapter and will give you the basics. You can stream The Rehearsal on Apple TV or HBO Max, or rent episodes on Prime Video.

Have more bandwidth before watching You Can See Everything, or want a deeper dive after the documentary has melted your brain? Here’s what else you can check out.

The companion podcast to Carreyrou’s book, Bad Blood: The Final Chapter, is well worth a listen. Hearing the journalist’s perspective about his investigation and work during and after Holmes’ trial offers additional insight into her personality and methods that will really resonate after watching her in Fielder and Oppenheim’s doc.

Once you’ve noodled on You Can See Everything for a moment, there are two more movies you should check out.

For more on Holmes’s specific grift and how she pulled it off, Alex Gibney’s excellent The Inventor: Out for Blood in Silicon Valley is the way to go, especially if you didn’t follow the Theranos story closely at the time and your main visual guide to Holmes is the new documentary. Gibney’s film is more traditional, but offers a wealth of insight into Holmes and her bubble. You can stream The Inventor on HBO Max or rent it on Prime VIdeo.

If you more from co-director Lance Oppenheim, watch Some Kind of Heaven, his 2020 breakout documentary about The Villages retirement community in Florida. It’s the film that put Oppenheim on the map, and offers hints of the same detached observational style that makes You Can See Everything so arresting. You can stream Some Kind of Heaven on Kanopy or Hoopla, or rent it on Prime Video.

Speaking of which, if you loved the visual style and “enhanced” reality of You Can See Everything and want to see more of that, catch the Robert Pattinson-starring Primetime, still in theaters. It’s Oppenheim's narrative film directorial debut, and combines his hyperstyled visual flair with thriller pacing and a narrative based on a true story.

The Curse, Fielder’s 2023 TV series, is his first work of fiction, and it offers some fascinating insights. It follows a newly married couple (played by Fielder and Emma Stone) who struggle to get an HGTV-style show off the ground as things get excruciatingly awkward (and, eventually, kind of surreal). After watching You Can See Everything, it will be interesting to see how Fielder views the power of editing, the ethics of reality TV, and working with a name actor to get the results that he wants. Plus, similarly to the film, The Curse swerves into a final act that will melt your brain. You can stream The Curse on Apple TV or rent it on Prime Video.

You should also definitely watch The Dropout, the 2022 Hulu series starring Amanda Seyfried. It’s a well-made film, and Seyfried’s performance was rightly praised for capturing the weirdness of Holmes' public persona. You can stream The Dropout on Hulu.
