#3619. Liam Neeson's New 2026 Action Movie Flopped At The Box Office

Another year, another Liam Neeson action movie. What else is new? This time, it's a police chase flick in the form of "The Mongoose." Ever since "Taken" became a box office hit that led to Neeson's unexpected action star makeover, the Oscar-nominated actor has been churning these pieces of genre fare out with regularity. His latest effort, however, failed to drum up much business.

"The Mongoose" opened to just $464,421 on 1,014 screens over the weekend, making for a terrible $458 per-screen average. It was duking it out with the badly reviewed horror comedy "Christmas at the Kringles," which bombed with just $710,526 on just over 1,800 screens. Because Halloween fell on a Saturday, it was a lousy weekend for new releases, so Samuel Goldwyn Films decided to throw this one at the wall to see if it would stick. It didn't.

Directed by Mark Vanselow, Neeson's new actioner centers on Ryan "Fang" Flanagan (Neeson), a man who, having been accused of a crime he didn't commit, leads law enforcement on a cross-country car chase with the help of his brothers in arms, all while the public roots for his getaway. The film's cast also includes Marissa Tomei ("Spider-Man: No Way Home"), Ving Rhames ("Mission: Impossible — The Final Reckoning"), and Michael Chiklis ("The Shield").

This is actually Leeson's second action flick to come and go while hardly registering with the moviegoing public this fall, as "The Fix" also opened in theaters in September, making roughly $1.2 million domestically in total. The days of the "Taken" trilogy are indeed very far behind us, it seems.

Like many of Liam Neeson's late career action movies, "The Mongoose" isn't exactly a critical darling, having only earned a 30% approval rating among critics on Rotten Tomatoes at the time of writing. That being said, this one was undoubtedly financed with the understanding that if it can be made at a certain price point, it'll find its audience on VOD/streaming.

Case in point, Neeson's "Blacklight" somewhat inexplicably took over Prime Video's streaming charts earlier this year, despite being considered one of the actor's worst films in recent memory. Similarly, in late 2024, Netflix breathed new life into Neeson's 2015 crime thriller "Run All Night." This sort of thing happens pretty regularly. People really enjoy these movies, even if it's more about enjoying them from the comfort of home. They may not be cinematic events, but they're good library titles that generate streaming revenue.

It's honestly been some time since one of Neeson's action movies was an out-and-out hit. 2018's "The Commuter" was like "Non-Stop" on a train and pulled in $120 million at the global box office. Ever since then, though, his films have tended to perform more like "The Mongoose." Setting aside the Neeson vehicles that were hampered by the pandemic, "The Marksman," "Blacklight," "Memory," "Marlowe," "Retribution," and "Absolution" are all real movies, yet each of them either disappointed or outright flopped at the box office.

We're arguably far removed from Neeson's best action movie "The Grey" or hidden gems like "A Walk Among the Tombstones." His recent efforts have tended to follow a very basic formula, and while it may not sell tickets in theaters, it clearly makes money elsewhere within the Hollywood ecosystem.

Liberty Mutual has gone too far with its latest ad campaign, and people are taking to the streets to protest it. While the general public often rallies behind commercials featuring popular actors or funny mascots, dozens gathered outside the headquarters of the insurance company to protest the existence of "Liberty Biberty." I'm sad I missed this protest, but I'm totally down to show up for the next one.

Led by YouTuber DimesAreTasty, people recently gathered in Boston in front of the Liberty Mutual headquarters to protest Liberty Biberty. Looks like the heat is officially off Limu Emu and Doug, because consumers decided they have bigger fish to fry.

In the words of the protest organizer himself, Liberty Biberty is a "nasty little pest" that was created by Liberty Mutual to "make the world worse." While his original video was directed specifically at how the new creature is a disgrace to all corporate mascots, the protest itself seemed to consist of people who were annoyed by seeing ads for the company while they watched sports or streamed shows with a Prime subscription.

The protest was only one day and only attracted dozens of people, and legitimate outlets like ABC News and others came out to cover the event. Unfortunately, I think the negative attention will only give Liberty Mutual more incentive to use the character, and maybe this all builds to a wild Super Bowl halftime ad. We shall see!

Liberty Biberty originally started as a joke in an older Liberty Mutual commercial, which featured an actor trying to say "Liberty Mutual" and instead saying "Liberty Biberty" instead. That character went on to do more commercials, with a running gag that he couldn't correctly say Liberty Mutual.

32 A-List Celebrities Who Have Appeared In TV Commercials

This gag evolved into a creature, which Liberty Mutual officially rolled out in July. The yellow fur ball was a puppet created in collaboration with the Jim Henson Workshop, so yes, I think that makes it a muppet. It's unlikely it'll be remembered as one of the best Muppets, but possibly the first to have a protest against it.

There is a part of me that suspects that Liberty Biberty was made in part to be annoying. The more people are making videos and content online about how much they hate the Liberty Mutual mascot, the more the company gets its name out there. It's not like having an annoying mascot is going to do much to impact the company's legacy and how it sells insurance. Heck, this might be the most I've talked about insurance all year, so if that was the play by the marketing team, kudos to them for pulling it off.

The Liberty Biberty ads will continue as the 2026 TV schedule rolls on. I'll be interested to see if any future ads address the backlash to the mascot, or if they'll phase out the mascot entirely after this negative attention.

#3617. James Talarico Flips Senate Seat In Texas, While Gina Hinojosa Takes Governor's Race

The polls closed in Texas at 7 p.m. local time (the state is split between Central Time and Mountain Time) Tuesday, and within hours, one of the state's most contentious battles in the 2026 midterm elections was over, with Democrat James Talarico prevailing over Texas Attorney General Ken Paxton, giving Democrats their first statewide victory in Texas since 1994.

As part of a campaign in the state's most closely watched race, Paxton embarked on a whirlwind tour across Texas, joined by President Donald Trump along the way. Given Trump's slumping approval, combined with popular discomfort around Paxton's scandal-plagued career, Talarico's lead continued to grow even as Elon Musk pumped cash into the Republican side.

In June, political advisor Mark McKinnon described Talarico in a piece for Vanity Fair as “a rare talent.” “He’s an eighth-generation Texan, a former middle school teacher, and a Presbyterian seminarian. In a state where the Scriptures amount to a kind of civic fixture, Talarico out-Bibles many Republicans,” McKinnon wrote. "What’s more, he is preaching a new kind of message that is not along partisan lines. Here’s a sample: ‘The biggest divide in this country is not left vs. right. It’s top vs. bottom. Billionaires want us looking left and right at each other instead of looking up at them.’”

Democrat Gina Hinojosa defeated incumbent Greg Abbott in Texas's governor's race, becoming the state's first Latina governor, as well as the first Democrat to hold the office in more than 30 years. The last one was also a woman: Democrat Ann Richards, who served from 1991-1995. Richards was the mother of Cecile Richards, the longtime president of Planned Parenthood.

#3616. The Best Apple Watch for Most People Is Over $100 Off

The Apple Watch Series 10 was released in September 2024, and it's one of the best ways to get into the Apple Watch in 2026 without breaking the bank. Right now, the titanium 46 mm case model with cellular capabilities is $112 off, bringing the price down to $637 (originally $749). That's the lowest price after Apple raised prices this summer due to the RAM shortage, according to price-tracking tools. The same model in gold titanium is also over $100 off, reaching $679 (originally $799), saving you the same amount compared to the latest Series 12 going for $799.

The Apple Watch Series 10 was considered the best Apple Watch for most people last fall and is a great replacement if you're still wearing the more budget SE. There are also some key upgrades from the Apple Watch 9, although they're less noticeable than previous Apple Watch upgrades. If you're curious to know how it compares to other flagship smartwatches from its time, you can check out our head-to-head comparison.

Some of the first things you'll notice on the Series 10 are a thin case and a big OLED screen (either 1.6 inches or 1.8 inches, depending on which model you get). The Series 10 has audio playback, meaning you can listen to podcasts, take calls, or listen to Spotify on its speakers. The sleep features allow notifications for signs of sleep apnea. What you're giving up by saving on this version over the latest Series 12 is a faster S11 chip, a newer Health Sensing System and the Readiness app (tracks daily insights, vitals, and other metrics), a longer battery life (from 18 to 24 hours), 5G RedCap support (it helps save on battery life and has better network coverage compared to 5G), and audio intelligence features like Live Rewind, Siri Recap, and Sound Recognition.

If those extra features don't matter to you, the Series 10 is a great Apple Watch to get in 2026 at a discount, when many are still suffering from their price hikes.

It's still early days for Warner Bros' new DC universe headed James Gunn and Peter Safran, but we just got one exciting update on one of the upcoming DC movies on the way. Dynamic Duo will officially star Mason Thames as Dick Grayson/Robin. It's perfect casting, especially since the actor once told us himself how much the character means to him.

In a new interview with Collider, Safran confirmed Thames casting, which has been rumored for awhile. Here's what he said about the 19-year-old from How To Train Your Dragon and The Black Phone movies earning the role.

We always talk about wanting volunteers and not recruits to be part of the DCU, to be part of DC Studios, and Mason always wanted to be Dick Grayson. He just did. And he came in, and auditioned the shit out of it, and was awesome. He's a wonderful young actor, but boy, did he want this. He was just obsessed. When he came over to the DC offices, he came over with his dad at the time, and we’ve got tons of great archives and stuff in there, and wanted to take a picture of everything and with everything. He's a fan.

When Mason Thames stopped by San Diego Comic-Con's suite back in July, he gushed with us about his deep love for the character. As he shared with us at the time:

I'm a big comic book nerd... Spider-Man's always been No. 1, but I love Robin, specifically Dick Grayson's Robin. I've loved his comic books. I have about a million of them. It's just fun to see his journey from him being first Robin to becoming Nightwing, to becoming kind of the symbol of what Batman wishes Batman was. And, he's always kind of been the best of him.

This new role for Mason Thames is absolutely deserved because he truly knows his stuff. In between chatting with him, I could see how genuinely stoked he was to be at his first San Diego Comic Con. He was asking me about all the tips to best enjoy the experience, and was hyped to walk the floor and get the full SDCC experience. He really and truly is one of us. Here's the video:

A post shared by CinemaBlend (@cinemablend)

DC's Dynamic Duo movie is set to have Thames' Dick Grayson working together with another Robin iteration, Jason Todd. Grayson grew up in a family of circus performers, but had to watch his parents fall to their deaths while trying to be complete one trick (after the act was sabotaged). He becomes Batman's first sidekick. Jason Todd, on the other hand, is a character who grew up on the streets of Gotham to a petty thief and a drug addict for parents before being taken in by Batman.

When the movie was announced it on X in October 2024, Gunn revealed it'd be "a mix of animation, puppetry, and CGI," making it a rather unique take on the characters. While Thames is presumably just taking on the voice role for Robin in this movie, Gunn has previously said this in 2023, per IGN:

And what we're doing with the DCU is we are having animation tied directly into live-action television and movies and games all intertwined within the same universe. We're going to cast actors that are going to be able to play the characters in this as well as in other things.

While we should keep in mind these comments are on the older side, Mason Thames looks absolutely ready to play Robin as is in live-action. And, I hope Dynamic Duo is the start of a long journey of the actor playing the role across a variety of mediums.

It's also worth nothing the movie is also produced by Matt Reeves, who's been the filmmaker behind The Batman films with Robert Pattinson. I wonder if we could see a version of his Dick Grayson in his universe? Dynamic Duo is set to hit theaters on September 22, 2028 following the release of Man of Tomorrow and The Batman: Part II next year. Congrats to Mason Thames on manifesting a dream role of his!

#3614. Star Trek's Gates McFadden And John De Lancie React To Death Of Patrick Stewart

It's never easy saying goodbye to heroes we grew up adoring, but some deaths take even longer than others to process. The loss of "Star Trek" and "X-Men" legend Patrick Stewart still doesn't feel quite real yet, even as it feels like we've spent every day since celebrating all of his greatest and most memorable moments on the screen. When it comes to the tight-knit bonds formed between members of the "Trek" family, well, they've proven that it really is a family. Some relationships have experienced more friction than others, such as the widely-publicized rift between William Shatner and the late Walter Koenig, but others have gone through the fire and emerged stronger than ever.

That sense of history through the decades is probably why two celebrations of Stewart's life hit harder than the rest. In a pair of separate posts, "Star Trek: The Next Generation" co-stars Gates McFadden and John de Lancie both memorialized their longtime friend and screen partner. Cast as Beverly Crusher and the enigmatic cosmic being Q, respectively, McFadden and de Lancie represent two of Jean-Luc Picard's most popular and well-established character dynamics throughout their collective run on "Trek." Both shared countless memories together with Stewart on- and off-screen, and, fittingly enough, both received satisfying send-offs alongside their captain on "Star Trek: Picard."

For those prone to bursting into tears over such heartbreaking tributes, be warned that this will likely unleash the waterworks.

Jean-Luc Picard meant so much to so many, and Patrick Stewart's portrayal of the venerated captain represented something deeper and more meaningful than a simple "Trek" character. And while fans all over the world have attempted to verbalize just how important he was, the woman behind Dr. Beverly Crusher has now captured it as eloquently as only she can.

Gates McFadden was one of the many Hollywood icons who initially reacted to Stewart's passing. But in a guest article in Variety, she's penned a full-length eulogy for her friend's well-lived life. However, though it's well worth reading in full, one particular passage draws a direct link between the integrity of Stewart's performance as Picard and our desperate need for genuine leadership in real life (a particularly poignant message on the U.S.' Election Day):

"One thing is for certain: Patrick's reach across the continents was massive. After word of his death surfaced, the internet, not surprisingly, was filled with thousands of tributes of admiration and overflowing love for the Yorkshire man. He touched so many people in so many ways. Not only was he the captain of the Enterprise crew, he seems to have been everyone's captain because of how he walked in the world.

What a breath of fresh air to have a leader who cared about the ethics of what he said! The result was eloquence. Seriousness. Intellect. The character of Jean-Luc Picard, which Patrick played brilliantly, was the antithesis of many of our leaders today."

McFadden sums up Stewart's life and his tragic loss thusly: "Jean-Luc Picard embodied that ideal. Patrick's death means the loss of Picard, which for some hurts even more than the loss of Patrick Stewart. Jean-Luc gave us hope."

Where Dr. Beverly Crusher brought both a platonic and romantic dimension to her relationship with Jean-Luc Picard, Q represents a very different extreme of emotions. Picard's longtime frenemy spent many an episode of "The Next Generation" annoying our good captain to no end, oftentimes outwitting our hero and proving himself an equal match in intellect or philosophy. But their two diametrically opposite perspectives on humanity added so much to their adventures over the years and, ultimately, reached a tearjerking crescendo in the Season 2 finale of "Star Trek: Picard" as they say an emotional goodbye to one another.

Actor John de Lancie struck that exact same tone in a Facebook post over the weekend. It's not easy to encapsulate such a complicated, prickly, but oh-so-entertaining dynamic between two such worthy opponents, but the Q scene-stealer certainly found a way. In a much shorter (though no less sincere) remembrance, he stated:

"For forty years, Q has been a thorn in Jean-Luc Picard's side. And what a pleasure it has been to be that thorn.

Patrick Stewart was a wonderful actor. He brought intelligence and depth to every role he played. It was a privilege to have worked with him.

The universe is a little smaller and a little less bright today with his passing.

We couldn't have said it any better than that. Most Trekkies would put the Q and Picard rivalry up there among the best in the entire franchise — a testament to Stewart and de Lancie's easy chemistry and witty repartee. It's devastating to know we'll never see that on-screen again, yet reassuring to know it'll always stand the test of time.

#3613. 'Wonder Man' Actor Officially Breaks Silence on the Marvel Show's Sudden Cancellation

'More shall be revealed, but a lot of people were disappointed'

Marvel Studios' six-year experiment in streaming television seems to be winding down, at least for the moment. This has been clear for a while now (despite some vague promises of more new series in the future), but perhaps the biggest sign that the Marvel Cinematic Universe was retreating from live-action TV was the sudden cancellation of Wonder Man.

Created by Destin Daniel Cretton and Andrew Guest, the series starred Yahya Abdul-Mateen II as Simon Williams, an actor trying to make it in Hollywood while hiding his secret superpowers. Ben Kingsley also reprised his MCU role of Trevor Slattery, who becomes Simon's unlikely mentor. Wonder Man was a hit with both critics and fans.

After quietly landing on Disney Plus in January 2026, it was renewed two months later in March. Then, in July, the series was suddenly canceled.

The news came as a surprise to everyone involved, including the show's most unexpected star, The Sopranos actor Joe Pantoliano, who played an exaggerated version of himself on Wonder Man. Polygon recently interviewed "Joey Pants" about his role in the upcoming movie Violent Night 2, and we wanted to ask how he felt about Wonder Man's cancellation.

Like everyone else, he was shocked by the news.

"Talk about heart, I thought that show was wonderful," Pantoliano tells Polygon. "And then, you know, Destin and his Spider-Man movie is like the hit of the year, then it falls apart. I think there's something going on there that nobody ever — more shall be revealed, but a lot of people were disappointed."

That last sentence is particularly interesting. What is Pantoliano trying to say? Does he know something we don't? Unfortunately, we didn't have time to ask a follow-up question, but we do have a few more details from Wonder Man himself.

In a series of interviews last August, Abdul-Mateen reflected on Wonder Man's cancellation and offered a few more details about his experience. Speaking to Vanity Fair, the actor said that Disney offered a vague explanation related to streaming numbers for season 1, but didn't provide any actual numbers.

"I was told that it had something to do with the viewership," he said. "I wasn’t told what those numbers were, but ultimately, I think they decided that it didn’t make sense for business."

Speaking to NPR, he was even more critical, pointing to Marvel's history of failing its Black stars.

"When you look at the history of those projects and when you put them all together, there's no way around it," Abdul-Mateen. "It does not look good. It does not look like good business. And it looks like it's certainly not favorable to its Black creatives."

For now, we still don't know why Disney renewed and then canceled Wonder Man. Could the character eventually show up in a Marvel movie instead? Was the show just a victim of Marvel's retreat from streaming? Or is Abdul-Mateen right that Black creatives aren't getting a fair shake in the MCU? If Pantoliano is correct, we may still find out.

We want to hear from you. Share your perspective in the comments below, and please keep the conversation respectful.

Disney has always been known for its animated blockbusters, but Frozen (which is streaming with a Disney+ subscription) became a full-blown sensation upon its release in 2013. Its sequel Frozen II crushed at the box office, and two more sequels were quickly announced. Although the studios' Head of Animation recently revealed a big change coming to the next two installments of the franchisee

The first Frozen III footage debuted at D23 over the summer, so anticipation for the threequel is steadily building. While we'll have to wait another year until it arrives in November of 2027, Disney's Jared Bush spoke to Collider about how the studio is approaching the next two movies. He revealed that they're putting a full emphasis on the third movie, rather than trying to put out 3 and 4 in quick succession. In his words:

Looking at Frozen 3 and what a Frozen 4 could look like, I know early on it was, 'We're going to put them right together, and they're going to be out in the world. It's going to happen quick.' That's not what we're doing, for a lot of reasons.

Rather than trying to produce a third and fourth Frozen movie as a cash grab (although they're sure to rake in the bucks), it sounds like the powers that be at Disney are putting story first. This is sure to be a relief for fans who might be worried about the property's legacy being soiled by the next two installments.

Fans are excited for Anna and Kristoff's wedding in the threequel, and to reportedly see Olaf get a love interest. Although we shouldn't expect Frozen III to do a bunch of set up for the developing fourth movie. As Bush went on to say:

To me, an important one is we want to make sure that Frozen 3 is the best movie it can possibly be, so that when you get to the end of the movie, do you feel like you've watched a complete story? That it feels like something that feels fulfilling. That doesn't always mean that everything is buttoned up, but it does mean that you have to be building to something that feels worthy of the end of a franchise that's that important to people.

Honestly, I love this strategy. Rather than getting too big picture about the Frozen franchise as a whole, it sounds like the next two installments will tell independent, fully formed stories. So we shouldn't expect any MCU-esque credits scene that help to set up the fourth movie once Frozen III hits theaters next year.

Sometimes thinking too far ahead can frustrate moviegoers when it comes to franchise films. For instance, Halloween Kills got some backlash upon its release for keeping Jamie Lee Curtis' Laurie Strode in the background and set up her role in the threequel. Luckily the third Frozen movie won't be doing that, and will instead tell its own complete narrative.

All will be revealed when Frozen III hits theaters November 24th, 2027. Since its not on the 2026 movie release list, we'll have to practice patience until footage get its wide release.

#3610. Johnny Depp Has One Condition To Return For Pirates Of The Caribbean 6

Will Captain Jack Sparrow suit up for one last ride? At the very least, Johnny Depp isn't ruling it out, but the actor has a condition to return for "Pirates of the Caribbean 6." Depp is in the midst of mounting a Hollywood comeback following his fall from grace several years ago, thanks to his highly publicized legal feud with his ex-wife Amber Heard. The Depp/Heard case was even explored in a two-part Discovery+ documentary. Now, though? He's back and may (emphasis on "may") yet return to his most famous role.

During a recent interview with Entertainment Tonight for his Hollywood comeback movie "Ebenezer," the actor was asked about reprising his role as Jack Sparrow in the next "Pirates of the Caribbean" film, which has been in the works at Disney for some time. Here's what he had to say about it:

"If things are exactly where they need to be with regard to how they are going to top off the 'Pirates' franchise ...The only involvement I really want to have, truly, is just to send them off on a better note.

"I will go to work with [producer] [Jerry] Bruckheimer tomorrow for anything," Depp added. "Doesn't matter ...If it's Jerry, I trust him. We have a deep friendship."

All of the "Pirates of the Caribbean" movies have been hits at the box office, with much of that attributed to Depp's work as Jack Sparrow. In light of everything that's happened in recent years, it's also easy to forget that he was nominated for an Oscar for his work on "Pirates of the Caribbean: The Curse of the Black Pearl." So, it's not hard to grasp why bringing him back might seem appealing. But Disney needs to decide if the inevitable circus that will create would be worth it.

Johnny Depp hasn't been in a big blockbuster in nearly a decade. He dropped out of the "Fantastic Beasts" franchise after a court case verdict related to the tabloid The Sun running a story where it referred to him as a "wife beater." Since then, he's taken on roles in smaller movies like "Jeanne du Barry."

Depp lost his suit against The Sun, but the actor and Amber Heard later settled a defamation case in 2022. And while that sort of paved the way for his attempted comeback, the optics surrounding Depp are still pretty lousy. Unfortunately, in Hollywood, money speaks louder than anything else. That is to say, should "Ebenezer" become a hit (suggesting the general public has an appetite for a Johnny Depp comeback), we'll be all the more likely to see Jack Sparrow again.

Setting aside the Depp of it all, Disney ultimately needs to decide how they want to handle this franchise's future. "Pirates of the Caribbean" remains the studio's only theme park ride turned hit film property, but getting a sixth movie made has proved difficult. At one point, it looked like "Pirates of the Caribbean 6" was going to set sail with Margot Robbie in the lead, but that has yet to happen.

At another point, it was suggested that the next "Pirates of the Caribbean" movie would be a total reboot. Multiple scripts have been developed, yet nothing has stuck. Basically, this movie is going to happen at some point, with or without Depp. So, Disney needs to decide what, exactly, it wants to do here. We'll see how it all shakes out.

"Pirates of the Caribbean 6" doesn't currently have a release date, but stay tuned.

#3609. As Donald Trump's Handpicked Candidates Flop Nationwide, the President Accepts Reality

As the results of Tuesday’s midterm elections began to roll in, Donald Trump’s mood seemed to darken, especially when it came to coverage from his network of choice, Fox News. But after a few posts complaining about the cable news channel, the president fell silent for hours, before telling the New York Times that he will accept the results of Tuesday's election.

As polls closed in Indiana and Kentucky at 6 p.m. ET, Trump termed the end to the latter state's election day “A BIG DEAL!” The president was likely aware of the closure as he was “Watching the Pre-Election Results on FoxNews,” he wrote, before complaining that he can't stand the voice of one of the network's few liberal leaning commentators, Jessica Tarlov.

“DUMB AS A ROCK,” Trump complained, his mood apparently turning. “Have to go somewhere else until that LOSER is off the air — I'll be back later!” After less than an hour, he returned, his anger at Fox increasing. “The FoxNews Poll, always the worst, is so insulting with the questions they ask,” he wrote. “Every question is a hit job, and every answer is ‘BULLSHIT!’ This has been going on for years.”

A few minutes later, he returned again, this time with a longer rant about the cable channel. “FoxNews Ratings are way down (27%!) because they’re spending too much time covering the Trump Deranged Dumocrats! All of those people who used to watch Fox, and no longer do, get it. It’s them, not me — My numbers are better than they have ever been.”

“No wonder FoxNews Ratings are collapsing, and they’re going to go down a lot further,” he continued. “They’re way down, not because of me, but because they are AGAINST me! This happened once before, and Fox almost collapsed. It’s happening again!”

In Georgia, Trump had earlier stumped for gubernatorial candidate Rick Jackson and US Senate nominee Mike Collins, who lost his race against incumbent Democratic senator Jon Ossoff. When that race was called, Trump made no comment. The same was true as Democrat James Talarico's lead over Texas Senate hopeful Ken Paxton continued to grow. Those who checked Truth Social after CNN projected that the Democratic party would capture the House of Representatives were also set up for disappointment, as the president has yet to comment on those results as well.

Instead, he returned some hours later with a post not about any candidate, but his own popularity. “I wasn’t on the Ballot and if I was, we would have won IN A LANDSLIDE!,” the president wrote. Shortly thereafter, at around 10:30 p.m. ET, the president spoke with the New York Times, where he struck a conciliatory tone. “I am absolutely willing to accept those results,” he told the paper. “We’ll work with the Democrats, and we’ll, you know, look forward to working with them. We’ll probably work something out.”

And, minutes later, another Truth Social post. “I'm going to become a Political Pundit, both good and bad, on the reasons these Candidates won and lost!” (Capitalization his own.)

An ultra-wide curved gaming monitor with ridiculous specs is every gamer's dream, but they (usually) don't come cheap. The Samsung Odyssey Neo G9 Series is not a regular ultra-wide gaming monitor. It has impressive specs, but you'll need a top-notch gaming computer with specific outputs to take full advantage of its 240Hz refresh rate potential.

This monitor came out in 2023 with an "excellent" review from PCMag, mainly due to its impressive 7,680 by 2,160 4K native resolution, the ridiculous 57-inch screen size, its great color range and accuracy, the 240Hz refresh rate, and its design. Although it is pricey, this monitor is a great value for the right gamer. #3606. Daniel Craig's Early-Career Miniseries Is A Masterpiece Every British TV Fan Has To Watch

We may receive a commission on purchases made from links.

When I saw a 24-year-old Daniel Craig play the sadistic South African Police Sergeant Jaapie Botha in John G. Avildsen's 1940s Apartheid drama "The Power of One," I can't say that I had him pegged for the next James Bond, but I did know that he was a remarkably hissable villain. The film quickly faded from memory, but every time Craig turned up in a movie during the 1990s, I'd remember how effective he was as Botha, and wonder why he wasn't getting meatier roles.

What I didn't know at the time was that he'd given a tour de force performance in the 1996 BBC drama serial "Our Friends in the North." The nine-part series spans 31 years in the lives of four friends from Newcastle upon Tyne, and boosted the careers of Craig, Mark Strong, Christopher Eccleston and Gina McKee. But no one demonstrated greater range than Craig, whose character, Geordie, flees an abusive, alcoholic father to pursue an unpromising life in low-level crime.

British television wasn't immediately accessible in the United States in 1996 (unless it was a pop cultural sensation like "The Office" or "Little Britain"), so I didn't find out about "Our Friends in the North" until a decade later, directly after Daniel Craig had rejuvenated the James Bond franchise in "Casino Royale." I can understand why it didn't leap over the pond. The historical references are specific and steeped in British politics, which, to American viewers, makes it somewhat daunting. But Peter Flannery's writing and the dynamite acting ensemble will hook you just as sharply as David Simon plunged you into the Baltimore social stratum with "The Wire."

Unfortunately, "Our Friends in the North" isn't readily available in the United States on streaming, but if you've got a region-free Blu-ray player you can purchase it for $33.00 on Amazon, and it's worth it. I grew up watching British crime movies like "The Long Good Friday," "Mona Lisa," and "The Krays," and Flannery's writing doesn't suffer fools. But his dialogue is so crisp and layered and immaculately performed that you feel compelled to understand it. You're thrust into a society that, from the corrupt parliament down to the alcoholic, homeless dregs, is foreign yet familiar.

Craig's Geordie faces the most dire swings of fortune. He's not a bad person, but, like so many people who choose a criminal lifestyle and succumb to substance abuse, he makes so many compromises that there's eventually no way out. It's a harrowing journey and I wish I could tell you it ends well for Geordie, but "Our Friends in the North" is not out to comfort.

#3605. Apple TV's Best Sci-Fi Show Begins Filming for Season 2, but the Wait Will Be Long

Cameras started rolling for Pluribus season 2

Apple TV's hit 2025 sci-fi show, Pluribus, has reportedly started filming for its season 2. On Oct. 1, Production List reported that Pluribus season 2 was in pre-production, with filming scheduled to begin on Oct. 31. While Apple has not released any official statements, Forbes reported on Nov. 2 that shooting for season 2 of Pluribus has begun in Albuquerque, New Mexico.

Pluribus was created by Vince Gilligan (Breaking Bad, Better Call Saul), and it stars Rhea Seehorn, who played Kim Wexler in Better Call Saul. In this post-apocalyptic sci-fi series, Seehorn plays Carol Sturka, an author of romantasy novels residing in Albuquerque, who is one of the only 13 people in the world immune to the effects of an extraterrestrial virus that transformed the rest of humanity into a creepy hive-mind collective known as Others. Pluribus won many awards, including Seehorn snagging the Best Actress in a Drama Series award at the Golden Globes, the Critics' Choice Awards, and the Primetime Emmys.

After her victory at the Golden Globes in January 2026, Seehorn confirmed that the team was already "back in the writers' room" and Gilligan was keen to get started on season 2 as soon as possible. Speaking to Polygon in March, Gilligan confirmed that he was "plugging away on it." While work wasn't going as fast as fans hoped, Gilligan reassured everyone that Pluribus season 2 would feature "lots more excitement and twists and turns."

Apple TV ordered two seasons of the show from the beginning, but Gilligan and his team only started working after the season 1 finale aired in December 2025. In September 2026, Gilligan teased that filming could start in late October or early November.

On Oct. 31, Ava Harper of SciFi Spiral posted on X a picture from the Pluribus set, adding that shooting is scheduled over a 225-day period. If this timeline is confirmed, taking post-production time into consideration, season 2 of Pluribus could not be released before the second half of 2028, making it close to three years since season 1 wrapped up. But some shows are just worth the wait.

#3604. Maine Senator Susan Collins Has Reportedly Conceded Race to Democratic Challenger Troy Jackson

One of the most closely watched states during the run-up to the 2026 midterm elections has been Maine, where incumbent US senator Susan Collins, a Republican, faced a significant threat from upstart candidate Graham Platner. Allegations of misconduct toppled the Democrat’s campaign, but his replacement, former logger and state senator Troy Jackson, has had a strong showing in the polls, and posed the first actual competition Collins has faced in nearly three decades. A little more than three hours after Maine's poll closure at 8 p.m. ET, Collins reportedly called Jackson to concede the race, even as most news outlets were reporting that the race was still ongoing.

Susan Collins was running for a sixth term, and was the only Republican representing a state President Donald Trump lost in 2024. As votes rolled in on Tuesday and into Wednesday morning, Jackson's lead continued to grow. According to outlets, including Maine broadcast station WMTW, Collins called Jackson shortly after midnight to congratulate him for his win. In an address to supporters early Wednesday, an ebullient Jackson celebrated his win. At the time of publication, the New York Times was forecasting that “Jackson is almost certain to win," and NBC had projected him the winner as well.

“20 minutes or so I spoke to Senator Collins and I thanked her for her service to Maine,” Jackson said. “I wished her and her family well.”

“To every Mainer who voted for her or supported her, you can count on me to be your senator now.”

Elsewhere in Maine, Democrats kept the governor’s office blue, as term-limited governor Janet Mills will be replaced by Democrat Hannah Pingree, the Associated Press said when they called the race Tuesday night. She bested Republican candidate Bobby Charles, according to the AP.

Maine only has two congressional districts, both of which are up for election every two years. The state’s First Congressional District is known as a Democratic stronghold, with Hannah Pingree’s mother, Chellie Pingree, expected to retain the seat she’s held since 2009. Its Second District is considered a battleground region, with former state secretary of state Matthew Dunlap, a Democrat, still locked in a tight race against Republican former governor Paul LePage as of publication time.

Homes with shedding pets, mixed flooring, and low furniture can quickly reveal the shortcomings of a basic robot vacuum. The CurvX earns that higher price by doing more than simply vacuuming an open stretch of floor—its 22,000 pascals of suction can handle pet hair, crumbs, and debris caught in carpet, while the DuoDivide main brush guides hair toward the center to reduce tangles. The Roborock app gives you further control, allowing you to clean specific rooms, create schedules, set virtual barriers, and mark areas the robot should avoid, while SmartPlan 2.0 adapts the routine to different rooms and floor types.

#3602. New Godzilla LEGO Set Builds A Big, Thick King Of The Monsters

Godzilla has been back in a big way since returning to theaters in 2016. Not only has Legendary's Monsterverse given the atomic kaiju plenty of screentime in the decade since then, but Japan also gave us one of the best Godzilla movies ever with "Godzilla Minus One," soon to be followed by "Godzilla Minus Zero." Ever since debuting in 1954, Godzilla just keep stomping through cities, and now he's entered the world of LEGO.

LEGO has announced the first official Godzilla building brick set, inspired by the kaiju's appearance in Legendary's Monsterverse movies. That will make it quite monstrous among the modular buildings out there, even LEGO's Marvel Avengers Tower.

All those LEGO pieces combine to form the massive monster, right down to the glowing spines on his back and his tail that's ready for to be whipped around as a weapon. Let's take a closer look below.

The official Godzilla LEGO set is the latest to come from the LEGO Ideas program, where master builders and fans can submit their own designs to be voted on and potentially considered for production by LEGO. Creator Matthew Esposito is behind the design, and it was perfected with the help of LEGO model designers Jim Clayton and Markus Rollbühler and creative design lead Jordan Scott.

This is the largest creature ever designed by LEGO, and the designers weren't even sure they'd be able to make it 50cm tall. But they ended up with a Godzilla LEGO set that stands at 70cm, making him a true titan in LEGO form.

While Godzilla probably looks coolest with blue blast out of his mouth, that element can be removed, and you can just have Godzilla's tongue sitting in there instead, roaring into the sky.

When we chatted with the SNL alum, I had to ask about the memories of playing the role IRL.

Of course, Mike Myers famously took the live-action approach for the 2003 book-to-screen adaptation. In our interview, Hader seems to counts himself lucky to have just lent the voice to the character after spending a day in the literal paws of the character way back when. In his words:

I’m very happy to do it animated because that suit was very hot. And the makeup took a long time. It was the second music number, and then another pre-tape thing that I wasn't in just so they could put all the makeup on me. It was the last sketch of the night, so we did it really fast. So yeah, it was really hot and I had all that stuff on my face. I don't know how Mike Myers did it.

Myers' own process took two and a half hours and was very hot to act in a yak-hair suit all day. Jim Carrey had it even worse as The Grinch. He had to go through such a grueling process a specialist in torture was hired to help him withstand the eight-hour get ready time. In our interview above, you can see Quinta Brunson school Hader on what happened and watch his real-time reaction.

Instead of going through all that makeup time for months, it was just for one night. He played the character on October 11, 2014 in an episode he hosted in the season right after his exit from the show following an eight-year run. You can check out the sketch below:

It’s such a funny spin on the classic children’s book. When two sibling children are bored on a rainy day, they conjure up The Cat in the Hat, but something unexpected happens: he’s already acquainted with their mom, Linda. Playtime with the whimsical figure turns into an awkward reunion between The Cat and Linda. The best line has to be when Linda says: “He’s reliable. I don’t have to say a rhyme to make him come home.” ‘

And then, Linda’s husband ends up being Thing 2, who goes by Jona-Thing now. He comes home disappointed to see The Cat In The Hat with his wife and kids. The sketch hilariously ends with The Cat In The Hat saying “But oh, the places she let me go!” as he leaves them, which is obviously a NSFW reference to another Dr. Seuss book.

When CinemaBlend also spoke to the movie’s writer/directors Erica Rivinoja and Alessandro Carloni, we had to ask if the SNL sketch was involved at all with casting Hader. Here’s what Rivinoja told us:

It was completely random, of course, but we might wanna do a sequel with that character and with Linda. We're very excited about Linda.

Hader’s animated version of The Cat in the Hat is much different than SNL because it isn’t a parody like his first run as the character was. It’s a more family-friendly retelling of the picture book with an expanded story about where The Cat comes from, and involves an imaginative plot line that’s perfect for the medium of animation. It hits theaters this Friday, November 6.

Now she's into covering YA television and movies, and plenty of horror. Word webslinger. All her writing should be read in Sarah Connor’s Terminator 2 voice over.

#3599. 5 Best Movies Like The Love Hypothesis

There was never any doubt that Lili Reinhart's rom-com "The Love Hypothesis" would become a big hit for Prime Video. Streaming platforms have struck gold by taking romance books and turning them into comforting crowd-pleasers for the small screen. Sometimes this results in films as vapid as "My Fault: London," but often it results in charming movies that take allow us to indulge romantic fantasies via two hot people falling in love.

That's exactly what we got when "The Love Hypothesis" transformed from "Star Wars" fan fiction, of all things, into a novel and then a streaming movie. Ali Hazelwood's book about a biology PhD student who pretends to date her professor, only for the two to fall deeply in love became a hit, and was promptly given a film adaptation in which Reinhart plays the student, Olive Smith, while British actor Tom Bateman plays the ornery professor, Dr. Adam Carlsen.

There were two main tropes to both the book and the film: mismatched lovers who cross a boundary to be together, and the good old fake relationship that becomes very real. Of course, this is far from the first time these tropes have been used in romance movies, which is why it's actually quite easy to recommend films just like "The Love Hypothesis." While there are plenty of golden-age romance movies that used these plot devices (1941's "Come Live with Me" saw James Stewart and Hedy Lamarr fake a marriage only to fall head over heels), we're betting that fans of Reinhart's movie will want more modern examples. With that in mind, here's a list of the best movies like "The Love Hypothesis."

"My Oxford Year" may have a controversial ending but it's got everything you could want from a modern-day streaming flick based on a book. Melodrama and fairytale romance combine in this Netflix movie, which stars Sofia Carson (who's fast becoming the streamer's go-to romantic drama leading lady) as American exchange student Anna De La Vega. Before descending into a life of corporate drudgery, Anna decides to study Victorian poetry at the University of Oxford for a year. Wouldn't you know it, once there she meets an unreasonably charming and handsome English DPhil student and tutor named Jamie Davenport (Corey Mylchreest).

"My Oxford Year" shares much in common with "The Love Hypothesis." Not only are both based on books (though the former actually began as a screenplay before it was adapted into a novel), they both feature a student/teacher relationship that gets off to a rough start only to flourish into a modern-day fairytale. Both also feature strapping English leading men (though Bateman plays an American in "The Love Hypothesis") who start out as jerks only to reveal a tender side as things progress.

It is worth noting that there's a tragic element to "My Oxford Year," so if you're looking for something that wraps up as neatly as "The Love Hypothesis," this might not be the ideal watch. But otherwise fans of Lily Reinhart's movie should fall madly in love with Carson's alternative.

These streaming movies are all well and good but there has to be at least one undisputed classic on this list. There's no better example of the fake relationship trope than this 1990 romantic comedy in which we got to see prime-era Richard Gere and Julia Roberts fall for one another. The movie did what "The Love Hypothesis" and its fellow streaming-age rom-coms did decades before Netflix was even a thing, bringing together impossibly beautiful stars via a fake relationship that blossoms into the real thing.

If you don't know the plot of what might just be Julia Roberts' best movie, I'm not sure what to tell ya. He's a corporate raider, she's a sex worker he asks for directions. So begins a love affair that sees Gere's Edward Lewis paying Roberts' Vivian Ward to spend a week with him and act as his girlfriend. Needless to say, this confected relationship becomes a real one. Ward melts Lewis' cold corporate heart and Lewis draws out the real Ward from behind a wall of dissociation built up over her time spent as a sex worker.

If you're somehow yet to see the film, and are worried the tale of a millionaire corporate raider falling for a sex worker might not have the wholesome charm of "The Love Hypothesis," don't worry. There's a reason Roger Ebert called the film "the sweetest and most openhearted love fable since 'The Princess Bride.'" "Pretty Woman" is as romantic a comedy as they come. But beyond that, it somehow manages to feel grounded thanks to its multi dimensional characters, without compromising the fairytale romance aspect.

Sofia Carson will soon have a monopoly on streaming romance movies. Her 2025 romantic drama "The Life List" dominated Netflix just prior to the similarly successful release of "My Oxford Year." But before either of these movies, Carson made her Netflix romance debut with the 2022 film "Purple Hearts." Guess what — the whole thing was based on a book, Tess Wakefield's 2017 novel of the same name.

In "Purple Hearts" we get a modern day version of James Stewart's "Come Live with Me." This Carson-led love story sees the former Disney Channel star play diabetic waitress and musician Cassie Salazar, who's working herself ragged just to afford insulin. Her salvation arrives in the form of hunky Marine Luke Morrow (Nicholas Galitzine), who agrees to marry Cassie so she can gain health coverage and he can benefit from a pay bump. You can see where this is going.

Much like with "The Love Hypothesis," this is a story about a couple who agree to act as though they're together only to develop real feelings along the way. There's plenty of BookTok-style melodrama on display here, too, which should please anyone who enjoyed the tension of the third act fall-out in "The Love Hypothesis."

It's the film that made Glen Powell a star and proved Sydney Sweeney could make popular stuff outside of "Euphoria." If your favorite thing about "The Love Hypothesis" was watching two attractive people make out, then "Anyone But You" should be right up your alley. In fact, "Anyone But You" is arguably the apotheosis of the modern day two-hot-actors-fall-in-love rom-com. But there's a stronger connection between this film and "The Love Hypothesis."

Lily Reinhart's Olive Smith and Tom Bateman's Dr. Adam Carlsen agreed to fake a relationship for mutually beneficial reasons, and the same happens with Sweeney's Beatrice Messina and Powell's Ben. The duo pretend to be a couple so that Bea's parents will stop trying to repair her relationship with her ex, and Ben can make his own ex jealous. We all knew where it was going from the very beginning but that didn't make it any less enjoyable to watch.

Unlike with "The Love Hypothesis," the guy in this romantic comedy isn't a complete jerk. Full of himself, maybe, but not an anti-social hermit like Bateman's "Dr. Evil." Still, he and Sweeney's law student don't exactly get along, especially after their first meeting ended on awkward terms. That, alongside the fake relationship trope, gives Powell and Sweeney's couple a similar dynamic to that of Olive and Adam in "The Love Hypothesis." So if you somehow missed the unlikely box office smash that was "Anyone But You" back in 2024, now's the time to remedy that.

In 2018, "To All the Boys I've Loved Before" became the new gold standard for teen rom-coms. It also happens to be a nice little companion to "The Love Hypothesis." Based on a book? Check. Fake relationship trope? Check. Academic setting? Sort of check. Rather than college, this tale of teen love, adapted from Jenny Han's YA novel, plays out in high school, where Lara Jean Covey (Lana Condor) writes secret letters to her crushes. Of course, she never intends for any of them to read her missives, but guess what — that's exactly what happens.

Lara Jean's biggest crush is Josh Sanderson (Israel Broussard), and when she sees him approaching with his letter in hand, she kisses another one of the letter recipients, Peter Kavinsky (Noah Centineo) in an attempt to throw Josh off. Soon, Peter and Lara Jean are fake dating. This allows the former to distract from the embarrassment of Josh receiving a letter, and the latter to make his ex-girlfriend Gen (Emilija Baranac) jealous. But you know how this goes. Real romance develops, melodrama ensues, feelings get hurt.

"To All the Boys I've Loved Before" is, however, more than your standard BookTook phenomenon turned Netflix romance movie. The film is surprisingly well shot, retains a heartfelt sensibility throughout, and isn't afraid to embrace its classic fake relationship rom-com influences. It's a touching little high school melodrama that's well worth a watch for anyone who even remotely enjoyed "The Love Hypothesis."

#3597. Republicans in Washington Watch The Midterms Wipeout as Trump Deflects Blame

It’s not easy to throw a party in Washington on election night when your side is bracing for a wipeout. But at Butterworth’s, the French bistro that has been a hub of MAGA Washington in Trump’s second term, the DC Republicans were intent on trying. Women in business casual and men in the Republican Party uniform—blue suits, white shirts, and red ties taut to the collar—drank specialty cocktails including “The Elephant in the Room” and “The Senate Majority Martini.” The bar may have been busy, but the mood was precarious. As Dua Lipa blasted from the speakers inside, a man on a smoke break out on the street took big gulps of a pint of lager and stared down at his phone. “Darline Graham just plummeted on Polymarket,” he said, exhaling from his cigarette. “I hate my fucking life right now. Everything just sucks. Jesus Christ we’re gonna lose it all.” A car drove past Butterworth’s with the windows down. A woman leaning out of an open window screamed, “Oh yeah, Democrats!”

Inside, at first, the mood was upbeat. It was early enough that the rising of the blue tide had yet to inspire fear. To an extent. A man waiting for drinks at the bar monitored the results in Florida, one of the few bright spots for Republicans. When informed that Senate candidate Ken Paxton and incumbent Governor Greg Abbott were down bad in Texas, he clutched his head dramatically. “Oh my god! I just got here. I need to go home.” He looked at his phone in anguish. Within minutes, he darted for the door. A White House staffer wearing a red hat emblazoned with “45/47” on the side and “WINNING” on the front made the rounds. “Optimistic? I was a lot more earlier,” he said. “If we lose Texas it’s a catastrophe.” Minutes later, Decision Desk called Texas for James Talarico, the first Democrat to be elected to the Senate in the Lone Star State since 1988.

As Ella Langley’s “Choosin’ Texas” blared through the speakers, two men at the bar lamented the cruel irony of the song playing as Ken Paxton, Talarico’s Republican challenger, saw his numbers plummet.

“I’m not trying to crash out,” said one of the men, a Republican organizer of the party. “But we nominated HITLER with DOWN SYNDROME. And guess what!? He lost! He lost! And now we lose a Supreme Court Justice. It is a fucking disaster.”

The mood at Paxton's watch party down in Dallas was not upbeat.

It was a fucking disaster indeed. Republicans lost almost every Senate seat that mattered, with the small consolation of Florida quickly washed away by the titanic loss of South Carolina. Trump had spent the election telling voters, “Pretend that I’m on the ballot.” By all measures, they had. By 10:40 p.m., Trump offered his verdict on the night: “I wasn’t on the Ballot and if I was, we would have won IN A LANDSLIDE! Thank you for your attention to this matter.”

Trump only has himself to blame for the Republican wipeout. The executive decisions that have defined his second administration were like something cooked up in #Resistance Laboratories to alienate the vast majority of Americans from his political project. The candidates he backed in these midterm elections, against the wishes of the Republican establishment, are those that wiped out the hardest. Darline Graham, the political neophyte sister of the late Senator Lindsey Graham, lost to Democrat Annie Andrews in South Carolina. Paxton, the scandal-plagued Texas attorney general whom Trump backed in the primary against incumbent Sen. John Cornyn, lost to young Democrat James Talarico.

“We got SMOKED. BIGLY,” one source close to Trump texted me. “He’s not the kingmaker he was, or still thinks he is. This is a referendum on him.”

In the 1994 midterms, when Bill Clinton’s presidency was bludgeoned half to death by the Newt Gingrich revolution, The New Yorker’s Michael Kelly described the punch drunk shock inside the White House. “No one can be expected to grasp immediately the full implications of being struck between the eyes by a two-by-four,” he wrote in the wake of the Gingrichian curb stomp, “so it was not surprising that the initial White House response to what had happened, and why it had happened, contained an element of stunned denial.”

The train that flattened Trump and Republicans this year had been barreling down the track for some time. No one could claim to be blindsided. Never in history has a party tethered itself so helplessly to one man, much less such a historically unpopular one. In December of last year, The Washington Post reported that Vice President JD Vance invited a conservative pollster to the White House to deliver an urgent message to the president: Americans don’t feel like you are fighting for them, Mark Mitchell of Rasmussen Reports explained as Trump ate a crab cake lunch. Mitchell urged him to focus on a message of “pragmatic economic populism.”

Trump ignored all that. Soon after the meeting, he started a war with Iran that triggered a global energy shock and by one study’s estimate has cost the average American household $2,000. “The Iran War is the greatest political blunder in the last two decades at least,” pro-Trump pundit Matt Walsh wrote on X. “A catastrophically stupid decision. An unforgivable betrayal of America First principles.”

A year after the calamity he dubbed “Liberation Day,” Trump conjured up a new plot to liberate Americans from economic security: A trade war with Canada that battered states in the upper Midwest that Republicans needed to hold the Senate. All the while, the president dismissed concerns about the cost of living in his public statements. He referred to “affordability” as a hoax, and fixated on lavish renovation projects, like the $600 million ballroom and the messy renovation of the Lincoln Memorial Reflecting Pool.

The pool, of all things, ended up anchoring Trump’s closing argument. In a press conference held there on Monday, Trump spent more than 20 minutes regaling reporters with war stories from his summer campaign against algae. “They’re brand new pipes put in, and the pipes being very important in terms of the algae and other things,” he said sternly, brandishing a posterboard with photos of the pool base. The next day, gasoline and diesel prices hit their highest national average in history. The president’s approval ratings sat firmly at a record bottom. “Trump simply doesn’t care,” said the source close to Trump.

The scene at soon-to-be House Speaker Hakeem Jeffries's watch party was starkly different.

The White House line on these elections is that Trump did all he could to help the party, holding a blitz of rallies in the run-up to Election Day and deploying $300 million of his sizable MAGA Inc. war chest to boost Republican candidates. The money may have helped, but it isn’t clear that the rallying did. Trump’s unpopularity is now seismic, and there’s a growing feeling that his movement is, after a decade of dominating the frontal lobe of the American mind, petering out. Even the president’s very generous offer to every American—$5,000 each if Republicans held both chambers of Congress—didn’t seem to sway our particularly plutomanic populace. Seventy percent of Americans, according to one poll, said they didn’t believe they would ever receive the money.

Trump’s approval among young men, a key voting bloc that ensured his return to power, has plummeted, and popular podcasters who cater to a younger audience have abandoned him. CNN’s exit poll on election day found Democrats won young white men by 17 points, two years after Trump won the same group by 28 points. “We all have to move to Florida,” said a dejected young Republican wearing a tie covered in elephants at Butterworth’s. “It’s a disaster.” Doja Cat’s “Paint the Town Red” was blasting.

Around 20 minutes north, at Metrobar, a few hundred Democrats assembled in the garden for a victory party. Emerging from a taxi, I was met with the roar of the crowd. NBC News had just announced that Democrats had won the Senate. As Steve Kornacki broke down the results from Ohio on a Jumbotron erected in the garden of the bar, the crowd chanted “USA!”

Michelle Meoh, a young Democratic volunteer, told me the night had gone “extremely well” for her party. “Basically every race, even races that I hadn’t thought would go in our favor, were wins.” What does she want Democrats to do with their newfound power? “I guess to show that we’re worthy of the trust that the voters are placing in us. I want us to prove that we’re tapped into the feelings of ordinary Americans and that we really do feel their pain. And that we don’t take that support for granted.”

Two burly men embraced. “Susan Collins is fucking gone!” one shouted.

I made my way to the exit as the hysterical celebrations died down and Kornacki on the Jumbotron read the latest results in Michigan, where Democrat Abdul El-Sayed held a narrow lead over Republican Mike Rogers. “How am I feeling!?” asked a visibly overserved woman. I hadn’t asked. “FUCKING GREAT!”

#3596. The Legend of Zelda: Ocarina of Time Is Still Perfect on Switch 2 | Review

Nintendo’s excellent Switch 2 remake recaptures the soul of a masterpiece

Somewhere among all its gods and ghosts, The Legend of Zelda: Ocarina of Time draws its true power from its human center: a familiar story about growing up and returning home after a long absence.

As the time-afflicted Link comes to learn in the seminal Nintendo 64 classic, a lot can change in seven years. Shifting political struggles leave a neighborhood in total disrepair. That one local eccentric he came to love is nowhere to be seen. There’s a Starbucks — or an archery range, I mean — in town now. Seriously? But underneath the jarring changes that taunt your memory, you know that the place that you love is still there. You can feel its heart beat when you plant yourself in the shade of that tall tree you played around as a kid.

It’s what makes the concept of an Ocarina of Time remake so challenging, but impossible to resist. How fitting — fated even, written in stars and ancient code — to bring generations of adventurers back to the sprawling field where they first learned to run. Like your hometown, a game as foundational as this is perhaps meant to be revisited throughout a lifetime rather than locked away in your long-term memory.

Nintendo doesn’t squander the opportunity for a meaningful homecoming in its lovingly crafted Switch 2 remake. The timeless classic is still a joy to reappraise in its dazzling new form, even if some of its modern developments might send protective fans marching to town hall. Yes, there’s a Starbucks where that quaint café used to be now, but Ocarina of Time’s soul still shines bright enough to guide you home.

One part faithful remake and one part modern retelling, the new version of Ocarina of Time is bound to take old players off guard in its opening moments. The story is unchanged: After getting paired with a fairy, Navi, for the first time, a young Link gets swept into a kingdom-trotting quest to save Hyrule from the nefarious Ganondorf. The sequence of events is unchanged from the original, but the presentation is very different. The Switch 2 remake leans into the fairy tale nature of the original game with storybook narration that clearly lays out the “legend” being told. It’s a smart bit of narrative framing, emphasizing that Ocarina of Time is a story meant to be passed down and retold like a fable.

What’s less successful, at least initially, is fully-voiced new dialogue that replaces the comparatively sparse text boxes of the original game, which featured no voice acting outside of a few stray grunts. An opening conversation between Navi and the Deku Tree, Hyrule’s guardian spirit, loses its moody texture in a brightly-lit cutscene where a squeaky-voiced Navi lays out all the exposition you need to know. It’s a common struggle that Nintendo faces anytime it tries to give its games a cinematic treatment; the more you scale a game like Star Fox 64 up, the more it starts to look like an Illumination-flavored animated kids movie. It’s no wonder that Nintendo saw enough of itself in the Minions studio to entrust it with Mario.

That change in energy takes some getting used to, as an introductory jaunt through Kokiri Forest teases a remake that has been overly polished to a modern sheen. That opening is more tutorial-heavy now, for instance — and that’s saying a lot considering that Navi is gaming’s original hand-holder. It’s not enough for a Kokiri child to tell you how to use your sword anymore; you now need to perform each action multiple times in a practice session before you’re trusted to explore your first dungeon. Those small changes have a way of stacking up early on, creating a shaky first impression as you learn all the ways an old favorite has changed.

But part of growing up is learning to accept, and even embrace, change. That’s where the remake’s controversial visual overhaul makes a statement. When the game was first revealed with a short teaser, it was met with some immediate disgust from players who feared that Nintendo was trading in its cartoon charm for flat Unreal Engine realism. That snap judgment is destined to age like Lon Lon Milk, because the remake is both highly stylized and stunning in motion. That’s apparent right off the bat when strolling through the dreamy Kokiri Forest, with streaks of light poking through the thick roof of greenery that protects the town. It’s a dreamy and nostalgic sight that sets the right tone for the rest of the adventure, one that has the emotional resonance of dusting off an old picture book you read as a kid.

What’s miraculous is how Nintendo is able to retain the grandeur of the world without scaling its locales up beyond recognition. Hyrule is compact by modern game standards, split into only a few tightly designed areas, but it still feels sweeping here. The open air of Hyrule Field is still breathtaking to take in, emphasized with more detailed grass instead of needless space-filling activities. Lake Hylia is just a round body of water, but the glistening light reflecting off of it makes it feel like a cool, serene getaway. Even Kakariko Village’s graveyard benefits from minor changes, with once low-poly headstones now detailed with embellishments that invite you to pull them to reveal the secrets buried underneath them. The only area that really loses some of its former aura is Hyrule Castle Town, as the pivot to smooth 3D camera controls does away with eerie fixed camera angles that were once so important to selling the village’s eventual decay.

If there’s an issue to take with the visual design, it’s that it can be inconsistent. While the detailed environments look spectacular, they aren’t exactly a match for the smooth character design. Link looks like a porcelain doll in hand-stitched clothing, which is a thematically appropriate choice that once again gets at an old childhood toy feel. It’s just a shame that the world doesn’t have a dollhouse look of its own to suit that style. Maybe that’s what has left fans so split as they see Princess Zelda’s glassy eyes or a hookshot that looks like a clay miniature contrasted against a more natural world.

Throughout Ocarina of Time, anything that felt off at first glance grew on me over time, especially once Link himself grew up in the story’s iconic turning point. The natural swap from a hokey animated cartoon to a Grimm’s fairy tale locks every artistic choice into place. The directed cutscenes become a highlight once Link is having tender musical duets with the mysterious Sheik. The reimagined visuals pay off once you get to see monsters like Redeads and Like Likes in their horrifying new forms, emphasizing Ocarina of Time’s roots as a true horror game. Freshly reorchestrated music makes everything feel more operatic without rewriting melodies that now feel as standard to musical canon as “Ode To Joy” — at least if you grew up humming “Zelda’s Lullaby.”

As jarring as the remake’s clean sheen can feel next to the meaningfully grungy Hyrule of olde, the changes don’t get in the way of what makes Ocarina of Time special. And how special it still is 27 years later!

While much has changed from an aesthetic standpoint, Nintendo is very careful not to adjust much about the adventure outside of handy quality of life tweaks. The addition of a dedicated jump button is an inoffensive touch, and Nintendo makes good use of modern controller layouts to make item swapping more seamless (even if Breath of the Wild’s dreaded horizontal item menu returns here), but the core of the game remains wisely unchanged. You still trek between locations across two ages, clearing elemental-themed dungeons full of monsters and puzzles, and obtaining items that gradually open up the world. It’s a structure that inspired an entire genre of adventure games in 1998, but the Switch 2 remake reaffirms that no game has ever nailed that formula as well as Ocarina of Time.

Upon revisiting the story for the first time in two decades, I came to appreciate so much about a game I thought I had mastered years ago. What immediately stands out about Ocarina of Time next to modern games — even modern Zelda games — is how not a moment feels wasted. Every interaction with a jolly Goron feels meaningful, hand-placed there for a reason. Every side-quest, minigame, or hidden grotto feels bespoke, like it was sculpted to contain one memorable secret. A gaggle of singing frogs perched next to a river, a pair of scarecrows baking in the sun, a diving tank in a mad scientist's house. No two activities feel like the result of designers copying and pasting assets throughout the world just to fill a game with more hour-eating busy work. It stands in proud contrast to modern adventure games that do so much less with so much more.

There was never a dull moment in my 20-hour playthrough, even when I was backtracking across Hyrule Field or up Death Mountain. That’s made possible in part thanks to Ocarina of Time’s fantastic dungeon design. Each one is a perfectly crafted puzzle box that builds unique enemies and challenges around the dungeon’s theme and key items. Navigating twisted hallways in the Forest Temple with your newly-discovered arrows or cutting your way out of an oversized fish belly is always a surprising delight that feels unlike anything you’ve done before. The remake keeps all of those iconic dungeon designs intact, only making some welcome tweaks to the dreaded Water Temple to make it easier to navigate at a glance. I have to wonder if the remake partially exists as a way to wean players off of Breath of the Wild’s open-world freedom, and reignite a desire for something crafted with more precise intent.

What I appreciate most of all is Nintendo’s restraint. It remains confident in the original game’s design, understanding that Hyrule Field doesn’t need to be an immersive playground full of new secrets to evoke an emotional response from new players. There’s a version of this remake in an alternate timeline that goes full Halo: Campaign Evolved, overhauling entire systems to bring an old game in line with its modern peers at the expense of the original game’s ethos. Nintendo largely rejects that, and that choice always pays off.

What a relief it can be to play something like the Ocarina of Time remake and find that the magic is still there.

Look to the remake’s swordplay for a shining example of that. Nintendo could’ve easily followed modern trends and buffed up Link’s move set by giving him a parry, a time-slowing dodge, or more sword-slashing combos to use against spongy enemies with bigger health bars. Instead, the remake sticks to the fundamentals of slashing and dodging to retain the Punch-Out!! style dynamics of Stalfos duels. Rather than aiming for artificial complexity, the remake puts its focus on giving every motion more feedback. When you land a successful slash on an enemy, you’re rewarded with a fireworks flash of particles and a grand slice sound to give your strike power. Even taking out a simple Deku Baba feels like a heroic act. It’s the best that combat has felt in a Zelda game since Wind Waker, and it’s accomplished by reinforcing the foundation instead of pulling up the floorboards.

That’s the strength of the remake at large. Like a good fable passed down through oral tradition, the heart of the tale remains intact; all that’s really changed is the embellishments. Little changes to room layouts in dungeons or exaggerated duels are akin to a storyteller putting their own flourishes on a story to make the fiery Volvagia sound like an even fiercer foe. It’s hard to lose the spirit of Ocarina of Time in that game of creative telephone because every word of it is unforgettable.

The Ocarina of Time remake’s technical excellence has nothing to do with why the adventure is actually special, of course. Revisiting Ocarina of Time feels a bit like plunging the Master Sword back into its pedestal in the Temple of Time; I’m young Link again, back in the peaceful shade of Kokiri Forest where I grew up. Part of that is because the original Ocarina of Time is so closely tied to my hometown; the first video game review I ever read was written by my late friend Andrew for our 4th grade newspaper. To me, Hyrule is a small town in Massachusetts, and I have always felt a fierce loyalty to it because of that.

There’s a sensitivity that comes with that, one that I’m sure many players feel when a meaningful piece of media from their childhood gets reappraised. Over the last two decades, I’ve watched the cultural consensus on Ocarina of Time shift from hailing it as an untouchable classic to a dated N64 game that downright sucks to play. I’ve always felt a protective instinct kick in every time a new player dips into it for the first time and starts complaining about this or that. You weren’t there! You couldn’t understand!

The reality is that I know it’s a defense mechanism. I’ve spent decades now scared to replay Ocarina of Time for fear that I won’t like what I find. Maybe I’ll find that it’s changed too much — or, worse, maybe I’ll find that I have. It’s not dissimilar to how I used to feel about coming back to my hometown after college; there is a discomfort in returning to something that once felt magical only to discover it’s small and mundane in the context of a wider world. Maybe that’s why video game remakes often elicit such strong reactions from players who lament their very existence or gasp at every minor change. It’s easier to protect the past by locking it up in our memories.

So what a relief it can be to play something like the Ocarina of Time remake and find that the magic is still there. Any fear I had that its design would feel antiquated or that a glossy visual overhaul would pave over its plucky spirit disappeared the first time I whistled out the jaunty notes of “Saria’s Song,” like a kid discovering how to make music for the first time by tooting out “Hot Cross Buns” on their dinky recorder. The world of Hyrule felt every bit as big and beautiful as I remembered, so full of discoveries for anyone curious enough to take a wrong turn in the Lost Woods.

A weekly cheat sheet to what you’ll eventually love to play. No buying, no commitment — just saving for later.

I’ve spent the better part of my life hearing people repeat the claim that Ocarina of Time is the greatest game of all time. At some point, it starts to lose all meaning, like saying The Beatles are the best band of all time based solely on an accepted cultural consensus. But the Switch 2 remake reminds us why Ocarina of Time earned that accolade in the first place. Set aside any nostalgia and you’ll still be met with a big-hearted fable set in a lively fantasy world filled with characters who are as familiar as close friends. Link’s journey to adulthood and back again remains a meaningful odyssey about finding the courage to save the soul of the place that lives in your heart — a love that transcends time itself. Every word in my friend’s 4th grade assessment of that epic adventure he connected with as a kid still applies here, and that’s a testament to what could have been a soul-crushing double dip.

That’s the intangible thing that I look for in a remake, something personal that’s hard to articulate in a technical breakdown. Forget the jump button or the smooth framerate: Does The Legend of Zelda: Ocarina of Time still feel like home? Yes, it does, even with a few changes that trigger a “back in my day” reaction. I’m no longer afraid of returning to Hyrule Field and watching the sun set again. I’ve only grown to appreciate the peace and quiet more with age.

The Legend of Zelda: Ocarina of Time will be released Nov. 5 on Nintendo Switch 2. The game was reviewed on Nintendo Switch 2 using a prerelease download code provided by Nintendo. You can find additional information about Polygon’s ethics policy here.
