If there’s one thing I know about Rebecca Yarros and her Fourth Wing books, it’s that she’s not afraid to kill anyone. That was clear from the moment Violet and co. stepped onto the parapet, and it became painfully obvious after our dearly beloved Liam’s death in the first book. Now, as we wait for book four (and the book-to-screen adaptation that just found its Violet and Xaden), the author has revealed that she had plans to kill off more characters than she did in Onyx Storm, and they’ll have to go in the next installment. So, yeah, I’m worried, and I’m really anxious about one specific character.

Listen, I spiral over comments Yarros makes about what’s going to happen in her books even harder than I spiral over updates and fancasts for the Fourth Wing TV show. So, you can imagine the panic I was sent into when she said the following at Iron Flame Night (via domloves2read):

So, I know when I’m in the book, when I start the book, who is going to die. Now, when I wrote Onyx [Storm] I actually was going to kill off other people at the end. And the way I had to shift the plot, and the way I had to shift things so that it wouldn’t feel like other books and it would have its own separate ending, it left some people alive that should not be alive that I will have to take care of in this book.

Yarros went on to clarify that she didn’t tell the audience if said characters “were good or bad,” and she poked fun at them, saying they are prone to jumping to conclusions that often involve her “plotting Ridoc’s murder.” She also said she always knows who she’s going to kill in a battle before she writes it, and she plants seeds ahead of time so we feel connected to those characters.

So, with all that in mind, I’ve realized I’m actually super duper worried about one character who (at least for now) is alive.

I know, I know, I can’t believe I’m writing this either: I really think Rhiannon could die in book four, and maybe Yarros had plans to kill her in Onyx Storm. So, let’s walk through why.

I actually got to this conclusion through a weird process of elimination. I was mostly thinking about what characters are either dealing with loose ends or are such a vital part of the story that they can’t die. Think characters potentially involved in the brother mystery, like Bodhi and Garrick, or those involved with Violet’s memory loss, like Imogen. Along with that, characters like Aaric are so powerful that it feels like they have a greater purpose to serve.

Plus, with the death of Violet’s mom, I don’t think Brennan or Mira will go (yet). I also don't think Dain or Sloane will die, considering their seemingly budding relationship. Then, just from a vibes perspective, I don’t think Ridoc will die (yet). And Swayer has already been through too much with going through first year twice and losing his leg.

Through that process, considering whose death would hurt Violet the most and just thinking about what’s happened in the first three books, I landed on Rhiannon as the character who was maybe going to die in Onyx Storm.

Other than Xaden and her siblings, I think Rhi’s death would hit Violet the hardest since she’s her best friend.

Now, adding to all that, a brutal Fourth Wing parallel led me to this conclusion, too. Think about it, of all the people in Violet’s crew, Rhi is probably the best of the bunch. She’s a natural leader, she was born to be a rider, and she’s simply a very good person. You know who else was near-perfect and all those things? Liam. And he died toward the end of Fourth Wing.

Yarros specifically said she didn’t kill a character in Onyx Storm because she didn’t want it to feel like the end of other books. If Rhi had died, it could have felt a whole lot like what happened to Liam. It would hurt Violet in a very similar way, and it would be the death of another hero, a good one, in this story.

So, yes, going into book four, I’m very worried for Rhiannon. However, for now, I’m going to choose to be very happy that she’s still alive and will live to see another page (for now).

#3594. How To Watch Other Mommy At Home

This has been a great year for horror, from the monumental successes of "Backrooms" and "Obsession," to more high profile favorites like "The End of Oak Street" and "Resident Evil." We've seen independent productions make waves, established filmmakers making their comebacks, and much more. There have also been plenty of lackluster horror movies with just enough interesting ideas to strike a chord with audiences.

Case in point, "Other Mommy," a pretty okay horror film that features Jessica Chastain doing her best Pennywise. That's it, that's the whole movie. Adapting Josh Malerman's novel "Incidents Around the House," Rob Savage helms a stylish horror film that is carried entirely by Jessica Chastain's unhinged performance and a fair amount of violence and spooky stuff.

In spite of less than stellar reviews, "Other Mommy" was a hit with audiences. The movie rose above its abysmal Rotten Tomatoes and CinemaScore evaluation, audiences showed up to theaters, and "Other Mommy" became a box office hit. It's a testament to the marketing department and the trailers for the movie, which hooked audiences on the premise of Savage's film long before the reviews dropped.

Now that Halloween has passed, it's slim pickings for horror at the box office. The good news is that all the horror films released before Halloween are going to start being released on home video soon. Universal Pictures Home Entertainment has announced that "Other Mommy" will release on digital platforms November 10, 2026 with a Blu-ray release expected later, on December 29, 2026.

One of the more intriguing and also confounding aspects of "Other Mommy" is its titular character, whose strange powers seem like Pennywise, Freddy Krueger, and a whole bunch of nightmares combined. It makes her a bit convoluted, sure, but also one of the most exciting horror villains in a while.

It remains to be seen if "Other Mommy" will warrant a sequel, or if Jessica Chastain would return to deliver more horrors. In the meantime, however, you can watch more than what was in theaters, because "Other Mommy" is bringing deleted scenes and other bonus features when it hits home video.

Jessica Chastain stars in a terrifying trip into the darkening world of a young girl, Bela, who forms a relationship with a disturbing entity in her home who looks uncannily like her own mother. 'Other Mommy' proves to be more than a mere figment of the girl's imagination as she becomes a sinister, manipulative presence determined to tear apart Bela's family.

The following bonus content is available when you purchase "Other Mommy" at participating retailers.

EFFECTING FEAR: An exploration of the ways special effects complemented each other to amplify the relentless tension, suspense, and fear driving the story.

A FAMILY IN PIECES: A behind-the-scenes look at the fractured family at the heart of the film and the standout performances that bring them to life.

BREAKING RULES WITH OTHER MOMMY: Cast and filmmakers discuss subverting horror tropes through Bela's perspective and disrupting the expected cadence of the genre.

#3593. You Should Enable This Chrome Feature That Flags Suspicious Websites

In addition to Lifehacker, her work has been featured on Wirecutter, Tom’s Guide, and ZDNET. Emily has also worked as a travel guide around the U.S. and as a content editor. She has a masters in social work and is a licensed therapist in Utah.

If you use Google Chrome, you can turn on a new safety feature that will warn you if you navigate to a suspicious website that looks like others already known for malicious behavior. The alerts are part of Enhanced Protection mode in Chrome's Safe Browsing, which checks your activity against potentially harmful sites and warns you if you're at risk of encountering malware, phishing, intrusive ads, or social engineering attacks.

Most internet users are familiar with the full-page alerts that appear if you navigate to a site that's known to be malicious. These red "dangerous site" warnings indicate a high risk of harm to the user and can't really be ignored since they take up the entire screen and urge you to go back to safety.

The new "suspicious site" alerts indicate possible risk of harm based on patterns consistent with other known malicious sites. This means that Google isn't as confident that the website is actually dangerous, but it looks a lot like others that are spreading malware or running phishing scams. These suspicious site warnings are smaller pop-ups with the text "This site doesn't seem right" and two button options: Mark as safe or Back to safety. The different colors, text, and formatting make it easy for users to distinguish between what Google deems dangerous versus suspicious.

Safe Browsing in Chrome has three options: standard protection, enhanced protection, and no protection at all (which isn't recommended). Standard protection checks your browsing activity, extensions, and downloads against Google's list of unsafe sites, which is updated periodically. By contrast, enhanced protection works in real time and uses AI analysis. Note that enhanced protection does require you to share more information about your activity to Google, and the data are linked to your Google Account.

#3591. TV Legend Ed Asner Appeared In This Classic '60s John Wayne Western

We may receive a commission on purchases made from links.

In 1966, John Wayne visited Vietnam and began formulating one of his biggest on-screen blunders, "The Green Berets." Before he could get around to making the one John Wayne film that Roger Ebert called "cruel and dishonest," however, he had another couple Westerns to get through. "El Dorado" was the first. It premiered in the United States in June 1967, exactly one year after Wayne made the rounds in IndoChina. At the time, the Duke was becoming increasingly irrelevant as the Western genre began its shift into the revisionist age. Nonetheless, "El Dorado," which saw Wayne reunited with his frequent directorial collaborator Howard Hawks, became a success. It also remains the only film to feature Wayne and Ed Asner, who at the time was just three years away from debuting in his best-known role as Lou Grant on "The Mary Tyler Moore Show."

Asner began acting in the mid-1950s. He made his TV debut in 1957 on "Studio One" and his film debut in 1962, appearing alongside Elvis Presley in "Kid Galahad." Oddly enough, he didn't appear in a Western film until 1966 when he joined Wayne in "El Dorado," which considering any working actor of the 1960s was bound to wind up in a Western at some point is surprising.

Asner did, however, appear in some classic Western TV shows, guesting on "Outlaws" in 1962 and "The Virginian" the following year. He also appeared in two episodes of "Gunsmoke" and in 1965 joined Robert Horton for a single installment of "A Man Called Shenandoah." When he set foot on the "El Dorado" set, then, while he hadn't yet appeared in a big screen Western, he was well acquainted with Hollywood's vision of the Old West. Now all he had to do was face down John Wayne.

"El Dorado" is directed and produced by Howard Hawks. His frequent collaborator Leigh Brackett wrote the script, which she considered to be her finest work. In Todd McCarthy's "Howard Hawks: The Grey Fox of Hollywood," Brackett is quoted as having said, "I wrote the best script I have ever written and Howard liked it, the studio liked it, Wayne liked it, and I was delighted." Unfortunately for her, Hawks wanted to play things a little safer by essentially remaking "Rio Bravo," the 1959 John Wayne-led Western that launched an unofficial trilogy.

"Rio Bravo" was the result of Hawks and Wayne's hatred for "High Noon," which featured a sheriff too scared to confront the antagonists alone. Hawks and Wayne's retort featured a more muscular hero who had no problem facing evil solo. It proved so successful and seemingly suited Hawks' sensibility so well he essentially remade it twice, once with "El Dorado" and again with 1970's "Rio Lobo" — both of which starred the Duke. The former was a more lighthearted movie, however, with James Caan as John Wayne's sidekick providing much of the comic relief due to his poor aim.

Otherwise, "El Dorado" starred Robert Mitchum, the film noir legend who was also no stranger to the Western, as the alcoholic sheriff of the titular town, J.P. Harrah. His old pal, gunfighter Cole Thornton (Wayne), arrives in El Dorado after being been hired by local tycoon Bart Jason (Ed Asner) to drive the poor MacDonald family off their land so he can claim it for himself. After talking to Harrah, however, Thornton refuses Jason's offer, and things don't exactly go smoothly.

Ed Asner — who passed away in 2021 at the age of 91 — played the villain of "El Dorado." It must have been intimidating for the early-career Asner, then in his mid-30s, to have to square up to John Wayne. "I found myself going into uncharted territory," he told Jake's Takes in 2021. "I regarded myself as a big liberal. I hadn't been proved yet as a liberal, but a big liberal, and here I was going against one of the biggest reactionaries of the times. I didn't know how I'd be treated." According to Asner he was "roasted on the first day" but "passed the roast test" and ultimately found the Duke to be "a nice reasonable fellow."

It probably helped that "El Dorado" was a success. Roger Ebert called it "the most entertaining Western to turn up this year" and according to "Howard Hawks: The Grey Fox of Hollywood," the film did "outstanding business" following its 1966 debut in Japan. It then went on to generate "rentals of $6 million on box office receipts of $12 million," which ultimately made it the 12th biggest picture of 1967. Not bad for Asner's first big screen Western.

Ironically, considering his initial collaboration with Wayne was so amiable, the very series that made Asner a star, "The Mary Tyler Moore Show," came to represent a form of TV entertainment that heralded the end of the TV Western as a result of the "rural purge." Not that Wayne himself was affected, but the more urban-focused TV slate of the 1970s was one major signifier that the world was moving on from the days when Wayne and his fellow Western heroes proudly rode the plains.

I can't imagine what it feels like to learn you've been cast as one of the most recognizable characters in the Harry Potter franchise, especially when you're following in the footsteps of the late Alan Rickman. That's exactly the position Paapa Essiedu found himself in when he landed the role of Severus Snape in HBO's upcoming book-to-screen series adaptation. While you'd expect some excitement after getting that phone call, the actor admitted his celebration lasted about as long as it takes to say "Expelliarmus" before reality came crashing down.

With the highly anticipated series arriving on the 2026 TV premiere schedule this Christmas, Essiedu recently spoke with People at the Time100 Next Gala about taking on the iconic Potions professor. The 36-year-old actor admitted he initially experienced "five to 10 seconds" of excitement when he found out he'd gotten the part. Then he remembered that accepting the job meant actually having to play Snape, and his reaction was wonderfully blunt:

It's like, wow, what an honor, what a privilege. And then there's a kind of crushing kind of reality of the reality of what is to come. 'Oh, fuck. I've got to do it now.'

I love how quickly that went from being honored to realizing he'd signed himself up for one heck of a challenge. Honestly, I get it. Rickman's portrayal of Snape remains one of the most beloved performances in the original eight-film franchise. His delivery, intimidating presence and ability to make even the simplest lines sound vaguely threatening helped turn the character into a fan favorite.

Those are some pretty big shoes to fill, and Essiedu knows it. He's already faced considerable backlash over his casting, including racist abuse and death threats from people upset about the decision. The actor previously addressed those reactions, explaining that he understood there would be criticism but remained committed to the role.

Still, despite the pressure surrounding the production, Essiedu seems genuinely excited about the experience. During the same interview, he credited the people working alongside him for making the enormous responsibility feel manageable:

It's a beautiful thing. And with something like this, it's also so much about the people that you're collaborating with, and I feel so much trust and endeavor in the people who I'm standing alongside on this journey. There's a lot of feelings, but they're all good.

That confidence extends to the show's young stars, too. Essiedu had particularly kind things to say about Dominic McLaughlin, Alastair Stout and Arabella Stanton, who are taking over the roles of Harry Potter, Ron Weasley and Hermione Granger, respectively.

Essiedu acknowledged the tremendous responsibility the three child actors carry, especially considering how closely audiences associate the characters with Daniel Radcliffe, Rupert Grint, and Emma Watson. He described his young co-stars as mature, hardworking performers and said he couldn't wait for audiences to see what they've accomplished.

I think that's worth remembering as we approach the premiere. Much of the conversation surrounding HBO's new Harry Potter adaptation has understandably focused on how the cast will compare to the original movies. But these actors also have the chance to explore the characters across an entire television series, potentially giving them room to develop aspects of the books that the films couldn't fit.

The eight-episode first season, Harry Potter and the Philosopher's Stone, premieres Dec. 25 on HBO and streams with an HBO Max subscription. John Lithgow will play Albus Dumbledore, Janet McTeer takes over as Minerva McGonagall, and Nick Frost steps into Hagrid's enormous boots.

As for Paapa Essiedu, I have to appreciate his willingness to admit that the thrill of getting the job wore off almost immediately. Hopefully, once audiences finally see him teaching Potions at Hogwarts, he'll get to enjoy a little more than 10 seconds of excitement.

Ryan graduated from Missouri State University with a BA in English/Creative Writing. An expert in all things horror, Ryan enjoys covering a wide variety of topics. He's also a lifelong comic book fan and an avid watcher of Game of Thrones and House of the Dragon.

#3589. What to Wear When Exercising Outdoors, Based on How Cold It Is

I fell in love with cold weather running while I was training for a spring marathon. It wasn’t a choice at first: Some weeks, the weather was bad for days on end, and if I stayed home, I would fall behind in my training. Everybody else in my training group was braving the elements, so I did too—with no regrets.

I got to run on quiet mornings while snow was softly falling. I signed up for a winter race that herded finishers into a heated barn for hot chocolate and soup. I set a personal record at a spring race, during which I pushed myself hard without breaking a sweat. I now find it sad when somebody tells me they’re afraid of running in the cold, or that they would run in the winter but don’t know what to wear.

No, cold weather doesn’t have to stop you from running, but getting dressed can be a puzzle: How do you keep from freezing your butt off at first and avoid overheating once you start to sweat? Fortunately, it isn’t as tough as it looks. With the right gear, your fingers and ears can stay toasty while you jog through a winter wonderland. Below, I’ll give you a temperature-by-temperature running cheat sheet, and then dive into the specifics on how to buy the best socks, shirts, and more.

When I get dressed to run in winter, I take a look at the “feels like” temperature, not the actual high or low. I also make sure to check the weather for the time I’ll go running, not for the whole day. It doesn’t matter how warm it will be at 2 p.m. if my run will be happening at 6 a.m., before the sun is up. I use the Carrot Weather app, but any app that gives you hourly feels-like temps will work just fine.

Next, use the 20-degree rule. Imagine that the temperature is 20 degrees (Fahrenheit) warmer than it really is. What would you wear then? Here's an example: if it’s 50 degrees out, you should dress as if it were 70: in a T-shirt and shorts, most likely. If it’s 30 degrees, you’d dress as if it were 50: long pants and maybe a light jacket. Get the idea?

Everybody has their own preferences. Some people wear shorts even when it’s snowing, while others will pop a beanie on as soon as there’s a detectable chill in the air. I’m a pretty middle-of-the-road runner when it comes to keeping warm, so here’s what I wear at each “feels like” temperature, starting with warmer weather and working our way colder. I'll give a guide to each type of garment or accessory at the end.

At 50+ degrees Fahrenheit, I’m wearing basically the same things I would for a summer run.

Head and hands: Nothing special. No gloves and no hat, unless it’s a baseball cap to shade my eyes from the sun.

We’re starting to feel the first bit of a chill. This is where I may start bringing gloves, although they’ll probably get stuffed into a pocket by the end of the run. Remember, with the 20-degree rule, it will feel like 60 degrees by the time you're warmed up.

Bottoms: Leggings, lightweight long pants, or shorts.

Top: Something with long sleeves, but ideally made of thin material (think long-sleeved T-shirt, not a full-on sweatshirt or jacket). If you wore a sun shirt in the summer, that's a good layering option for these cool temps. I like my REI Sahara Shade hoodie here, but any long sleeve will do. If you run fall and winter races, you'll probably be handed a free long-sleeved version at some point.

Hands: I usually just pull my shirt's sleeves over my hands, but you could wear knit gloves if you want. Consider something like Flipmits for an intermediate option (they can be folded down into a wrist cuff when your hands warm up).

Head: A headband if you need protection for your ears.

You may see a few snowflakes drifting down, but don’t bundle up in a snowsuit. Once you’re warmed up, it will only feel like 50 degrees—so go for something in “light jacket” territory.

Bottoms: Leggings or running tights. The fleece-lined kind can be nice. (I have these.)

Top: You’ll want some kind of jacket or sweatshirt. A lightweight, reflective rain jacket is great here, or just throw on a regular hoodie over your T-shirt. (I go with cotton sweats in dry weather or light snow, but I'd go for synthetics or wool if there's rain or sleet.)

Hands: Definitely wear gloves. The cheap knit ones are usually good enough, but consider treating yourself to a nice pair of running gloves.

Head: Your choice of hat or headband; I’d stick with the headband.

Feet: This is around the temperature you may start to want warmer socks. That goes double if snow is in play: snow that falls onto your shoes will work its way through the mesh, melt, and make your feet wet. Wool is a good material here, so consider something like these from Smartwool.

This is where I’ll officially say it’s “cold.” Whatever warm-weather gear you were getting away with at warmer temps, you’ll probably have to swap it out now. Shorts people will break out their long pants. Headband people will wear a real hat.

Bottoms: Leggings and shorts. I don’t care if you think it looks goofy to wear both; this is an A+ hack. Or try a puffer skirt.

Top: It’s definitely jacket weather. Rather than getting a warmer jacket, I like to wear the same light jacket as I did at 30 degrees, but this time with a long-sleeved fleece or wool base layer underneath.

Hands: Real gloves, please. You can keep wearing your little knit gloves if you’re able to tuck your hands inside your jacket sleeves, or if you have a pair of mittens to wear over top; otherwise, get windproof gloves.

Head: A hat, and maybe also a buff for your nose and mouth. (If you have any cloth masks still hanging around from the early COVID days, they’re perfect for cold weather runs.)

Feet: Warm socks for sure. If you’ll be doing a lot of running in these temperatures, you may want shoes that are specialized for the elements. Look for ones with Gore-Tex uppers, like the Brooks Ghost GTX.

This is where I tap out. If a run is just barely in the teens, I’ll make do with the 20-degree items I mentioned above, adding an extra layer wherever needed. But if that isn't enough, I opt for the treadmill. You certainly can run in this weather if you are determined. You’ll want windproof everything, some kind of face covering, and you may need eye protection such as goggles.

Whenever the weather gets to your own personal “too cold” temperature, remember that you still have options. The early afternoon is often the warmest part of the day, so a run may be tolerable then. There’s also no shame in using a treadmill (even if you have to join a cheap gym for this reason alone).

Everybody has different preferences, and with practice you’ll figure out if you’re the kind of person who wears three shirts before it hits freezing or the type to run through the snow in shorts. But this should give you a starting point when you head out for your first (or next) cold weather run.

As you continue on your cold-weather running journey, you may need to buy some new gear or repurpose things from elsewhere in your closet. And yes, the first few minutes of your run will feel chilly. But if you’re wearing the right shoes and clothes (and planning routes with a few extra factors in mind, which I’ll discuss below), winter running is not just feasible; it’s actually fun. So here are the items you may want to consider.

Your feet need to be warm and, if possible, dry. Warm socks go without saying, but there are some extra considerations when you’re picking socks to run in. Wool socks are ideal because they keep your feet warm even when they get wet. You may not think of winter as a wet time, but any snow that meets up with your body heat will turn into water. If you don’t have wool socks, synthetic wicking fabrics are a good second choice. Cotton is a no-no

First, the socks have to be able to fit into your shoes. If you’ve been running in super thin cotton or synthetic socks all summer, thick socks may not fit. Smartwool run socks are available in a thin version that can fit no problem—but in colder weather you’ll want some thickness for extra warmth. That thickness, in turn, may mean that your winter running shoes need to be roomier than the shoes you wear in summer. If you’re buying a new pair, make sure to try them on with the type of socks you intend to run in.

If your warm socks fit, you can make do with the same shoes you wore in the summer. Your feet will stay dry if the weather is dry and you stay out of puddles. If you encounter snow and slush, though, your feet will have to endure warm-but-wet conditions for the rest of your run. That can be okay for short runs, but for serious winter running, consider upgrading your shoes.

Some running shoes are available with water-resistant uppers. This level of water resistance will keep stray snowflakes out of your socks, but it isn’t reliable if you’ll be stepping in slush puddles. In that case, you’ll want something more waterproof, like Gore-Tex shoes, many of which are made for running trails.

If you expect to run on a lot of ice or packed snow, especially on trails, spikes can give you a little extra grip.

Yaktrax makes a rubber harness that stretches to fit your shoe, with steel coils and small spikes, for about $40.

Microspikes are a notch up from there, costing around $90 for what look like a miniature version of the chains you’d put on car tires.

And if you’re really dedicated—and are seeking a purpose-built pair of snow shoes—you can attach individual spikes: either these traction spikes from IceSpike, or via a DIY approach using sheet metal screws. (There’s a tutorial here.)

The versions that include rubber, like Yaktrax, can wear out quickly on pavement, so it’s best to save these for runs on trails or on unplowed paths. You’ll also want to be careful about the fit. I tried a pair that were similar to Yaktrax, but they were a tad too big. Shortly into my run, I found that the rubber stretched enough to pull the front set of spikes up over the top of my shoe. I've since gotten better-fitting ones, and they work great.

Spikes and specialized shoes help you go more places, in worse weather—but remember that they’re not required to just head out on a chilly day. Regular shoes are fine if the weather is cold but dry, or if you’re willing to put up with a little moisture.

I actually love when the weather gets cold enough that I need a jacket, because then I get to wear something that gives me extra pockets! Stick with thin jackets that have some room inside. By the time temps dip into the 20s or below, you’ll be doing some serious layering: for example, an undershirt, a long-sleeved warm layer, and a jacket. A great option for that warm layer is a wool base layer like this one. (Don’t worry, it’s not itchy.) If you can’t wear wool, a synthetic fleece is a good alternative.

Before you run out to buy all new clothes, experiment with what’s in your closet. Try repurposing a thin sweater, for example. Some people would never wear cotton for running (it can be cold when wet), but I wear it as my undershirt layer and have lived to tell the tale. Just make sure to shower or change after your run, so you aren't sitting around in cold, wet clothes.

The jacket is the most important layer. You can grab a sweatshirt in a pinch, but to be really well-equipped for nasty weather, you’ll want a jacket that is windproof and water-resistant. Jackets made for running are lightweight, for layering. Consider ones that are visible at night, with bright colors and reflective areas, and that come with zippered pockets.

Once it’s too cold for shorts, you’ll want to start layering your bottoms, too. Loose pants let cold air in, which is why leggings or “running tights” like these are standard winter wear for all genders. Running tights come in different thicknesses; go for something fleece-lined for your coldest runs, or layer two pairs.

You need to keep your ears warm, but don’t reach for a winter hat right away: an ear warmer or headband can cover your ears while still letting heat escape from the top of your head. And if anything is falling from the sky (say, snow), a baseball cap will keep it out of your eyes.

Fleece or knit hats are great for cold enough days, of course. The dividing line between earwarmer weather and hat weather is a personal one, and depends on whether you’re overheating. If you’re wearing a hat but sweating into your base layers, the hat is probably overkill.

Gloves, however, are essential. I keep a pair of cheap knit gloves in my jacket pockets, but windy or very cold days call for something stronger. You can layer gloves; I find gloves under mittens work well. You can also get windproof insulated gloves, which are warmer than any number of layers of holey knit gloves.

Your face will freeze on windy or very cold days, so this is where your old stash of pandemic face masks really shines. Consider a balaclava or even a fleece-lined bandana. A neck gaiter stays on better than a scarf if your neck is cold. At this point, every inch of you is covered but your eyes. Sunglasses can take care of that.

#3588. Netflix's Assassin's Creed Live-Action Series Officially Wraps Up Filming

The Assassin's Creed series returns to Rome

Netflix unveiled its plans to make a live-action Assassin's Creed series in 2020. Development only began in 2025 when Halo's screenwriter David Wiener and Roberto Patino came on board. Six years after the announcement of this project, as reported by Matt's Inside Line, filming is complete. It's now time to get it ready for the TV screen as the series enters the post-production phase.

Netflix's live-action series isn't the first attempt to take the Assassin's Creed franchise beyond the world of video games. In 2016, Michael Fassbender entered the Animus as Cal Lynch to access the memories of his ancestor Aguilar de Nerha, a 15th-century assassin from Spain. Unfortunately, the movie was not well-received, scoring a mere 18% on Rotten Tomatoes.

Assassin's Creed fans have traveled all over the world as different members of the Assassin Brotherhood. Netflix will take them back to Rome in its upcoming live-action series, the city where Ezio Auditore fought the Borgia family in the early 16th century in Assassin's Creed: Brotherhood. However, they won't come across one of the series' most beloved characters, as the show will take place in 64 AD, a long time before Ezio Auditore.

Instead, they will find themselves in an ancient Rome ruled by Emperor Nero. According to Netflix, its focal point will be the secret war between two "shadowy factions," — presumably the Templar Order and the Assassin Brotherhood — played out across "pivotal historical events." Beyond that, not much is known about the plot; more is likely to be revealed soon.

Shooting for Assassin's Creed took place in Italy and Bulgaria. The series cast includes Lola Petticrew (Say Nothing), Toby Wallace (Euphoria), Zachary Hart (Black Doves), Laura Marcus (Bad Education), Tanzyn Crawford (A Knight of the Seven Kingdoms), Nabhaan Rizwan (KAOS), and Claes Bang (The Square).

There is still no expected release date for Netflix's Assassin's Creed. Post-production is next, and that is when we can expect a trailer and more details.

#3587. I'm Not A Star Trek Fan – Here's What I Learned After Watching Patrick Stewart's Best TNG Episodes

I love my job and promise I'm qualified to do it, but sometimes, I have to admit that I, as the kids or Taylor Swift might say, don't "know ball." After admitting that I'd never seen "Jurassic Park" or ever sat down and watched "The Mummy," I wrote about the experience of watching these gems for the first time right here at /Film, and across the board, I'm always excited to learn about some new corner of the pop culture world for the first time.

Then my editor asked me to watch "Star Trek."

I need to be exceedingly clear: I don't have any actual beef with the Star Trek universe, but I am a spiteful and deeply stubborn person who has been asked — begged, at times — to watch this show by some of its more passionate fans who have flitted in and out of my life. There came a point where I felt like proving some sort of inane point by not watching this show, even though my refusal to do so affects nobody and nothing anywhere in the world. Then, Sir Patrick Stewart died, and my lead editor asked if he could give me a list of five particularly fun Picard episodes of "Star Trek: The Next Generation" and I could write about them. I said yes, because despite my well-documented spite, I'd like to pay my respects to Stewart's legacy. (A note! "Best of Both Worlds," "Family," and "Chain of Command" were only excluded from this list because they're multi-part episodes.)

Some important context! I've never watched this show before. I don't really know who most of the characters are, nor do I know what's going on at most given moments. So what do I think of these handpicked Picard episodes of "Star Trek: TNG?" Let's see.

I started with "The Measure of a Man," a relatively somber Season 2 episode of "Star Trek: The Next Generation" that involves a legal, ethical, and moral dispute over whether the ship's android guy Data (Brent Spiner) is a sentient being or the property of Starfleet, to be dismantled and studied. The whole thing progresses into a miniature legal drama where Captain Philippa Louvois (Amanda McBroom) has to oversee Data's case and make a declaration one way or another. (Also, I love that this show goes out of its way to remind us, regularly, that Patrick Stewart's Captain Jean-Luc Picard is way hot. Louvois is practically panting at him during most of their scenes.)

"The Measure of a Man" is a relatively somber treatise on what it means to possess a soul, artificial intelligence, and what can and should be sacrificed in the quest for more knowledge, but I really can't stress this enough: it's also the first Star Trek anything I've ever watched. With that in mind, I admittedly didn't follow every single plot beat but instead paid close attention to Stewart's performance, which is, obviously, outstanding. The way he approaches a world where the guy next to him is in full body paint as if it's a Shakespearean drama is incredibly rad, but it also lends some gravity to the entire situation. (Get it? "Gravity." The show's about space! Nevermind.)

As news spread of Stewart's passing, it became quite clear to me that he was a massively important actor for so many people thanks to the Star Trek franchise, and this episode was a perfect first introduction that helped me understand why. How could you not side with the guy arguing to save his friend?

"The Drumhead," the second Patrick Stewart episode of "Star Trek: The Next Generation" that I turned on, is a tiny courtroom drama focused on an explosion on the Starship Enterprise that may or may not have been outright sabotage. After the arrival of retired rear admiral Norah Satie (Jean Simmons), the crew tries to officially get to the bottom of it, as Worf (Michael Dorn), a Klingon dude that I referred to as "the guy in a Chewbacca mask" to tick off one of my Trekkie coworkers for fun, reveals that his hilariously named fellow Klingon J'Dan (Henry Woronicz), is betraying them; it turns out he is, but he didn't cause the explosion.

Satie turns on Picard, angry that he's vehemently defending his own crew — even though the explosion wasn't sabotage at all, as it turns out. The reason that "The Drumhead" ended up on this list is, indisputably, because of Picard's masterful monologue defending himself; Stewart, of course, performs it beautifully and with the solemnity of a soliloquy delivered by Hamlet or Macbeth. (The scene with him and the Klingon whose name is definitely Worf and not Not-Chewbacca is also quite nice.) Again, there's a steadiness to Stewart's performance that's obviously what drew in "Star Trek" fans for decades. Even as you know that Picard is falsely accused, Stewart's real concern and frustration in the moment is palpable, and his moral center remains clear even as he deals with political scapegoating and fear-mongering. That's not just a prescient message for our current times; it's a message that has remained relevant in the decades since Stewart turned in this performance in "The Drumhead," and it's easy to see why Picard is so important to so many.

In this episode, which my editor insists is a must-watch because it shows off Captain Jean-Luc Picard's sillier side — and Patrick Stewart's by extension — Picard is bullied into going on vacation by his colleagues because he won't stop working and just go already. (As a freelance writer, I find this sadly and disturbingly relatable.) Picard finally agrees to go to a planet called Risa when he finds out that Deanna's (Marina Sirtis) mother is coming to visit — I asked around, and apparently, she's a real pain in the butt — and when he gets there, a woman he ultimately learns is named Vash (Jennifer Hetrick) kisses him to try to get away from an enemy. (They do it later, probably crazy style. I don't know what the sexual norms are in the Star Trek universe and am only sort of afraid to ask.)

After that, Vash and Picard have a whole subplot involving some sort of MacGuffin called the Tox Uthat — and a brief borderline kidnapping by that aforementioned Ferengi character Sovak (Max Grodénchik) — and by the end of the episode, Picard goes ahead and destroys the Uthat with the Enterprise's help because I guess it's very dangerous or whatever. I don't know about all that. What I do know is that "Captain's Holiday" is an episode of "TNG" that reminds you that Picard is a hot captain who f***s. In that sense, it's incredibly effective, and I am sorry for how much I objectified Sir Stewart throughout this episode. (No, I'm not.) In all seriousness, though, Stewart took the challenge of this silly, relatively fluffy episode and performed it with the utmost sincerity and wit.

I was given next to no information about "The Inner Light" and the assigned episode that follows (more on that in a second, obviously), and that definitely improved my viewing experience ... because not only do these feel like relatively standalone episodes, they're also both incredible showcases for Patrick Stewart as a performer. After getting hit by some sort of energy beam in a probe on the Enterprise, Jean-Luc Picard wakes up in another universe as a guy named Kamin, who lives with his wife Eline (Margot Rose) on a planet called Kataan. Picard then spends several decades there hanging out with his wife and his friends, raising children, and noticing, all the while, that the sun's radiation will eventually cause widespread drought, something he hopes to prevent despite the government repeatedly telling him that they don't have the technology to prevent it.

Spoilers for this pretty old episode, but when I learned that the whole thing was a series of memories implanted in a probe to show others what life on Kataan was like before it was lost to time, I was pretty shaken! (Also, the fact that 40-odd years only take 25 minutes for Picard is nuts.) All in all, this was the most emotionally resonant episode of "Star Trek: The Next Generation" I watched in this bunch. As I watched Stewart's Kamin try, over the course of years, to save the planet he calls home and protect his loved ones in the process — despite that mission ultimately being doomed — I ended up weirdly hoping that Picard wouldn't return to the ship, only because Kamin seemed so happy and comfortable with his loved ones. Picard was a cultural father figure, and this episode explains why pretty perfectly.

A sort of "Sliding Doors," "A Christmas Carol" episode completed by journey into the Star Trek universe — and yes, I'm talking about "Tapestry." (No, I did not know who John de Lancie's Q was going into this, and I still don't! Sorry!) After Jean-Luc Picard is wounded on a mission — an understatement, considering it's a large sucking chest wound — he's taken something that may or may not be the afterlife where he meets up with Q and is able to revisit a crucial moment in his life, seeing what would happen if he didn't get wounded in a bar fight and receive an artificial heart in the aftermath.

After changing his past and sleeping with his fellow cadet Marta Batanides (J. C. Brandy) — I love that all of these episodes drive the point home that Picard is super popular with the ladies — Picard decides to not fight the alien who stabs him in the heart, only to learn that, without taking that massive risk and nearly dying, he doesn't become the captain of the Enterprise ... but becomes a loser junior officer that nobody really respects. I genuinely did not see the "Picard goes back and gets stabbed" conclusion coming here, but it ends up making a weird amount of sense that he needs to push himself to end up on the correct life path. Once again, Stewart delivers a deeply considered and serious performance as a man grappling with a fork in the road that he actually has the power to change (or not), but this is probably the most complicated look at Picard in this bunch, and Stewart sells that conflict in him throughout every single second. Stewart was one of our finest actors, bar none. Episodes like "Tapestry" prove that handily.

"Star Trek: The Next Generation" is streaming on Paramount+.

#3586. Anker’s New Soundcore Space 2 Headphones Are Already 18% Off

Anker released the noise-cancelling Soundcore Space One headphones a few years ago, and while they were a more budget-friendly alternative to premium models from Bose and Sony, their performance and fit still fell short in several areas. The brand’s updated Soundcore Space 2 headphones are a major upgrade across the board: They’re comfier, have better ANC, and are currently 18% off at $106.49 (originally $129.99), a rare price cut for a still-new release from a popular brand.

Battery life is one of the Soundcore Space 2’s most attractive features: They last up to 50 hours with ANC on and 70 hours with ANC off, and a five-minute charge gives you up to four extra hours. The noise cancellation is strong for the price, blocking out lower-frequency sounds well. Comfort is also a major upgrade from its sparser predecessor, with roomier, more plush memory foam earcups and a padded headband. They’re also travel-friendly, as the earcups rotate and fold.

The Soundcore app allows you to customize EQ and sound presets, giving you added flexibility if you don’t like the default tuning. Instead of touch-sensitive panels, these headphones use conventional buttons, which help prevent accidental commands while adjusting the earcups and are easy to operate. Along with supporting Bluetooth 6.1, they also have a wired-cable option, which isn’t always the case with modern wireless headphones. That said, they don’t support USB-C audio.

If you want over-ear noise-canceling headphones that perform well but don’t have $200 to shell out for a more expensive model, the Anker Soundcore Space 2 headphones are a comfortable, effective, and long-lasting alternative that hover around $100 at the current discounted price.

The process of reading a Christopher Nolan script sounds like a spy thriller.

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

Director Christopher Nolan is the rare unicorn filmmaker who can draw audiences to the theater and bring in the kind of box office numbers that every major movie studio dreams of. Seeing a Nolan movie feels like special event viewing, partly because audiences go see his films with a level of anticipation and excitement that only comes with not having many details and never fully knowing what to expect. And, apparently, the head of Universal had an even more unique experience when Nolan pitched her The Odyssey.

There is a level of secrecy surrounding the Oppenheimer director’s projects, though I'm only now finding out that it carries over to even the Chairman of NBCUniversal Entertainment, Donna Langley. During an interview with Maria Sharapova for Pretty Tough, Universal’s Head Honcho described her experience with reading Christopher Nolan’s adaptation of The Odyssey, which sounds a bit like its own spy thriller. She revealed this about the IMAX savant's method, which includes his wife and producing partner, Emma Thomas:

It’s terrifying…. I’m terrified. Because well the way that Chris does it, or the way he did it on The Odyssey and on Oppenheimer, actually is I was invited over to their house, and I went by myself both occasions. And I didn't know what I was going to read because he doesn't say ahead of time. So you don't know until you're sitting in his library on the couch and he hands you the script. And so it’s a bit intimidating.

Not only does that sound intimidating and terrifying, I can’t imagine what would happen if you had a negative reaction while you were sitting in the home of the filmmaker responsible for writing it. Granted, Nolan is considered to be one of the best filmmakers in the entire world, but even the best at something has a bad day (or project) every once in a while, don’t they?

What strikes me as particularly interesting is the fact that even the biggest of big wigs at Universal doesn’t get to know ahead of time what she’s going to read when she knocks on Nolan’s door. I can’t imagine the level of heightened emotions that one experiences when reading a script from such an expert storyteller for the first time, as everything unfolds. But according to Langley, the pitch experience for this book-to-screen adaptation doesn’t just end there:

Then they leave, and I get a couple of hours to read the script on the same sofa…. And they leave me to it with a cup of tea. And then they leave, and then they come back when I'm finished and we talk about it.

It would probably be hilarious to watch the facial expressions of someone as they read a Christopher Nolan script. Especially someone so high up at the studio, as they realize what kind of budget they’ll need to do the story justice when it’s a story as epic as The Odyssey, one of the biggest blockbusters from the 2026 movie schedule. But knowing that, once finished, the Memento director and Thomas, will return to chat about it seems even more daunting. I wish I could have been a fly on the wall to hear everything that they talked about once Donna Langley finished reading the Odyssey script. Langley added:

It’s a process that — I love it, because it feels very old school, and it’s very intentional. And it makes you pay attention, but it is slightly intimidating. But I think, in the best way possible, it makes me feel very alive.

I have to admit, there is something really cool about making everyone involved with getting a movie into production feel like they’re a part of a private little club of people let in on a secret that the world is not yet ready for. It’s an old-school approach, keeping technology out of it, and that tracks for Nolan, given he doesn't even own a smartphone. However, I understand how exhilarating it must be to be a part of the cool club. And Langley said that the scripts for The Odyssey and Oppenheimer were both brilliant and easy to talk about once she finished them.

The Odyssey's reviews were largely positive from general audiences and critics alike, even if some did point out historical inaccuracies and that side character problem. This historical epic lit up the 2026 box office in a big way, proving that if you release a movie people want to see, they will go see it, likely over and over again. Now, I'm just wondering when Nolan and Thomas might reach out to Langley with another script that would lead them to repeat their unique process.

#3584. Inside LA’s Election Night Parties as DSA-Backed Nithya Raman Threatens to Unseat Karen Bass

Ta-Nehisi Coates (Vanity Fair senior staff writer) recently said that if he reads “another scene from a DSA party in Brooklyn where people are drinking beer, and doing whatever, I’m going to scream.”

But I can report that there were a lot of ecstatic and tipsy socialists in oversized vintage jackets at the DSA election party on the edge of Skid Row in Los Angeles Tuesday night. And boy did these socialists have a lot to celebrate.

Democrats were trouncing Republicans nationally. Democratic Socialists are projected to take at least seven seats in the House, up from two. And in Los Angeles, the DSA’s preferred mayoral candidate, Nithya Raman, appeared poised to unseat Karen Bass. The incumbent Democratic mayor held a less than 1% lead in early returns, but ballots are expected to skew towards the more progressive candidate, Raman.

Karen Bass during an election night event in Los Angeles, November 3, 2026.

“Karen Bass said that she would need to be up 10 points on election night to be comfortable,” one DSA-LA leader told the crowd. He gestured at a graphic showing Bass’s narrow lead and said: “I’m not good at math because I’m gay. Is that 10 points? I don’t think so.” (Bass didn’t actually say that but a pundit on KTLA did say something to that effect.)

At the DSA party, people cheered victories elsewhere in the country by socialists and establishment Democrats alike, but they booed when Bass appeared on television, and laughed when a Fox News commentator suggested the economy was doing well. At one point, organizers put on Hasan Piker’s livestream, and at another they played an AI-generated video showing Raman dancing while wearing a traditional Russian fur hat with ear flaps and a red star. When local TV station KTLA suggested Raman would likely win and Mayor Bass’s face appeared on screen, someone shouted, “Woah get fucked Karen.” It kind of encapsulated the strongest force animating the DSA members I talked to in this mayoral race: their dislike for Mayor Bass. They even called her the c-word on stage: “conservative.”

The DSA and Raman have had something of an on-again, off-again relationship. The organization helped propel her to an upset City Council victory in 2020, only to censure her over disagreements about Israel, housing policy, and the city’s mansion tax. The local DSA chapter endorsed her candidacy late in the campaign but the national organization almost stripped it from her at the 11th hour. The national DSA voted last week to preserve its Los Angeles chapter’s endorsement of Raman by a single vote, after a dispute over her refusal to embrace the movement to boycott Israel.

“I think people here have varying levels of begrudgingness about supporting Raman but I think everyone here voted for her,” said one DSA-LA member at the party who worked on the chapter’s video team and declined to give her name.

Still, the DSA members at the party seemed to think this mayoral race offered another encouraging sign for their organization, even if Raman isn’t quite New York Mayor Zohran Mamdani. She was attacked consistently by her opponents—mainly Spencer Pratt—as a “dangerous” extremist but with the help of the DSA—they said members knocked on more than 110,000 doors this election cycle—she might be the first LA mayoral candidate to defeat an incumbent in over 20 years.

Meanwhile, at the Raman campaign’s official election night party at the Greek Theater in Los Feliz, there weren’t any signs calling to "Tax the Rich" or to implement “Medicare for All,” as there were at the DSA party, but comedian Guy Branum from Apple TV’s Platonic sounded pretty similar to those socialists. He argued that Raman’s coalition reflected a class divide within Hollywood.

“Nithya has way more of entertainment’s middle class,” Branum said, describing workers worried about their next job. And Raman’s husband, television writer Vali Chandrasekaran, understands the industry’s problems firsthand, he argued.

Branum, who hangs with the couple socially, also wanted voters to appreciate one of her less-discussed qualifications. “They lead with the masters in urban planning, and the Harvard, and the MIT,” he said. “But what you really need to see is that she can dance. She really lets her hair loose.” (Vanity Fair did not stick around at the party long enough to verify Raman's dancing skills.)

Raman’s campaign manager, Ian Manheimer, was pretty psyched when he took the stage outside the Greek. “Holy shit! What is good, Los Angeles?” he shouted. Nearly three-quarters of his campaign staff had never worked on a political campaign before, he told the crowd. Regardless, they managed to knock on over 100,000 doors, according to Manheimer.

The campaign’s grassroots operation had apparently become a bit of a competition. Volunteer Leo Blain, 25, told VF he’d knocked on more than 300 doors, putting him near the top of the campaign leaderboard. But the person to beat was Raman’s father, who volunteers said had knocked on more than 1,000. All of that knocking was crucial, especially since Raman didn’t have a lot of institutional support or name recognition. Many of California’s most prominent Democrats stayed on the sidelines, because most of them would do anything to avoid the choice between an establishment incumbent and a rising DSA-endorsed challenger. But their neutrality didn’t necessarily mean indifference. A high-ranking official in Sacramento told me that plenty of state legislators were privately rooting for Bass, who had served as speaker of the California Assembly before heading to Congress.

John, a DSA member who volunteered for Raman after having worked on Tom Steyer’s gubernatorial campaign, expected strong support for Raman among the local socialists, arguing that her independent thinking was a positive.

Raman’s party also included some unlikely converts. Kathleen Jensen, a Toluca Lake resident who previously supported Republican Rick Caruso, told me she considered Raman brilliant and wanted a “doer” in City Hall. Although she said some of her Democrat friends remained uneasy about Raman’s DSA association.

By 10:30 p.m., Bass’s election night party at the Loews Hotel in Hollywood had grown considerably quiet as her supporters began to digest the initial results. But the people who remained were still getting down to Snoop Dogg. The demographic differences between the parties were striking. Raman’s crowd skewed whiter, and more Asian, and the music was more alternative and disco. Bass’s crowd was notably more Black, reflecting the mayor’s decades of relationships in the city’s African American community.

Vaval Victor, 28, a member of Alpha Phi Alpha, the historically Black fraternity with which Bass has worked, remained confident that she would pull through. “She started the LA Black Dems Club in her kitchen,” he said, invoking her long history of organizing. “People are thirsty for hope.”

Bass had spent the campaign defending her record on homelessness, city finances, and last year’s catastrophic fires. Caruso, whom she defeated four years earlier, had swooped in at the end to endorse her, giving some of the city’s more conservative voters permission to support the incumbent. But early election-night returns were not the decisive advantage her campaign hoped for.

For all the divisions this mayoral race exposed, the three parties shared something that had been in short supply among Democrats lately: liberal joy.

Meghan Markle and Prince Harry have been making headlines for a number of reasons as of late but, most notably, the pair have been drawing attention for their recent move. A few months ago, it was reported that the royal couple were planning to move back to the United Kingdom with their two children. The pair eventually did just that and reportedly got there on a private jet that apparently cost them a pretty penny to use. Now, it would seem that while back in the UK, Harry and Markle have just relocated again.

Since being back in the UK, the Duke and Duchess of Sussex – along with children Prince Harry and Princess Lilibet – have reportedly been living with friends in the Cotswolds. More specifically, the brood had taken up residence in what’s been referred to as the “main house” on the property. According to a report from Daily Mail, however, the family is now moving from that house to what’s simply described as a “property on the estate.” Reps for the royals have not provided any concrete information on the matter.

Recent rumors have suggested that Markle and Harry have been searching for a new abode in the British countryside. However, the state of that search remains unclear, given their current stay with their friends. As for this latest move, it purportedly took place while Archie and Lilibet were on their half-term vacation from school.

Why Geography Always Seems To Be A Problem For Prince Harry And Meghan Markle

This latest move comes amid questions about the Duke and Duchess’ decision to leave the United States in the first place. Prince Harry and Meghan Markle initially moved to California in March 2020, only months after stepping back as senior members of the British Royal Family. At that point, they stayed in a house owned by filmmaker Tyler Perry and, by July, they took up permanent residence in Montecito. Around 2023, it was rumored that the two were considering a move to Malibu, but that didn’t come to fruition. It was also in 2023 that the couple formally relinquished their UK home, Frogmore Cottage.

Reports of the Duke and Duchess’ intention to move back to the UK began to surface in August 2026. Shortly after that came the reports of the pair using the private jet to get their family to Harry’s home country. Per numbers that were shared, the jet reportedly cost $12,000 per hour for the 10-hour flight, which apparently brought the grand total of the trip to $120,000. The couple’s exact reasons for returning to the UK remain unknown, though it’s been speculated that the health of Harry’s father, King Charles III, was a contributing factor.

The royals may be back in the UK now, but it’s already been reported that they may return to the US, at least for visits, very soon. Sources allege that Meghan Markle and Prince Harry could be back for the holiday season, considering Markle’s mom, Doria Ragland, still lives in the states. That piece of speculation also came with the claim that Harry and Markle wouldn’t be celebrating with the Royal Family. If any festivities take place in the UK, though, it seems the Duke and Duchess now have a new spot in which they can celebrate.

#3582. Jake Gyllenhaal's 124-Minute Sci-Fi Disaster Movie Is Officially Netflix's Biggest Streaming Hit

In 2004, "The Day After Tomorrow" clumsily delivered a message about climate change via a movie in which Dennis Quaid and Jake Gyllenhaal try to save the world from a new ice age. The questionable part of the film was the science, which as NASA Goddard Space Flight Center meteorologist J. Marshall Shepherd told USA Today, warranted "a D minus or an F." Otherwise, "The Day After Tomorrow" was a grand old time at the movies, and now it seems modern audiences are having a similarly wonderful time with the end of the world over on Netflix.

The sci-fi disaster film was co-written, co-produced, and directed by Roland Emmerich, who prior to this had taken a break from big-budget sci-fi fare to make "The Patriot" with Mel Gibson. "The Day After Tomorrow" saw him return to familiar territory, with a film based on on Art Bell and Whitley Strieber's 1999 book "The Coming Global Superstorm."

Dennis Quaid stars as Paleoclimatologist Jack Hall, who's dismayed to find that global warming has finally brought about a new ice age that's preceded by extreme weather events which batter major cities around the world. His son Sam Hall (Gyllenhaal) happens to be in New York just as the big freeze sets in, prompting Jack to set off on a rescue mission.

The movie isn't the most critically acclaimed thing Emmerich has ever done. But it did gross $552.6 million on a $125 million budget and remains an impressive showcase of early 2000s CGI and arguably the best natural disaster movie of the era. If it's been a while, or you're yet to catch "The Day After Tomorrow," why not join in the celebration over on Netflix?

"The Day After Tomorrow" hit Netflix on November 1, 2026 and immediately took over the streamer's charts like an unstoppable climactic event. Streaming viewership tracker FlixPatrol shows the movie debuted at number one on the Netflix Top 10 movie charts on November 2, 2026 in the United States. What's more it maintains that position at the time of writing and it will be interesting to see just how long Jake Gyllenhaal's disaster flick can hang on to the top spot.

Otherwise, there are plenty of other disaster movies streaming on Netflix, just in case you don't necessarily fancy the early 2000s stylings of Roland Emmerich and co.

#3581. 10 Shows Like 'A Different World' You Should Watch Next

Ross Johnson writes about television, film, and literature for Lifehacker. He has a degree in political science from the University of Rochester and has previously been a legal writer and editor for Thomson Reuters, for which he later traveled around India and the Middle East as an educator specializing in American English style and grammar for adults.

Ross has been an actor on stage, in commercials, and in independent films since childhood, and has written hundreds of articles and essays on genre literature and cinema for Barnes & Noble, Gizmodo, Kotaku, and Yahoo! Entertainment.Ross produces the Swan Songs film podcast and hosts The Sound of Tomorrow, a pop culture and current affairs radio show based in Rochester, New York, where he lives with his husband and dogs and supports the local arts and cinema scene. You can find him on Bluesky.

This is Streamalikes, where you can find a curated list of recommendations to stream based on what you already like.

The original A Different World was a groundbreaking sitcom in its era, spending six seasons highlighting Black academic drive among a cast of characters so indelible that we're now checking in on them decades later. Spearheaded by Queen Sugar's Felicia Pride, the update has been a critical and ratings hit for Netflix, earning the rarest prize of all in streaming television: a quick second season renewal. While you're waiting for season two, here are some other smart coming-of-age shows that blend heart and humor with realistic drama.

An easy pairing with A Different World, this show follows Black-ish's Zoey Johnson (Yara Shahidi) as she leaves home to attend a (fictional) California liberal arts college (the last couple of post-graduation seasons shift the focus to her brother Andre, played by Marcus Scribner). The emphasis is on driven young people who are capable of making big mistakes on the path to adulthood. A true comedy-drama, Grown-ish feels real(-ish) in a way that few other college shows have managed. Stream Grown-ish on Hulu.

Adapted from and expanding upon the 2014 movie, this show takes us to a (fictional) Ivy League school for a comedy-drama that tackles campus life and politics from a rather different perspective than that of Rooster. Logan Browning leads the ensemble cast as Sam White, who kind of inadvertently starts the titular radio show following a racially charged incident on campus. Far from the racial screed that some bad-faith YouTubers seem to find it, it's never shy about confronting the complicated and occasionally silly contradictions of campus activism, with each episode approaching life at Winchester University from a different character's perspective. Stream Dear White People on Netflix.

Kimberly (Pauline Chalamet) is an endlessly naïve scholarship student; Bela (Amrit Kaur) is an aspiring comedy writer on the make for the hottest guys; Whitney (Alyah Chanelle Scott) is an overachieving athlete and senator’s daughter; and Leighton (Reneé Rapp) is a closeted sorority girl. They're all randomly assigned to room together as freshmen at the fictional Essex College in Vermont. Created by Mindy Kaling and Justin Noble, this comedy-drama isn't nearly as salacious as its title suggests. There's sex for sure, but mostly it's a funny, queer-friendly show that's a little less about one overarching romance than it is about growing up, and the value of female friendship. Stream The Sex Lives of College Girls on HBO Max.

Even though we're backing up a couple of years to follow teens in their high school years, this British import's setting is a decent match, finding its students living away from home and family for the first time in their lives. At the fictional prestigious boarding school St. Gilbert’s, five Black teens are newly attending on scholarships, but their integration into the existing cliques is less than smooth—especially given that they're there largely as a PR stunt. Boarders blends teen romance, coming-of-age drama, and a delightful willingness to take the piss when it comes to the whole "rich private school" thing. Stream Boarders on Tubi.

Another modern take on a beloved '80s/'90s sitcom, this one's a bit different, serving as a total reimagining with no narrative connection to the original. And while A Different World is a comedy with dramatic heft, this one's more of a straight drama. It’s jarring for fans of the beloved original to tune in to find a serious show with the same premise as the Will Smith original—one that often leans into heavy realism. Jabari Banks plays, er, Will Smith, a 16-year-old from West Philadelphia who moves in with his auntie and uncle in Bel-Air following a gun charge and a run-in with a Philly drug lord. Banks is charismatic and believable, bringing a ton of personality to a show that occasionally veers down dark alleys. Stream Bel-Air on Peacock.

Comedian Benito Skinner plays himself, kinda, in this buzzy comedy that sees a former high school jock facing his freshman year in college while desperately trying to convince himself and everyone else that he's as straight as they come (relatable, except for the jock part). Much of the appeal is in its deft blending of tones: It's both a frequently raunchy college comedy and a sweet coming-of-age story about accepting yourself without worrying about what everyone else thinks. The cast includes Adam DiMarco (The White Lotus) and Rish Shah (Ms. Marvel), and, though it's more a story of one young man's coming of age, there's a strong ensemble backing him up. Stream Overcompensating on Prime Video.

The heart of All American (for most of its run) is Spencer James (Daniel Ezra), based on real-life NFL linebacker Spencer Paysinger. A star player for his high school team in Crenshaw, he's recruited by the coach (Taye Diggs) of a team in Beverly Hills to come and play for them, forcing Spencer to navigate two very different worlds while trying to build a life and potential career. Stream All American on Netflix.

Following a family tragedy, the already awkward 15-year-old Devi Vishwakumar (Maitreyi Ramakrishnan) has a pretty terrible freshman year of high school, and decides that she’s going to turn things around the following year, hoping that a nearly academic study of sex will get her the boyfriend(s) her raging hormones have begun to demand. It works, to a point—but getting a surprise yes to sex from her crush leads her to question what she’s really ready for. More about burgeoning sexuality than sex specifically, this Mindy Kaling-produced series is both honest and charming. Stream Never Have I Ever on Netflix.

For realism in a show about the college experience, you could do a lot worse than this docuseries following several students at Gallaudet University, a school for deaf and hard-of-hearing young adults. In one sense, it's a specific setting where perspectives on deafness vary wildly, even in Gallaudet's self-contained world (aside from being a show about academically driven and horny college students, this is also a great primer for hearing people about some of the issues). But even for all of that, the challenges in building a life and future away from home are pretty universally relatable. Stream Deaf U on Netflix.

There's a reason A Different World has returned in 2026, and a lot of that has to do with the fact that there was nothing else on TV quite like it back in the late '80s and early '90s. For all of its sitcom sensibilities, the show tried hard (especially after multi-hyphenate creator Debbie Allen arrived to rework things after its first season) to paint a realistic picture of college life and an HBCU. Of the few shows on TV with largely Black casts, almost none would go so far as to highlight achievement and excellence; A Different World managed to do so while building a cast of characters so memorable that we're more than willing to catch up with them nearly forty years later. Stream A Different World on Netflix.
