#3543. 8 Classic Books That Are Still Perfect From Start to Finish

Feel free to connect with him or check out his work. He's everywhere — Upwork, YouTube, Spotify, SoundCloud, Collider, LinkedIn, Instagram.

A lot of the books on this list were probably assigned to you at some point, which is a good reason to avoid them. School has a way of making a great story feel like homework, and I’ll admit I rolled my eyes at a couple of these before I actually sat down and read them. Then I got to the end and wished I’d done it sooner.

What they share is that none of them lose steam. Some are short, some are enormous, and a couple are more than two hundred years old, but you never reach a chapter where you start counting the pages left. Here are some of the most iconic books I’d pick up on a quiet weekend which I think everybody should read at least once.

Mary Shelley was only eighteen when she came up with the idea for Frankenstein during a rainy summer in 1816 at a villa near Lake Geneva. She was stuck inside with her future husband, Percy Shelley, and Lord Byron, and the group decided to see who could write the scariest ghost story. The weather was so bad that year, after a volcano erupted in Indonesia, that nobody could go out, which gave her plenty of time to think. She finished the novel at twenty and published it anonymously in 1818.

Victor Frankenstein, the young scientist who builds a living creature out of dead body parts, is arguably the real villain of the story, even though most people call the monster Frankenstein. The creature never gets a name, and he teaches himself to speak by secretly listening to a family through a hole in a cottage wall. Shelley tells it through letters from a sea captain in the Arctic, which makes everything feel like a confession. It’s much sadder than you’d expect, and the creature is hard not to feel sorry for.

Scott Fitzgerald first wanted to call The Great Gatsby “Trimalchio in West Egg,” which is a mouthful, and he only gave it up close to publication. Nick Carraway, a young Midwesterner who moves to Long Island in the summer of 1922, tells the story of his mysterious neighbor, Jay Gatsby, a millionaire who throws huge parties every weekend hoping that Daisy Buchanan, the woman he loves, will walk through the gates. The book is short, around 180 pages, and every sentence is carefully chosen.

It barely sold when it came out in 1925, and Fitzgerald died in 1940 thinking it had been a failure. What changed things was World War II, when roughly 150,000 copies were handed out to American soldiers overseas, and a whole new generation of readers fell for it. The green light at the end of Daisy’s dock and the giant eyes on a faded billboard are probably the most analyzed images in American fiction. It ends quietly, and it hurts.

Charlotte Brontë published Jane Eyre in 1847 under the name Currer Bell, because she worried that critics wouldn’t take a woman writer seriously. Jane is an orphan who gets sent to a harsh boarding school, grows up determined to be treated as an equal, and takes a job as a governess at Thornfield Hall, where she falls for the moody owner, Mr. Rochester. The school, Lowood, is based on a real place, Cowan Bridge, where two of Brontë’s older sisters caught illnesses and died.

Jane tells her own story, and she often speaks straight to the reader, which makes you feel like she’s confiding in you. Strange laughter in the night and a locked room on the third floor hint at a secret that takes a long time to come out, and when it does, the story takes a turn nobody saw coming. Jane’s refusal to give up her self-respect for love is why the book is contemporary. Jean Rhys later wrote Wide Sargasso Sea to tell the story of the woman in the attic.

Jane Austen wrote the first version of Pride and Prejudice in her early twenties under the title First Impressions, and her father tried to sell it to a London publisher in 1797, who turned it down without even reading it. Years later she rewrote it, and it came out in 1813 with “by the author of Sense and Sensibility” on the cover instead of her name. Elizabeth Bennet, the clever second daughter of a family with five girls and no son to inherit the estate, meets the proud Mr. Darcy at a dance and decides she can’t stand him.

Austen sold the rights for just £110, a small sum even then, and the publisher made a good profit from it. She called Elizabeth “as delightful a creature as ever appeared in print,” and it’s hard to disagree. Mr. Collins’s marriage proposal is one of the funniest scenes in English fiction, and the slow shift in how Elizabeth sees Darcy is what keeps you reading. Everybody jokes about it being a romance, but it’s really a sharp comedy about money, class, and first impressions.

J.R.R. Tolkien was a professor grading exam papers when he found a blank page and scribbled a single sentence about a hobbit living in a hole in the ground. He didn’t know what a hobbit was yet, but he kept going, telling the story to his kids at bedtime, and The Hobbit came out in 1937. Bilbo Baggins, a comfortable homebody, gets talked into joining thirteen dwarves and the wizard Gandalf on a trek to take back a mountain from the dragon Smaug.

Tolkien’s publisher let his ten-year-old son, Rayner Unwin, read the manuscript and give his opinion, and the boy’s short report helped get it printed. The chapter where Bilbo plays a game of riddles with Gollum in a dark cave is one of the best pieces of writing in fantasy, and Tolkien later rewrote it so the magic ring would feel more dangerous in The Lord of the Rings. He drew the maps and illustrations himself. It’s funny, warm, and quick, and it never feels like it’s trying too hard.

Gabriel García Márquez spent about eighteen months in Mexico City writing One Hundred Years of Solitude, while his wife, Mercedes, kept the family afloat and reportedly pawned their appliances to pay for the postage to send the manuscript to a publisher. The novel follows seven generations of the Buendía family in the made-up town of Macondo, which is based on Aracataca, the Colombian village where he grew up. The first print run of 8,000 copies sold out in a week.

Strange things happen in the book as if they were completely normal. A girl floats into the sky while folding sheets, yellow butterflies follow a man everywhere he goes, and it rains for almost five years straight. García Márquez said the style came from his grandmother, who told impossible stories in a flat, matter-of-fact voice. He won the Nobel Prize in 1982, and the book has sold tens of millions of copies. It’s dizzying, funny, and sad in equal amounts.

George Orwell wrote 1984 on a remote Scottish island, Jura, while he was seriously ill with tuberculosis, and it came out in June 1949, only about seven months before he died. Winston Smith, a quiet clerk at the Ministry of Truth, spends his days rewriting old newspaper articles so they match whatever the government wants people to believe. When he starts a secret relationship with a colleague named Julia, he knows that even thinking against the Party is a crime.

Room 101, where prisoners face their worst fear, was reportedly named after a boring BBC conference room where Orwell sat through meetings during the war. The Ministry of Truth was modeled partly on the Senate House in London, where the wartime Ministry of Information worked. Words like Big Brother, doublethink, and Newspeak have become part of everyday language. It’s one of the few books where the ending leaves you cold, and you finish it feeling like you’ve seen how easily the truth can disappear.

Harper Lee published To Kill a Mockingbird in 1960, and for fifty-five years it was the only novel she let anyone read. Scout Finch, a six-year-old tomboy in Maycomb, Alabama, tells the story of the summer when her father, Atticus, a lawyer, defends a Black man named Tom Robinson, who is falsely accused of assaulting a white woman. Scout and her brother Jem spend the same summer trying to figure out their reclusive neighbor, Boo Radley.

Dill, the imaginative boy who visits every summer, is based on Lee’s childhood friend Truman Capote. Friends gave her a year’s pay one Christmas so she could quit her job as an airline clerk and write, and her editor had her rewrite the book several times. It won the Pulitzer Prize in 1961. Atticus’s quiet courage in the courtroom has made him one of the most loved fathers in literature, and the book’s mix of humor, childhood, and injustice is why it keeps topping lists of the greatest American novels.

Four of the largest communities on the planet, and four completely different reasons to belong to one. Here is yours, what it would give you, and the argument you would be having within a week.

You belong to the fandom that is really about comfort. Hogwarts works on people because it is a place rather than a plot, and the pull is not the wizard war so much as the corridors, the food, the weather and the sense that somebody is expecting you.

You belong to the deepest fandom on this list, the one where somebody has always read further than you and is quietly delighted to say so. Middle-earth rewards patience more than any other world in popular culture.

You belong to the loudest and largest tent of the four, the one where three generations are all watching the same thing and none of them agree about any of it. That disagreement is not a flaw in this fandom, it is the main activity.

You belong to the thinking fandom, the one that turns up for the argument rather than the explosion. Trek has always been a series of ethical problems in space, and the people who love it love being asked what they would have done.

#3542. The Out-of-Touch Adults' Guide to Kid Culture: What Is 'Ballhog'?

A weekly deep dive into the current trends, slang, and viral videos of youth culture in terms that even the squarest can understand.

This week's zeitgeist snapshot explains what ballhog means, how a video of someone wrapping a burger led to a new meme format, and the dangers of Benny tripping. So strap in, and let's go.

Ballhog or ball hog is a streetwear fashion style growing in popularity among younger people. The cool ones, anyway. The idea is to wear vintage clothes that look normal, even drab, to most, but that people in the know can recognize as interesting or unique. Like the best youth trends, it's an insider vs. outsider thing that takes connoisseurship to understand. Some examples: If you're wearing a late 1990s Helmut Lang denim jacket, most people will think "thrifted," but a ballhog-enjoyer would recognize it as a seminal piece of streetwear history. If you want to be ballhog, rocking a pair of skinny jeans isn't going to cut it unless they're from Dior Homme or at least Cheap Monday.

The style is named after the Ball Hog Collective, a group of rappers, Twitch streamers, and content creators founded by the Atlanta-based indie record label Ballhog. It was popularized by streamer Brady Goodwin, seen below looking quite ballhog:

The #ballhog hashtag is blowing up (as people used to say) lately with a growing collection of kids posting videos to show off their ballhog fits, like so:

The popularity of the style comes down to, I think, how difficult it is to commodify. Most truly organic trends are recognized quickly by culture vulture types, and in a few months, there's a line of clothes at Target, but you can't do that with ballhog. There's no way to make "new" ballhog gear, as that would mark it as inauthentic immediately. Gotta hand it to the kids for adopting a style that is at once exclusionary and impossible to rip off.

On the opposite edge of the spectrum from ballhog fashion is the "while they're out partying btw" meme, videos made to show off the strange, specific, and usually useless talent one develops while others are out wearing cool clothes and socializing. The phrase has been kicking around since last year, when TikToker @tacobella posted this video

but it's taken off more recently, thanks to the huge number of views on this video showing off some truly mind-blowing burger wrapping skills:

This led to an influx of videos of people showing off what they were doing instead of partying. Like this mechanic:

This is the second youth trend I support wholeheartedly. We can't all be cool ballhoggers and we don't all have talent, but we can all learn to do a thing really well through brute force and repetition.

The past tense of "cringe," "crunged" is often used to describe extreme cringe, like "I cringed so hard I crunged."

As for "scuba," it now describes something that is very smelly, which might be because the word conjures the dead air of unventilated, underwater spaces. But it's often accompanied by a pinch-your-nose gesture, which looks like the gesture in the Scuba Dance that was popular on TikTok a few months ago, so that's a more likely origin for the term.

There has been a steady stream of news stories about kids overdosing on Benadryl over the last few years. They call it "Benny tripping," and it's achieved by taking too much of the allergy medicine, like 10 times the amount recommended. Among the active ingredients in Benadryl is Diphenhydramine, and it's a particularly nasty drug. Unlike most recreational substances, tripping on Benadryl is not fun. It's a deliriant, and taking too much results in hallucinations that are usually described as terrifying—swarms of spiders, shadow people, whispering voices, etc. Benadryl overdoses can result in loss of short term memory, displacement from time and space, and panic attacks that last for hours or even days. Or you die from tachycardia. Here's how Reddit user Reasonable-County971 described their experience,

I lost access to my memories. I couldn’t recognize my mom—I mistook her for a 'pretty nurse'. Early in the trip, before you lose yourself, you develop tremendous anxiety, far far beyond anything else I can compare it to. Also, you have motor skills affected, including losing access to your bladder.

So yeah, it's a bad drug. And it's easy to get—just pop down to CVS. On the plus side, despite sometimes overly hysterical reporting on Benadryl as an "online trend" or challenge, tripping on Benadryl is such a harrowing, not-at-all-fun experience, its use isn't particularly popular among young people. But if you want to scare yourself, read some trip reports, watch this YouTube video, and imagine someone you love going through this.

This week's viral video is very meta, and it's hilarious to anyone who follows the trajectory of viral internet sensations. Brought to us by the great @ariisaysso, this video lays out the history of the fictional Cheezit Girl as she becomes an internet sensation, quits her job, sells merch, releases a rap single, releases a remix, reheats the nachos, and falls into obscurity, all in about two and a half minutes. We've seen this story before with the Hawk Tuah Girl, Dah Bih Gah Kid, and many more future members of the "remember that thing" club, and we'll no doubt see it all again soon. Such is the circle of life.

#3541. Ebenezer’s Venmo and ‘How to Rob a Bank’ ATMs: Studios Are Now Promoting Movies by Just Giving Away Money

Clipfarming, influencer screenings, and meme-bait popcorn buckets: promoting a movie in the internet age is often a full-court offensive to get noticed. In that spirit, why not just get down to business and resort to modern civilization’s oldest method for seeking attention: dangling some money in people’s faces?

That’s what the marketing teams behind “How to Rob a Bank,” from Amazon MGM Studios, and “Ebenezer,” from Skydance’s Paramount Pictures, have tried in the weeks leading up to their shared November 13 release to North American theaters.

For the former ensemble heist thriller, a branded ATM was moved between multiplexes throughout the Los Angeles area over the course of four days. Those who learned of the campaign on the film‘s social media channels could gain clues about the machine’s location and a specified PIN number, which would spark payouts of a single one-hundred-dollar bill to those who bothered to seek out (or stumble upon) it. Related Stories What Are Local Movie Theaters Showing on Election Night? Don’t Forget, Oscar Watchers: ‘The Odyssey,’ ‘Project Hail Mary,’ and Other Big Guns Are Coming Back

“Ebenezer” took a more cheeky, trifling approach, promoting an official Venmo account for Johnny Depp’s Christmas crab apple that users could request funds from. Those who scrolled through the account’s transactions would see it shares the character’s penny-pinching spirit: the only completed transactions were those giving away one single cent. The Venmo account was only active for a few hours, though a Paramount Instagram post from last week teases followers to “check back” as “Ebenezer might be feeling generous on @venmo again.”

Several film news aggregation accounts like Culture Crave and DiscussingFilm reported that the account “crashed” due an overwhelming amount of requests, though Paramount declined to comment on if such a description was accurate. Venmo did not respond to a request asking if the company partnered with the studio on the sponsorship.

Much like that line, there is also a tackiness du jour to both money-mindset stunts, especially in a world where awards shows, professional sports and geopolitical events can hardly be watched without outlets asking you to bet — erh, predict — on them. A video posted to Paramount’s socials opens with a Venmo request for $500, asking Scrooge to help pay off a user’s student loans.

Not to mention the real inadvertent quirk: the account has been able to receive payments from users. Considering the scant number of one-cent payouts from the account and the number of influxes, it is almost certain that Paramount could have made money on the stunt, though an individual with knowledge of the account shared that all received funds were sent back to users via private transactions.

Krystyna Ursta, a 27-year-old actress, video editor, and Depp fan in Los Angeles, shared that she gave about $30 to the account and received a full refund a few days later — plus an extra penny and an invitation to a special screening of the film in New York on Monday. She will be attending a local press screening instead. Ursta also posted a video of herself reacting to the account, one of many fan responses that flooded in on social media.

“I kind of figured that they will probably return it,” Ursta wrote over text after being reached through her Instagram handle, which she included in her Venmo transactions. “I’m such a big fan. I was happy to support the film.”

The rather gimmick-less gimmick of waving around money also helps capture the attention of people that aren’t necessarily interested in seeing the movie, but are going through the average modern experience of thinking about one’s financial situation. Aggregation accounts were quick to post graphics reporting on both stunts, with captions like “HOW TO ROB A BANK ATM’S ARE BEING SET UP AROUND LOS ANGELES AND GIVING PEOPLE FREE MONEY AND IT COULDN’T HAPPEN AT A BETTER TIME” and “EBENEZER SCROOGE WILL SEND YOU REAL MONEY ON VENMO BUT THERE’S A CATCH SWIPE FOR MORE.”

There’s also people like Scott, a 35-year-old based out of Atlanta that couldn’t help but engage with the “Ebenezer” Venmo account after seeing it on X. He sent a penny, then received one in return. (A disclaimer: six Venmo users were reached for interview about their Ebenezer experience by sending them $0.01 with this reporter’s contact information in the caption; Scott was the only response that timed out before publication.)

“Seeing Ebenezer is now on Venmo was too funny and stupid to not engage with,” he wrote over text. “There’s something very boring dystopia about it: the idea of a fictional character from a 200-year-old Christmas story being commercialized on Venmo just shows how dumb Hollywood can. … It’s like McDonald’s Monopoly: take our slop and we might give your money.”

Also helpful for the studios is how little dangling the potential of money actually costs. Sans staffing fees, producing the “Ebenezer” Venmo account and its activity used a sum less than the coins between the couch cushions on the Paramount lot. Per the “How to Rob a Bank” promo’s website, each location’s prize pool gave away ten one-hundred-dollar bills and twenty twenty-dollar-bills ($1,400 total), plus some theater-supplied prizes like gift cards. An employee at the Regal Sherman Oaks that worked on the day of the on-site promotion said the ATM seemed to deal out the rewards in a random order, as opposed to $100 dollar bills for the first finders. Amazon MGM declined to comment, while Stellar Agency Inc., which sponsored and administered the promotion, did not respond to a request.

Both had much smaller overheads than a “Now You See Me: Now You Don’t” promotion than ran in April 2025. To launch the magician threequel’s first trailer, Lionsgate reportedly gave away roughly $250,000 to those that texted a mysterious phone number displaying in Times Square in the hours up to the drop. Like “Ebenezer” and “How to Rob a Bank,” it was a promotion that sparked a viral moment with plenty of user-generated content, each sharing the widely desired fantasy of receiving free money.

Neon handed out basic resources for an “I Love Boosters” promotion in May, where stars KeKe Palmer and LaKeith Stanfield took over a Shell gas station in West Pico to give out complimentary refills to the first 70 cars that arrived. The stunt played on then-peaking fuel prices, which had skyrocketed in the wake of the U.S.’ initial bombing of Iran in February and the subsequent blockade of the Strait of Hormuz.

In the months since, President Trump has promised $5,000 checks to every adult U.S. citizen if the Republican Party retains control of Congress in Tuesday’s midterm elections. Trump announced the idea, his approval rating was at a dismal 35 percent, per a CNN aggregate of various polls. Though the offer is unprecedented and dubious on its face, it has been covered extensively — and it cost nothing to float it.

#3540. The Fitbit Edge Is Everything the Charge 6 Should Have Been

I’ve been using the new Fitbit Edge for a little over a week, and am happy to report that it’s quite good at its job. It shipped with more features than I expected (Google Maps directions were there from the jump) and corrects the missteps that Google made with the Fitbit Charge 6. After running the Fitbit Edge through its paces, here’s my breakdown of what works well, what doesn’t, and what I think of the device overall.

When I reviewed it in May 2025, I liked a lot about the Charge 6, but found it had a few serious flaws. Tightening the strap messed up its GPS readings (weird but true), and some of its features required a subscription (like the music controls that only worked with YouTube Music). Its promised side button wasn’t really a button, and didn’t even always work.

I’m happy to report that all of my biggest gripes have been fixed in the Fitbit Edge. Or to put it another way: the Edge is what the Charge should have been in the first place.

Accuracy tests are always one of my top priorities in testing, but honestly I wasn’t expecting much from this device. A Fitbit can still be successful in my eyes even if its heart rate sensor is only “good enough.” Nobody should expect lab-level precision from a Fitbit.

But I was pleasantly surprised by just how capable the Edge is in this regard. It sometimes takes a few minutes to lock on to a heart rate signal (as most optical devices do), but after it does, it is spot-on—I think it might be in the running alongside the Apple Watch and high-end Garmins as one of the better heart rate wearables on the market. The Edge’s accuracy is notably better than the Fitbit Air's, even though they seem to share the same sensor hardware.

Location accuracy is also quite good, only deviating slightly from a Garmin I tested alongside the Edge. It may not be the best out there, but it’s miles ahead of what the Charge 6 was able to do.

The Fitbit Edge has real music controls, unlike the Charge 6. I can play something in Spotify or in Castro (my favorite podcast app) on my phone, and then control the audio from my wrist—and you no longer need to use YouTube Music or have a subscription to get this feature.

When the Fitbit Air and the Google Health app first launched, it was possible to pair both a Fitbit and a Pixel Watch to the same phone, but not two Fitbits. That has finally changed: I was able to connect the Edge to my phone without losing my connection to the Air. It also works to swap seamlessly between the two Fitbits. For example, one night the Edge was low on battery, so I slept with the Air on, and then swapped back in the morning once the Edge was charged. The app happily showed my sleep data from the Air and my activity data from the Edge without my having to do mess around in the app.

As a nice bonus, the charger for the Fitbit Edge is the same as for the Fitbit Air. (The chargers for the Pixel Watch and for the Fitbit Charge 6 are not compatible with the Edge.)

The Fitbit Edge is a similar size as the old Charge 6, but with noticeably more screen real estate. The strap fits pretty much the same way as a Pixel watch band—that is to say, normally, not with the strange hang-off-the-wrist stiffness of the Charge 6.

The Fitbit Edge also has a physical button—not a haptic nub like the Charge 6, but an actual, physical button. And it even works (to return you to the home screen) nearly every time I press it. The Charge 6’s nub was not as reliable.

Overall, I’m quite happy with the Fitbit Edge. It’s much better than the Charge 6, and adds accuracy and a screen to the things I already liked about the Fitbit Air. But there are a few things I don’t totally love.

One is that there is no NFC chipset, which means no option to use Google Pay. I don’t mind using my phone or card at checkouts (and I always carry my phone), so this isn’t a big deal for me, but I know a lot of folks love a wrist-based payment, and that’s missing from the Fitbit Edge. (Google reportedly said most Fitbit users didn’t actually use Google Pay, so they removed the functionality—presumably to fit in the other components while keeping the device small.)

The other downside is, I hate to say it, the Google Health app. It’s OK, but I still find myself arguing with the AI when it assigns me workouts I never asked for, and I have to agree with the redditors who are commiserating about the lack of a “yesterday” view. (On the bright side, Google recently added a feature that lets you turn off the AI insights, which helps a lot.)

Overall, the Fitbit Edge is a great fitness tracker. It measures heart rate and running/walking mileage accurately; it can control music in a sensible way; and it looks good, feels good to wear, and works smoothly. The price also tracks: It’s definitely worth the $20 premium over the Charge 6, and it’s not quite double the price of the Air, which I think is fair. For anyone who doesn’t want a smartwatch or a running watch and will be satisfied with just “a Fitbit,” this one is pretty much perfect.

#3539. The MCU's X-Men Is Immediately Correcting Fox's Biggest Missed Opportunity

The Marvel Cinematic Universe is taking advantage of Fox's missed opportunity with X-Men from the very beginning. While Marvel Studios has brought mutants into the MCU over the years through many means, it won't be until 2028 that the franchise introduces its first proper X-Men team.

After making Jean Grey (Sadie Sink) the villain of Spider-Man: Brand New Day, she'll return as a central figure in the new film. Amid speculation about Sink's role, questions swirled about what other mutants would join her. Answers continue to come as Marvel Studios fills out X-Men's cast with actors playing known heroes and villains from this corner of the universe.

The assembled talent for the MCU's X-Men have brought plenty of insights into Marvel's approach, especially regarding how it compares to Fox's handling of the IP for decades. The MCU's X-Men skews younger than the originals, but older than Fox's prequels. Adam Driver's Mister Sinister will be the villain, rather than Magneto. The X-Men team he'll fight is notable, too.

While Fox delivered multiple iterations of X-Men teams throughout its various timelines, they missed out on uniting the original comic team. That mistake in the eyes of Marvel Comics readers is immediately being fixed for the MCU, as that's the team X-Men is starting with based on how casting has shaped up.

The X-Men were introduced in 1963's The X-Men #1 by Stan Lee and Jack Kirby with a roster constructed of Angel, Beast, Cyclops, Iceman, and Jean Grey, with Professor X teaching them. While the team has grown and changed in many ways throughout the years since then, those characters are the core of X-Men storytelling.

Marvel Studios is ensuring that is the same for the MCU by having all of them appear from the very first X-Men movie, as all of these characters have been cast. Jean was cast first for Spider-Man: Brand New Day, while Professor X (Christopher Abbott) and Cyclops (Kit Connor) were announced at D23 2026.

Since then, trade reports have come announcing the casting of Angel (Asa Germann) and Iceman (Ben Wang). There is also a report that Game of Thrones' Peter Claffey will play Beast, but that has yet to be confirmed. But given previous rumors that Charles Melton was in consideration for that role, all signs point to Beast being in the movie.

This makes the six founding X-Men members part of the team from its inception in the MCU. Jean, Cyclops, Angel, Beast, and Iceman should all be active team members, while Professor X remains their teacher. There may be more mutants on the team or teaching the students, but this will be the first time these six X-Men will be together in a movie.

Fox's X-Men movie franchise repeatedly missed the chance to bring the founding mutants together. Beast and Angel were missing from the first team in X-Men and X2. All but Professor X and Beast were absent from X-Men: First Class' initial roster, and that carried over into X-Men: Days of Future Past. The new-look team introduced in X-Men: Apocalypse brought Cyclops and Jean into the mix, and Angel eventually, but Iceman remained missing.

The closest Fox ever came to assembling X-Men's founding members was in X-Men: The Last Stand. The trilogy ender included all six characters in some capacity, but they did not all interact. Jean killed Cyclops early on and Professor X later before abandoning the X-Men to join Magneto's Brotherhood of Mutants. Angel and Beast joined Iceman as official X-Men members, but the rest of the team was different: Wolverine, Storm, Kitty Pryde, and Colossus.

It's a stunning oversight for Fox (one that likely left Kevin Feige scratching his head as he worked on those films early in his career). The franchise had seven core X-Men movies to bring these six characters together but failed to do so at every turn. Now, that missed opportunity has become the linchpin to the MCU's take.

Starting the X-Men franchise with the original team is the latest example of the MCU going back to fundamental comic elements when redoing previously adapted characters and stories. For instance, Tom Holland's Spider-Man spent an entire trilogy in high school, rather than speeding him to adulthood. Something similar is happening with the X-Men, as Marvel has clearly made the founding members a priority for the MCU.

This immediately sets the reboot apart from past adaptations and brings it closer to the comics fans know and love. X-Men may target younger audiences, but it will have the nostalgic lineup that lifelong comic readers know. It will feel incredibly familiar and new at the same time.

However, the MCU isn't just blindly following the comics either. Storm (Maya Boyd) and Rogue (Inde Navarrette) are confirmed to appear, and both should be part of the X-Men team. Emma Frost (Samara Weaving) also remains a wildcard regarding what side she will fall on. Some of these characters could have larger roles than some of the founding members, but the important thing is they all get to be together at last.

Other mutants are sure to appear in X-Men, with Gambit and Nightcrawler two popular suggestions. Wolverine's potential presence looms over the whole project, as the MCU needs to figure out if the iconic hero will be recast, replaced by X-23, or continue to be played by Hugh Jackman (until he's 90). But that decision can be delayed thanks to X-Men's focus.

With the founding members taking precedence for the MCU, Wolverine sitting out the movie becomes easier to explain away. He is not part of the original lineup, as his comics debut didn't come until 12 years later. Wolverine's popularity quickly led to him taking a prominent role in X-Men titles, and that will happen for the MCU once he is properly introduced.

Rather than have Wolverine overshadow the rest of the X-Men from the start, he can sit out the first movie and allow the founding members more time to shine. This will be a better approach for the health of the MCU's future, as audiences need to care about more than just the adamantium-strengthened mutant.

X-Men could still wind up referencing Wolverine, but it's easier for comic readers and general audiences to understand why he isn't in the 2028 movie if Marvel sells the founding members' focus. Those mutants could then encounter him in a follow-up project after being more established as the core of the team concept in the MCU.

#3538. 5 Big Challenges in Creating Criterion’s ‘The Complete Kubrick’: From Navigating HDR/4K to Preserving Stanley Kubrick’s Love of Mono Sound

In 2024, archivist Michael Chaiken was approached by the Criterion Collection about what was being described as a “big Kubrick project.” It would start with remastering the director’s last film, “Eyes Wide Shut,” but for months the scope of the ambitious project remained an open question: Was a complete Stanley Kubrick box set even possible?

Kubrick was a precise director, and his control over every aspect of his filmmaking process extended to its home video presentation. But home video technology has developed in ways (widescreen TVs, high dynamic range, 4K resolution, Dolby Atmos) that Kubrick could never have imagined before he died in 1999. As a result — from the image to sound to design of the box itself — there was the underlying question driving Chaiken and the team’s work: “What would Stanley do?” Related Stories Ebenezer’s Venmo and ‘How to Rob a Bank’ ATMs: Studios Are Now Promoting Movies by Just Giving Away Money What Are Local Movie Theaters Showing on Election Night?

“I had to research the history of Stanley Kubrick on home video, and that’s a very specific thing,” said Chaiken. “It’s almost like for a biographer that would be [an important] footnote.”

In an interview with IndieWire, Chaiken broke down the challenges and key work behind “The Complete Kubrick,” which hit stores and mailboxes last week.

Home video fanatics are often completists. And if you are going to invest the time in a $599.95 box set (on sale for 30 percent off at most retailers), the motivation to make it comprehensive and definitive is obvious, but with a career spanning five decades, that isn’t always possible.

“You have to kick around the idea, ‘What does ‘complete’ mean? And how would we make that so?,” said Chaiken.

The heart of Kubrick’s feature film career has been well preserved. His final five films were made with Warner Bros., and the studio’s archive team has kept the original elements well preserved. Meanwhile, Criterion, back in its laser disc era, in the 1980s and ’90s, had a good working relationship with Kubrick himself (more about that later) and was already familiar with what was available (and already in-house) when it came to having to remaster his key films into the HDR/4K standards of today.

“It’s the early stuff that was tricky because he wasn’t working for a studio; he was an independent,” said Chaiken. “[A complete box set] almost didn’t happen; it was really at the 11th hour that it came together.”

In the case of “The Seafarers,” a 1953 30-minute documentary Kubrick was commissioned to make for the Seafarers International Union, the issue became untangling the project’s rights. “We thought we knew [who owned the rights], and then somebody said, ‘Hey, by the way, I’m actually the rights holder of that,’” Chaiken chuckled, retelling the story and imagining Kubrick himself groaning at the idea that Criterion had dug it up and restored it. “ I laugh because it’s a work for hire, but at the same time, it’s a very beautiful film, and it’s his first color film, and there’s elements in it that are so Kubrickian.”

The final missing piece was the original 12-minute version of the 1951 documentary “Day of the Fight,” which Kubrick shot and edited independently for Look magazine in 1949.

“There’s a version that [Kubrick] financed and made himself, and then there’s the version that exists,” said Chaiken. “He sold the film to RKO Pictures, and they re-edited the film; they added footage that he didn’t shoot, and they changed the narration and the soundtrack that Kubrick had commissioned Gerald Fried to make.”

Kubrick’s original version had never been presented in 4K, and locating the original elements was the final piece, in Chaiken’s mind, to the set being “complete.”

“Why do you need two cuts of Day of the Fight?” Chaiken rhetorically asked before answering the question: “They are different, and to reinforce that completeness, especially with [this being] Stanley’s very first film.  His cut is actually [four minutes] shorter than the one that RKO made [and] the very first film edited and produced and directed by him.”

Chaiken’s need to present both versions of a film also applied to “The Shining,” which, after it was released domestically in May 1980 — where it bombed with critics — Kubrick spent three months re-editing, making it 25 minutes shorter, for the international release in September 1980.

What’s fascinating is that both versions have been widely available for decades; they just didn’t cross the ocean. The shorter international version is Kubrick’s final cut, and what he considered his director’s cut, never made its way to the U.S.

“[Kubrick] never pulled the U.S. theatrical version, so that version is what has existed here on video. And if you’re doing complete Kubrick, the final edit of ‘The Shining’ has to be on there. It  just has to be,” said Chaiken, noting the significant differences. “The international version is a different experience. The tone of it does shift. It does leave open the possibility that none of this is happening, and it’s all happening in Jack’s head. You really don’t understand [Jack’s] relationship with Danny in the same way in the international version.”

As IndieWire’s Jim Hemphill fully explored, the significant differences between the versions are disorienting for those who grew up loving the longer U.S. version. Chaiken anticipated what “a headscratcher” the international version would be, which is why he commissioned a new commentary track. In the new box set, the U.S. version preserves steadicam operator and founder Garrett Brown’s original Criterion commentary track, but the international version features a newly recorded track by the great Pixar animation director Lee Unkrich, who co-authored a decades-in-the-making, 1,396-page, two-volume “Stanley Kubrick’s The Shining” book, which drew from rare documents, script notes, and storyboards in the Kubrick Archive, and is based on extensive interviews with the surviving cast and crew, to tell the definitive story of the legendary and misunderstood production.

“I imagine American audiences, who love the movie, saying, ‘Why would I want to watch a shorter version of ‘The Shining’? But I think having Lee Unkrich there walking you through it and talking about some of these decisions, and talking about the production of the movie, makes it a rewarding experience,” said Chaiken. “If you’re a skeptic, it’s at least worth watching once with Lee’s commentary because it is like a master-class in ‘The Shining.’”

Twenty years after Francis Ford Coppola and Walter Murch’s groundbreaking “Apocalypse Now” sound design and roadshow ushered in surround sound, and George Lucas used the box office power of his “Star Wars” franchise to leverage theaters into adapting the new technology he was pioneering at Skywalker, Kubrick was still avoiding even doing stereo mixes of his final films.

“He stuck with mono until the end,” said Chaiken. “He was obsessed with presentation, and he truly felt, ‘I would rather have good mono than bad stereo,’ and he didn’t trust that these theaters were set up in such a way that the stereo mix.”

For the box set, Criterion does offer 5.1 mixes of Kubrick’s films, but the default audio is Kubrick’s preferred mono mix. Chaiken and Criterion audio supervisor Ryan Hullings felt it important to go back to original mono mixes, which hadn’t been touched for home video in 30 years, to do new masters for the box set. In most cases, locating the original mono mix assets was not a problem, but there were exceptions, most notably “Full Metal Jacket.”

While Warner Archives had preserved all the original assets, identifying which was the final mono mix proved difficult, explained Chaiken, “ ‘Full Metal Jacket’ was a tricky one because they were trying to convince Stanley to do it in stereo. So there was the beginning of a stereo mix.” In going through what Hullings thought were the final mono mixes, they didn’t conform with the 35mm print he was using as a comparison. As they did throughout the process of making the box set, the Criterion team turned to Kubrick’s surviving collaborators, in this case “Full Metal Jacket” editor Martin Hunter and Nigel Galt, who would go on to edit “Eyes Wide Shut,” but had done Foley and sound work on “Full Metal Jacket.”

According to Chaiken, it was Galt who helped them solve the puzzle, telling Hullings, “You’ll know you have the right mono mix of ‘Full Metal Jacket’ because during the end credits, in the original mono theatrical mix, we screwed up.” The final song over credits is The Rolling Stones’ “Paint It Black,” but according to Galt, ‘When it went out originally theatrically, we had it at 25 frames per second, so it’s actually sped up. So if you have the mix that has ‘Paint It Black’ at 25 frames per second, that’s it.’”

And yes, on the new Criterion, the “Full Metal Jacket” mono mix preserved “Paint It Black” playing approximately four percent faster than The Rolling Stones recorded it.

“Stanley passed away in 1999, and that was the beginning of when the DVD revolution was starting to happen,” said Chaiken. “So, the idea of Blu-ray and then 4K, you’re in a realm that Kubrick could never have imagined.”

Chaiken confronted this head-on, starting the project with “Eyes Wide Shut”—which he described as one of Kubrick’s hardest films to bridge the gap between the filmmaker’s original intention and the latest in modern home video technology. In working with “Eyes Wide Shut” cinematographer Larry Smith, Chaiken came to understand how much of a “dreamy quality” is a product of the unique way Smith and Kubrick exposed and developed the celluloid.

“It’s never going to be a one-to-one correlation between film and video; you can get close, but video is getting sharper and sharper and sharper,” said Chaiken. “I saw it with ‘Eyes Wide Shut,’ that you could go very hardcore into the 4K, and you could see details in the shadows and things that Kubrick would never have wanted you to see.”

Chaiken and Criterion worked closely with the Warner Archives, Smith, and other collaborators, going back and forth with different passes to figure out how best to find a happy medium, which, with most films, meant sometimes dialing down the HDR and leaning into “more filmic, warmer curve” with the color grade.

The more Chaiken researched, the more he learned just how obsessive Kubrick was about the presentation of his films, and admitted he would get obsessive wondering if they had gotten the colors of a particular transfer right. He sought out advice from Maria Palazzola, long-time restoration supervisor, colorist, and former transfer expert at The Criterion Collection during 1980s and ‘90s, having overseen “director approved” versions of Kubrick’s Criterion laser discs.

“I had assumed that there was an intermediary, or Leon Vitali, Stanley’s longtime assistant, helping Maria,” said Chaiken.”But when I talked to her, she said, ‘No, no, Stanley was calling me directly.’”

Chaiken said he flooded Palazzola with questions trying to find out just how obsessive Kubrick was about his home video transfers and what, in particular, he obsessed about. Chaiken had heard the stories that Kubrick had made Palazzola re-transfer films countless times.

Chaiken explained his assumptions were wrong, “She said that was absolutely not the case. That  [Kubrick] understood the limitations of the technology at that time, and he wanted them to look as good as they could possibly look on home video.”

For example, according Palazzola told Chaiken with “2001: A Space Odyssey,” Kubrick only pressed hard on two key sections.

“He wanted to be sure that the Dawn of Man sequence — that was front projected: The backgrounds were projected when they were filming it — and so he wanted to make sure that you couldn’t see any reflection in the eyes of the apes from that front projection,” said Chaiken. “And she said the one reel that he made her re-transfer a few times was the last reel, in the French boudoir, because [Kubrick] didn’t want it to be too bright.”

Chaiken said the anecdotes of Kubrick’s collaboration with Palazzola changed his perspective on his own work: “Hearing that he was relatively easy to work with was a bit of a relief because he cared about this stuff immensely, but he understood that film is not video. It’s a completely different medium.”

Chaiken gives full credit to visual artist Drusilla Adeline (aka Sister Hyde) for the design of the Kubrick box set, and in this video, you can hear them discuss how the fonts, color, layout, and the box itself were built around the theme of “Kubrick at work,” and how, in going through his archive, you get a sense of him leaving his fingerprints (literally and figuratively) on the making of his films.

One of the things that is striking about the box set, loaded with 16 different films, extras, and supporting materials, is how — compared to most box sets — it is laid out in a way that it is very easy to find what you are looking for, but also clear explanations for each film (each separated by a tab and film poster) of what versions, audio, and extras are available. Chaiken said that in going through Kubrick’s work, it was clear what an organized and clear archivist the filmmaker was himself.

“In my mind, I was thinking about the Library of America —  what would a Library of America compendium of Stanley Kubrick look like? That  was definitely a touchstone,” said Chaiken. “Library of America editions, where they’ll [be] a single compendium of a great American author and you have the major works, but then you also have these interesting tangential pieces, and they’re laid out so beautifully, they’re just so uniform. They have the little tab that marks a page.”

#3537. If You Loved 'Crystal Lake,' There's One Movie You Need to Watch Next

Jeff Somers is a freelancer who has been writing about writing, books, personal finance, and home maintenance since 2012.

Jeff has published nine novels and more than 70 short stories; his story Ringing the Changes was selected for inclusion in The Best American Mystery Stories 2006. In 2018, Jeff published the book Writing Without Rules: How to Write & Sell a Novel Without Guidelines, Experts, or (Occasionally) Pants. He holds a bachelor’s degree in English and previously worked in medical publishing as a production editor.

When not writing, Jeff spends his free time fixing up his old house. He has tackled a wide range of DIY projects, including remodeling a bathroom entirely on his own in two weeks, and building a roof deck that hasn't fallen down yet. You can find him on Bluesky.

This is Streamalikes, where you can find a curated list of recommendations to stream based on what you already like.

Peacock’s Crystal Lake is an unexpected treat in a lot of ways, taking one of horror’s most iconic figures—Jason Voorhees of the Friday the 13th franchise—and digging into the universe’s background by focusing on his mother, Pamela. Famously the actual serial killer in the original film, Pamela’s development into a psychotic killer who inspired her son to become the psychotic killer of all time is the engine that drives Crystal Lake, finding the damaged humanity behind the terror. If you’ve burned through all eight episodes of Crystal Lake’s first season, and you’ve worked through the streamalike series with similar DNA, it’s time to check out some movies—starting with the perfect companion film, 2022’s Pearl.

The second film in Ti West’s X trilogy (starting with X and concluding with 2024’s MaXXXine) is the ideal film to watch after Crystal Lake. Like the series, it explores a female serial killer’s backstory and recontextualizes your understanding of their motives and psychology. It also requires that you be familiar with the original story—while you can certainly watch Crystal Lake or Pearl without having seen the Friday the 13th films or X, you’ll be missing out on a lot if you do.

In X, a group of young people descends on a dilapidated old farm to film an adult movie in Texas in 1979, and by the end of the film most of them are dead, killed by the farm’s elderly couple Howard (Stephen Ure) and Pearl (Mia Goth), with Pearl presented as the most deranged and dangerous of the two. It’s a riveting update to the classic splatter movie template, and Goth nails her dual role as the Final Girl Maxine and the psychotic, murderous Pearl. The prequel, Pearl, jumps back to 1918, when Pearl (Goth again) was a young woman living with her strict mother and paralyzed father. Pearl has big dreams of being an entertainer, but her mother tries to trap her to ensure she’s there to care for her parents and work the farm. Pearl’s lonely unhappiness and frustration (both mental and, er, physical) inspire a slow boil of tension as her grip on sanity frays, and her anger toward her parents curdles into something frightening.

Like Crystal Lake, Pearl takes a killer who seems fairly one-dimensional in their original presentation and gives them a deeper back story and psychological framing. Pamela Voorhees wasn’t just crazy—she was driven to madness by the horrible things that happened to her and her son, and the awful way she’s treated by her fellow humans. Similarly, Pearl is a hopeful and innocent young woman who is slowly molded into a killer by the events of her life. Both the series and the film serve as reminders that monsters are rarely born—they’re made. And it’s usually the casual cruelty of the people around them that does the making. If you loved Crystal Lake’s fresh take on Pamela, Pearl is the perfect choice for a movie night. Stream Pearl on Hulu or rent it on Prime Video.

Need more serial killer movies that hit the Crystal Lake vibe? Never fear—here are some other excellent choices to pair with the series.

If you’ve never actually seen the original Friday the 13th (or if it’s been a while), this is a must-watch for fans of Crystal Lake. Although the series takes some liberties to update the timeline, it’s still intended as a glimpse into the events that shaped both Pamela and Jason Voorhees into inhuman (and somewhat supernatural) monsters. Initially given savagely bad reviews, the film was a surprise blockbuster and is now regarded as a classic of a genre it helped to create in the first place; rewatching it today not only helps contextualize Crystal Lake, it puts the entire slasher genre into perspective. Stream Friday the 13th on Netflix or rent it on Prime Video.

The success of Friday the 13th led to a rush of copycat films, of course. Most of those weren’t particularly good or even interesting, but Sleepaway Camp is an exception (although it was similarly savaged by critics at the time). Now a cult classic, Sleepaway Camp has two things that recommend it to fans of Crystal Lake and Friday the 13th: a weird sensibility that gives it an otherworldly atmosphere that enhances the sense of dread, and what is probably the most unexpected twist ending in the history of slasher films (and it’s probably a Top 10 twist in general). Stream Sleepaway Camp on The Roku Channel, Kanopy, or Tubi, or rent it on Prime Video.

One reason Crystal Lake exists is the enduring power and influence of slasher films in general and Friday the 13th specifically. Few recent films have tapped into that dreamy nightmare feel like Jane Schoenbrun’s Teenage Sex and Death at Camp Miasma. As with most of Schoenbrun’s work, the film delves into themes of identity, subverting queer tropes, and the malleable nature of reality itself. If you’re looking for a slasher story that’s less straightforward than Crystal Lake while dealing with some similar themes of transformation and destiny, this is it. Stream Teenage Sex and Death at Camp Miasma on Mubi.

If you’ve seen all the Friday the 13th movies and want more slasher horror with a bit more edge, check out The Burning. Is it a great film? Not really. Combining the straightforward slasher thrills of Friday with some of the villain motivations of fellow classic franchise A Nightmare on Elm Street, The Burning dials the blood and guts up to 11 (and beyond) and remains notoriously gory even by today’s standards. But if your fave part of Crystal Lake is the frequently over-the-top gore and violence, this is an ideal movie choice. Stream The Burning on The Roku Channel or Kanopy.

Want a slasher film that explores the psyche of a female killer the way Crystal Lake deconstructs Pamela Voorhees? Check out May. A fragile young woman, May struggles to find connection with the people around her, and slowly descends into a fantasy world that inspires her to literally make her own ideal friend. What makes May so interesting is the depth of the exploration of May’s personality that’s similar to how Pamela is handled in Crystal Lake, tracing each step of her stumble into a bloody hell. Stream May on Tubi or rent it on Prime Video.

#3536. 'Jimmy' Gets To the Heart of James Stewart, but Fails To Explore His Depths | Review

In Frank Capra’s classic It’s a Wonderful Life, a defeated George Bailey sits alone at the local Bedford Falls bar and prays for God to show him the way. It’s one of the most heartbreaking scenes in the 1946 classic, made all the more powerful by James Stewart’s trembling voice and anguished expression. But for a scene hailed as one of the best in movie history, what if some of George’s pain actually came from Stewart himself? That’s the heart of Jimmy, director Aaron Burns’ new biographical drama starring KJ Apa as the beloved actor. Following Stewart’s experiences during World War II and his difficult return to acting, Jimmy offers a moving portrait of the man behind the iconic character, even if it doesn’t always dig deep enough into who Stewart really was.

Written by Justin Strawhand, Jimmy explores the period between the height of Stewart’s Hollywood success and his decision to join the military, where he eventually works his way up the ranks to become a decorated combat pilot. While there’s a great deal of sincerity in Apa’s portrayal, particularly through Stewart’s compassion and patriotism, Jimmy rarely explores the experiences that shaped him. The result is an affectionate, occasionally moving biopic that feels more like a polished dramatization of familiar history than an intimate portrait of an extraordinary man.

Fresh off his Oscar win for The Philadelphia Story in 1941, Jimmy finds the 32-year-old Jimmy Stewart (Apa) evolving into one of Hollywood’s most prominent rising stars under the MGM banner. With Louis B. Mayer (Jason Alexander) guiding him through a career so many actors envied, Jimmy shortly after admits he has other plans. With the influence of his father, Alexander (Neal McDonough), and a rich family history of military service behind him, Jimmy wants to enlist despite doubts about whether an actor could handle the realities of war. It’s a compelling starting point for a film about a man willing to leave behind everything he has worked so hard for, even if Jimmy only briefly explores these primary relationships and experiences that shaped his determination.

Under Lieutenant Colonel Terrill (Rob Riggle)’s command, Jimmy eventually earns the responsibility of leading his own squadron, while quickly needing to prove he can bring his men home safely and isn’t just some Hollywood leading man. The film also introduces Lady Julia (Kara Killmer), a British aristocrat who helps him escape from the realities of war. As we see them interact, their growing affection brings out a boyish, vulnerable side of Jimmy as we learn he longs for ordinary conversations and companionship. Yet those moments of joy outside the war become increasingly difficult to keep as the losses mount around him, particularly after he forms meaningful bonds with his men.

Burns, whose prior work has been in faith-based independent films, handles this progression with sensitivity, allowing the consequences of war to build rather than rush from one tragedy to another. Through this, we see Jimmy’s own devastation slowly grow between having to write condolence letters to grieving families and his struggle to reassure others while privately questioning his own confidence. There’s also a sincere appreciation for Stewart’s patriotism and faith that never feels overtly preachy and becomes the emotional foundation of a story about a man whose experiences would eventually reshape who he is and the profession he once loved.

It should be known that an excellent portrayal of a beloved actor doesn’t automatically make it an excellent biopic, but Apa no doubt gives Jimmy its strongest reason to exist. For as long as I can remember, Stewart has been one of Hollywood’s most recognizable, but also frequently imitated actors, often exaggerated to the point of caricature. Somewhere along the way, between Dana Carvey’s impressions on SNL and a massively popular indie podcast from the 2010s lampooning him as a relationship advice guru, those mockeries have almost made it too easy to forget the sincerity that made Stewart so beloved in the first place.

Thankfully, Apa understands that distinction. He nails Stewart’s unmistakable voice, right down to its familiar cadence and hesitant delivery, without ever letting it become a parody. The former Riverdale star also captures the smaller shifts in his expressions, gentle manner, and the quiet vulnerability beneath his Hollywood persona. Sure, there’s an uncanny resemblance from certain angles, but more importantly, Apa makes Stewart feel like a real person again, rather than the impression of one.

That humanity becomes even more effective as the wartime experiences begin to change Jimmy. In one particularly affecting moment, he reassures his squadron about their plans, only for the camera to linger on his face afterward, revealing a quiet anguish beneath his encouraging words. Apa also shares some rather tender moments with Killmer, who brings a gentle counterbalance as Julia, the fictionalized romantic interest whose presence brings out his desires for an ordinary life.

Elsewhere, Max Casella brings warmth to director Frank Capra, who was a longtime friend and collaborator with Stewart, having worked together on 1938’s You Can’t Take It With You, and 1939’s Mr. Smith Goes to Washington before It’s a Wonderful Life. Alexander lends Louis B. Mayer an appropriately imposing presence, while Riggle is convincing as Terrill, but his role is largely functional and doesn’t give us much to go by. But this is unquestionably Apa’s film, as he carries much of the screenplay’s emotional weight even when the writing never quite gets to his level.

For all its sincerity and heart, Jimmy is more interested in what Stewart endured rather than exploring the man he was before these experiences changed him. And that’s a big difference when telling the story of one of America’s greatest actors and war heroes. Burns wisely avoids squeezing an entire lifetime into one film, but the screenplay still overlooks relationships that could have given its central character more depth. For starters, the dynamic between his father and his connection to his Pennsylvania hometown is under-explored — yet, in reality, the love was so mutual that there’s a museum and statue dedicated to him in its historic downtown.

Even Ginger Rogers (Jemma Donovan) is introduced without much development, despite the two having briefly dated. More frustrating is the attention given to Julia, a fictional composite of Stewart’s romantic relationships. While their scenes reveal his vulnerability and bring out another layer of Apa’s performance in the middle of war, she remains thinly written. It’s not that the film needed to include every important person in Stewart’s life, but the relationships it chooses to explore don’t always tell us enough about the man himself.

It’s only when Jimmy turns his attention to Capra’s It’s a Wonderful Life that the biopic finds something genuinely moving. After serving for four-and-a-half years, Jimmy’s wartime trauma gives weight to George Bailey’s despair, particularly while filming the famous bar scene at Martini’s. It’s here that we see Apa beautifully convey the pain of a man struggling to find his way back to himself. The film earns that emotional and heartfelt payoff, even if a vision of Stewart’s fallen comrades beforehand feels unnecessarily heavy-handed. Unfortunately, his introduction to Gloria (Jen Lilley), the woman he eventually falls in love with and marries, arrives almost like a bright resolution, never exploring how he rebuilt his life after the war and PTSD.

The film ends on archival footage of the real Stewart, surrounded by family and reflecting on his extraordinary life in his own words, which is undeniably touching. As a longtime fan, it’s this part that made me sob like a baby. But it also highlights how much of the man remains unexplored. Jimmy understands the compassion and decency that made Stewart so beloved, and its depiction of wartime sacrifice carries genuine emotional weight. But seeing what the war took from him isn’t quite the same as understanding everything that made him who he was. Apa gives us a wonderfully human portrait of an American icon, but the film and its writing stop short of becoming the richer biopic that Stewart deserves.

Jimmy opens nationwide in theaters on November 6.
